messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Theoretic question about HMC
messages.body_plain:
The general state space version of Metropolis-Hastings works
in a similar way.  Basically, you double your target space,
\Omega -> \Omega \times \Omega, and then the
Metropolis-Hastings proposal is just switching the the states
in the two components of the product space (formally, the
acceptance probability is the Radon-Nikodym derivative
of the transition from component one into component two
with respect to the transition from component two into
component one).

Anyways, the point is that detailed balance follows immediately
from the permutation-like construction of the general
Metropolis-Hastings algorithm.  In fact, most Markov transitions
can be framed in this way.

On May 29, 2015, at 10:47 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> You can think of continuous versions of MCMC the same way --- you
> just partition the space into two pieces, A and B, and look at probabilities
> of transitioning between them (or generalize to more states).  It makes
> much more sense (to me at least) than thinking about densities --- for
> instance, it makes the Goodman and Weare ensemble sampler clearer as to
> why it needs to do the Jacobian adjustment it does.
>
> This is going on a slide or two for our upcoming class where I believe
> I'm on the hook to do a day of Bayes and MCMC.

log[p(y|c,d)] = log_sum_exp(a=1,A) [ log(Uniform(a)) + log(sum(b=1,B) [Uniform(b) + log (Poisson(y(t)| a, b, c, d))]]

Best,

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Jolly-Seber model, state-space representation
messages.body_plain:
Bob,

Thanks for the extensive help with this. I really appreciate it.

I've implemented the earlier, less efficient, suggestion. I made the changes you suggested, and I think it works/makes sense now. I'm sticking with the less efficient version for now as I currently understand it better, but I will most likely revisit efficiency later after I've done some more testing etc.

I'm glad the King paper has been useful. Of the paper's I've found on this topic, it was one of the better recent reviews.

Cheers,

Peter

On Friday, May 29, 2015 at 4:31:56 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The answer I gave you before was right, but inefficient.
>
> Reading Ruth King's paper made me think about the whole model
> as an HMM and thus realize that the value chi[t] computed in
> the Stan Manual's CJS model for the probability of being uncaptured (not sighted)
> after time t was just the backward probability from the forward-backward
> algorithm.   By analogy, I'm going to define a forward variable alpha[t]
> that represents the probability of being unsighted up to time t-1 but being
> alive at t.
>
> Then, given first[i] as first sighting of i and last[i] as last sighting
> of i, we can use the forward value up to first[i] and backward value back
> to last[i] and condition everything in the middle knowing that all the x[i,t] = 1
> (the individual can't die and come back to life between first[i] and last[i]).
>
> So I'd probably write this as a likelihood function for y conditioned on
> a whole bunch of things:
>
> real
> log_likelihood(int[] y,       // observations
>                int first,     // first sighting time
>                int last,      // last sighting time
>                vector alpha,  // in study at first sighting
>                vector chi,    // unsighted after last sighting
>                vector phi,    // survive from t to t+1
>                vector p) {    // sighted given alive
>   real ll;
>   ll <- alpha[first] + chi[last];
>   for (t in first:(last-1))
>     ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t]);
>   for (t in first:last)
>     ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(y[t], p[t]);
>   return ll;
> }
>
> The first loop is that it survives from each point to the next
> point between first and last (you don't know if you survive beyond
> last, which is why phi[last] isn't included).  The second loop just
> takes the sighting/capture probabilities for each point.
>
> The first, last, and alpha values all get computed as in the previous model.
> I'd define first and last as transformed data so as not to have to recompute.
>
> Im assuming alpha and chi are defined on the log scale.
>
> You can then define alpha and chi as locals in the model block, where
> b[t] is chance of entering study at time t.
>
>   alpha[1] <- log(b[1]);
>   for (t in 2:T)
>     alpha[t] <- log_sum_exp(alpha[t-1] + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t-1]),
>                             b[t]);
>
> The log_sum_exp is for the mixture of either being in the study at time t-1
> and surviving to time to or entering the study at time t.
>
> Moving on to the abundance study, you'll also have a bunch of individuals
> who were never sighted.  So you have to increment the log density by the
> probability of that, too.  Which is another calculation like the others,
> because they can come into the study or exit the study, but at each point they
> are in the study, they are unobserved.
>
> I think that's it.  Let me know if you have more questions.
>
> This is fun!  Especially when I don't have to debug it all.  You
> really want to check all the boundary conditions in the above to make
> sure they're right.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm using the ode_integrator which work very well. thank you.

just one think, for some of my data, I have several measures at the same time, hence the following error message:

"times is not a valid ordered vector. The element at 2 is 1, but should be greater than the previous element, 1"

I understand this is not possible but how can we deal with such things ?

I thought about 2 things:
1 - I could provide a kind of "mean" using transformed data and then having one for a single time.
2 - I could "trick" the ode_integrator by transforming data at the same time to an ordered sequence: for instance, if I've 3 data at time 1, I can spread them around 1: 0.999, 1.000, 1.001.

What is the best way ?

messages.body_plain:
Just use the given solution multiple times,

y <- integrate_ode(…);
y_hat ~ normal(y, sigma); // vectorized statement for each time point
y_hat_extra_1 ~ normal(y[duplicate_time_1], sigma); // additional data at t = ts[duplicate_time_1]
y_hat_extra_2 ~ normal(y[duplicate_time_2], sigma); // additional data at t = ts[duplicate_time_2]

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Marginalising out two discrete parameters
messages.body_plain:
The simplest thing to do is this:

  matrix[A,B] lp;
  lp <- rep_matrix(0, A, B);
  for (a in 1:A)
    for (b in 1:B)
      for (t in 1:T)
        lp[m,n] <- lp[m,n] + log prob of y(t) given a, b, c, d

  increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(to_vector(lp)));

That is, you need to marginalize both out jointly.  Better to
just do the log_sum_exp once for efficiency, though you can
nest:

  log_sum_exp({a, b, c, d})

  = log_sum_exp(log_sum_exp(a, b), log_sum_exp(c, d));

  = log(exp(a) + exp(b) + ... + exp(d))

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] [Whishlist] Ability to export a quantity computed in the "model" part of a Stan model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] [Whishlist] Ability to export a quantity computed in the "model" part of a Stan model
messages.body_plain:
Other people have asked for this, too.

Basically, the idea is to completely get rid of the transformed
paramters block and instead flag variables declared at the top of
the model block as save or no save.

Right now, the transformed parameters may depend on "uninteresting"
quantities, as in

  transformed parameters {
    real a;
    real b;
    {
       real c;  // uninteresting
       real d;  // uninteresting

       ... define a and b ...
    }
  }

but the uninteresting variables will not be available in the model
block.

The alternative that makes most sense to me would be this:

  model {
    save real a;
    save real b;
    real c;
    real d;
    ....
  }

- Bob

> On May 30, 2015, at 5:01 PM, Emmanuel Charpentier <emanuel.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I'd like to be able to export quantities used in the computation of the log-posterior without having to re-declare and re-compute them in the "generated quantities" part of a Stan model. After attentive perusal of the Stan manual, I saw no way to do this.
>
> Could it be possible to add, for example, a keyword (e. g. "exported") to the declaration of the quantity ?
>
> Nota Bene : I am aware of the possibility of declaring transformed parameters. But the interesting quantities might be function of other "uninteresting" quantities computed earlier in the model part. Including them in a "transformed parameter" part would export also those "uninteresting" quantities.
>
> Possible applications : DIC, WAIC, mixtures of already-fitted models, etc...
>
> What do you think ?
>

> > On Friday, May 29, 2015 at 4:31:56 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > The answer I gave you before was right, but inefficient.
> >
> > Reading Ruth King's paper made me think about the whole model
> > as an HMM and thus realize that the value chi[t] computed in
> > the Stan Manual's CJS model for the probability of being uncaptured (not sighted)
> > after time t was just the backward probability from the forward-backward
> > algorithm.   By analogy, I'm going to define a forward variable alpha[t]
> > that represents the probability of being unsighted up to time t-1 but being
> > alive at t.
> >
> > Then, given first[i] as first sighting of i and last[i] as last sighting
> > of i, we can use the forward value up to first[i] and backward value back
> > to last[i] and condition everything in the middle knowing that all the x[i,t] = 1
> > (the individual can't die and come back to life between first[i] and last[i]).
> >
> > So I'd probably write this as a likelihood function for y conditioned on
> > a whole bunch of things:
> >
> > real
> > log_likelihood(int[] y,       // observations
> >                int first,     // first sighting time
> >                int last,      // last sighting time
> >                vector alpha,  // in study at first sighting
> >                vector chi,    // unsighted after last sighting
> >                vector phi,    // survive from t to t+1
> >                vector p) {    // sighted given alive
> >   real ll;
> >   ll <- alpha[first] + chi[last];
> >   for (t in first:(last-1))
> >     ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t]);
> >   for (t in first:last)
> >     ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(y[t], p[t]);
> >   return ll;
> > }
> >
> > The first loop is that it survives from each point to the next
> > point between first and last (you don't know if you survive beyond
> > last, which is why phi[last] isn't included).  The second loop just
> > takes the sighting/capture probabilities for each point.
> >
> > The first, last, and alpha values all get computed as in the previous model.
> > I'd define first and last as transformed data so as not to have to recompute.
> >
> > Im assuming alpha and chi are defined on the log scale.
> >
> > You can then define alpha and chi as locals in the model block, where
> > b[t] is chance of entering study at time t.
> >
> >   alpha[1] <- log(b[1]);
> >   for (t in 2:T)
> >     alpha[t] <- log_sum_exp(alpha[t-1] + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t-1]),
> >                             b[t]);
> >
> > The log_sum_exp is for the mixture of either being in the study at time t-1
> > and surviving to time to or entering the study at time t.
> >
> > Moving on to the abundance study, you'll also have a bunch of individuals
> > who were never sighted.  So you have to increment the log density by the
> > probability of that, too.  Which is another calculation like the others,
> > because they can come into the study or exit the study, but at each point they
> > are in the study, they are unobserved.
> >
> > I think that's it.  Let me know if you have more questions.
> >
> > This is fun!  Especially when I don't have to debug it all.  You
> > really want to check all the boundary conditions in the above to make
> > sure they're right.
> >
> > - Bob

> > On Friday, May 29, 2015 at 4:31:56 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > The answer I gave you before was right, but inefficient.
> >
> > Reading Ruth King's paper made me think about the whole model
> > as an HMM and thus realize that the value chi[t] computed in
> > the Stan Manual's CJS model for the probability of being uncaptured (not sighted)
> > after time t was just the backward probability from the forward-backward
> > algorithm.   By analogy, I'm going to define a forward variable alpha[t]
> > that represents the probability of being unsighted up to time t-1 but being
> > alive at t.
> >
> > Then, given first[i] as first sighting of i and last[i] as last sighting
> > of i, we can use the forward value up to first[i] and backward value back
> > to last[i] and condition everything in the middle knowing that all the x[i,t] = 1
> > (the individual can't die and come back to life between first[i] and last[i]).
> >
> > So I'd probably write this as a likelihood function for y conditioned on
> > a whole bunch of things:
> >
> > real
> > log_likelihood(int[] y,       // observations
> >                int first,     // first sighting time
> >                int last,      // last sighting time
> >                vector alpha,  // in study at first sighting
> >                vector chi,    // unsighted after last sighting
> >                vector phi,    // survive from t to t+1
> >                vector p) {    // sighted given alive
> >   real ll;
> >   ll <- alpha[first] + chi[last];
> >   for (t in first:(last-1))
> >     ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t]);
> >   for (t in first:last)
> >     ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(y[t], p[t]);
> >   return ll;
> > }
> >
> > The first loop is that it survives from each point to the next
> > point between first and last (you don't know if you survive beyond
> > last, which is why phi[last] isn't included).  The second loop just
> > takes the sighting/capture probabilities for each point.
> >
> > The first, last, and alpha values all get computed as in the previous model.
> > I'd define first and last as transformed data so as not to have to recompute.
> >
> > Im assuming alpha and chi are defined on the log scale.
> >
> > You can then define alpha and chi as locals in the model block, where
> > b[t] is chance of entering study at time t.
> >
> >   alpha[1] <- log(b[1]);
> >   for (t in 2:T)
> >     alpha[t] <- log_sum_exp(alpha[t-1] + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t-1]),
> >                             b[t]);
> >
> > The log_sum_exp is for the mixture of either being in the study at time t-1
> > and surviving to time to or entering the study at time t.
> >
> > Moving on to the abundance study, you'll also have a bunch of individuals
> > who were never sighted.  So you have to increment the log density by the
> > probability of that, too.  Which is another calculation like the others,
> > because they can come into the study or exit the study, but at each point they
> > are in the study, they are unobserved.
> >
> > I think that's it.  Let me know if you have more questions.
> >
> > This is fun!  Especially when I don't have to debug it all.  You
> > really want to check all the boundary conditions in the above to make
> > sure they're right.
> >
> > - Bob

messages.body_plain:
You're right. Looking log_sum_exp(lp) where lp is a vector of log probabilities, it sometimes has a value of -inf.

I think the issue is the definition of lp. it is defined vector[first_capture(y) * (size(y) - last_capture(y))] lp; What happens, is that if last_capture is equal to size(y) the vector has length 0. And that is bad. This causes further problems when trying to loop from (last_capture + 1):size(y).

So, I add 1 to the length of the vector lp, then it is no longer degenerate in the case where last_capture(y) == size(y). I then also changef the t_last_alive loop to last_capture:S. This seems to have fixed it.

The stan file is attached.

Thanks again, Bob. Your help has been really illuminating.

Cheers,

Peter

> > > Reading Ruth King's paper made me think about the whole model
> > > as an HMM and thus realize that the value chi[t] computed in
> > > the Stan Manual's CJS model for the probability of being uncaptured (not sighted)
> > > after time t was just the backward probability from the forward-backward
> > > algorithm.   By analogy, I'm going to define a forward variable alpha[t]
> > > that represents the probability of being unsighted up to time t-1 but being
> > > alive at t.
> > >
> > > Then, given first[i] as first sighting of i and last[i] as last sighting
> > > of i, we can use the forward value up to first[i] and backward value back
> > > to last[i] and condition everything in the middle knowing that all the x[i,t] = 1
> > > (the individual can't die and come back to life between first[i] and last[i]).
> > >
> > > So I'd probably write this as a likelihood function for y conditioned on
> > > a whole bunch of things:

> > > log_likelihood(int[] y,       // observations
> > >                int first,     // first sighting time
> > >                int last,      // last sighting time
> > >                vector alpha,  // in study at first sighting
> > >                vector chi,    // unsighted after last sighting
> > >                vector phi,    // survive from t to t+1
> > >                vector p) {    // sighted given alive
> > >   real ll;
> > >   ll <- alpha[first] + chi[last];
> > >   for (t in first:(last-1))
> > >     ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(1, phi[t]);
> > >   for (t in first:last)
> > >     ll <- ll + bernoulli_log(y[t], p[t]);
> > >   return ll;
> > > }

> > > The first loop is that it survives from each point to the next
> > > point between first and last (you don't know if you survive beyond
> > > last, which is why phi[last] isn't included).  The second loop just
> > > takes the sighting/capture probabilities for each point.
> > >
> > > The first, last, and alpha values all get computed as in the previous model.
> > > I'd define first and last as transformed data so as not to have to recompute.
> > >
> > > Im assuming alpha and chi are defined on the log scale.
> > >

> > > b[t] is chance of entering study at time t.

> > > and surviving to time to or entering the study at time t.

> > > who were never sighted.  So you have to increment the log density by the
> > > probability of that, too.  Which is another calculation like the others,
> > > because they can come into the study or exit the study, but at each point they
> > > are in the study, they are unobserved.
> > >
> > > I think that's it.  Let me know if you have more questions.
> > >
> > > This is fun!  Especially when I don't have to debug it all.  You
> > > really want to check all the boundary conditions in the above to make
> > > sure they're right.

messages.body_plain:
As long as there's no undefined variables floating around.

I'd think what you want to do is this:

vector[first_capture(y) * max(size(y) - last_capture(y), 1)] ...;

BUT, that runs into a bug we have in using max() within bounds
that I'm currently in the process of fixing.  So you'll have to do it like
this:

  vector[foo(first_capture(y), size(y), last_capture(y))] ...;

with

  int foo(int fc, int s, int lc) {
    return fc * max(1, s - lc);
  }

The fix for max in vector declarations probably won't make it into
Stan 2.7.0, which we're trying to rush out the door to deal
with BH (Boost headers) changing versions on us so that nobody can
get RStan to build.

- Bob

My question is in regards to this statement in the Stan manual: "we found that normalizing the data to unit sample mean and variance sped up the fits by an order of magnitude"

Does this apply to normalizing the parameter values too? I have a model where the actual values of different parameters vary over a few orders of magnitude, could this be slowing my model down?

Thanks,
Cameron

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Scaling data and parameters
messages.body_plain:
The parameters are actually what matter.  Stan tries
to fit the scale of each during adaptation (technically by
estimating a diagonal mass matrix used to scale each parameter
during the Hamiltonian updates) but it helps immensely to keep
everything on roughly a unit scale.

I don't know how much this matters for parameters that are
small.  So if you have some regression parameters that due to
pooling are pulled very close to zero.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Scaling data and parameters
messages.body_plain:
To add another data point — scaling helps in both modeling
and computational.  As Andrew notes scaling is essentially
identifying the natural units of the problem which makes it
much easier to define weakly informative priors (a weakly
informative prior essentially identifies the expected order of
magnitude of a parameter — if the parameters are all
scaled appropriately than these are all O(1) ).  Additionally,
when all of the parameters are scaled the posterior becomes
more or less isotropic which makes it makes any computational
algorithm much better conditioned.  For example, in HMC this
means a much more stable and efficient integrator as the cost
of the leapfrog integrator goes as largest_scale / smallest_scale
which is minimized when largest_scale ~ smallest_scale.
Moreover, floating point arithmetic is essentially the most accurate
when the parameters are all O(1), further avoiding computational
problems.

-----------------------------------
> fit <- stan('dir_rand.stan')

TRANSLATING MODEL 'dir_rand' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL 'dir_rand' NOW.

SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'dir_rand' NOW (CHAIN 1).

Iteration:    1 / 2000 [  0%]  (Warmup)Error : Invalid value of beta: modele264fa804e_dir_rand_namespace::write_array(d): beta is not a valid simplex. sum(beta) = nan, but should be 1

error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

-------------------------------

The worst part is that errors in generated quantities just kill the whole
process because there's no recovery possible (it's too late to reject a
sample and we don't want feedback from generated quantities anyway).

The problem is that everything's under or overflowing internally and we're
getting draws like this:

iterations [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5]
      [1,]  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN
      [2,]    0    1    0    0    0
      [3,]  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN
      [4,]  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN
      [5,]  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN
      [6,]  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN
>

So you can't even solve the problem by relaxing the declaration of the simplex.

I'll try to fix it by scaling the RNG draws internally, but it won't land
before the 2.7.0 we're working on getting out the door right this second.

- Bob

P.S.  The Dirichlet (and Beta) is traditionally parameterized
with "prior counts" plus 1 and this is always what's used in Stan.
For example, Dirichlet({1,1,1,1}) is uniform over 4-simplexes and
the mean of Beta(2,3) is 1/3 (The (2,3) parameters corresponding to 1
prior success and 2 prior failures).

Re: [stan-users] Problems with dirichlet_rng
messages.body_plain:
That's how we're currently generating Dirichlet variates.
The problem is that when  alpha = 1e-5, most of the probabilty
mass of gamma(alpha, 1) is for values so small that they underflow
to 0 in practice when using double-precision arithmetic.

So what I'm working on in the way of fix is to use the technique
from this paper:

  G. Marsaglia and W. Tsang. A simple method for generating
  gamma variables. ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software, 26(3):363-372, 2000.

  http://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=358414

as discussed here:

  http://www.hongliangjie.com/2012/12/19/how-to-generate-gamma-random-variables/

That lets me generate a gamma (P)RNG x ~ gamma(alpha, 1) as:

  x_raw[i] = gamma_rng(1 + alpha[i], 1); // now first arg > 0
  u[i] = uniform_rng(0, 1);

  x[i] = x_raw * pow(u[i], 1 / alpha[i]);

Then I just do all the fussy work that might underflow on the log scale,
so that

  log_x[i] = log(x_raw[i]) + log(u[i]) / alpha[i];

Then I generate the denominator

  log_sum_x = log_sum_exp(log_x),

which is numerically stable, then generate

  log_theta[i] = log_x[i] - log_sum_x

and then take

  theta[i] = exp(log_theta[i])

at which point we get mostly underflow to 0 because of the way Dirichlet works,
but that's the best we can do without returning results on the log scale, that is
returning log(theta) where theta ~ dirichleta(alpha).

It's testing now, but it seems to work OK.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Time complexity of HMC algorithm used in stan
messages.body_plain:
Too dependent on the exact geometry of the posterior.

The basic cost per transition is cost(gradient) * N_leapfrog steps,
where cost(gradient) will depend on your exact model — it often
scales linearly with the data, but not always, and the scaling
with respect to parameters depends sensitively on your model.
Then N_leapfrog steps scales as integration_time / step_size,
where integrate_time and step_size depend very sensitivity
on the geometry of the posterior.

Heavy tails?  Integration time goes way up.
Strong constraints from data?  Step size goes way down.
Etc, etc, etc.

Best you can do is try an empirical study, where you vary
the data in your specific model and see you if you can
identify a natural scaling.

Hi Bob,

thanks for your comments and suggestions.

As you must have noticed, we were trying to fit a hierarchical model.

First, taking the learning rate (lr) as an example. lr must be between 0 and 1, that's why we chose a beta distribution. lr_mu is the population mean of all the lr(s), lr_kappa is the concentration of the beta distribution.
Our thought of using something like:

     transformed parameters {
        lr_kappa <- 3.0 / (lr_kappa0 * lr_kappa0) - 1.0;

is to prevent bimodal posterior beta distribution (such as beta(0.5,0.5) ). Or perhaps Stan is clever enough to prevent this case automatically?
Then, lr_mu and lr_kappa were used to derive lr_a and lr_b for the beta distribution at the individual level.

Second, the idea for the temp parameter is basically the same, with temp could be a between 0 and 20. That's why we used the same procedure for temp0 and multiplied with 20 afterwards.
Based on your experience, would you suggest some other distribution for a positive parameter constrained at (0,n], instead of multiplying n with a beta?

Third, I've tried to declare v as a vector to avoid transpose, however there is an indexing error.
Suppose v is now declared as 'vector[2] v[nTrials+1]', how do I put that into the categorical_logit?
I tried both categorical_logit( temp[s] * v[:,t] )
and categorical_logit( temp[s] * v[,t] ), but neither worked.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Time complexity of HMC algorithm used in stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Time complexity of HMC algorithm used in stan
messages.body_plain:
> On Jun 3, 2015, at 5:00 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Too dependent on the exact geometry of the posterior.
>
> The basic cost per transition is cost(gradient) * N_leapfrog steps,
> where cost(gradient) will depend on your exact model — it often
> scales linearly with the data, but not always,

The scaling is with the number of edges in the expression graph
for simple expressions (which is the number of operands used in
functions and operators) --- things like ode solvers can take longer
because they're encapsulating iterative algorithms that depend on
state, much like HMC itself.  Sometimes the number of edges scales
more than linearly in the data, for instance in a GP.

- Bob

> Hi Guido,
>
> thanks for your comments and for sharing your experience. I will contact Steingrove for more details.
>
> > softmax temperature 20
> From a not-so-optimal estimate, I do see this parameter doesn't extend that wide on the parameter space. I'll consider to compress it, and this may save some memory.
>
> > bimodal beta
> I agree with what you mentioned. Later, we would plan to employ a transdimensional modeling method to let the model categorize which sub-group a person may belong to.
>
> Cheers,
> Lei
>
>
> On Thu, Jun 4, 2015 at 9:59 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Steingrove, Wetzels & Wagenmakers (2013) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3847555/] used stan to fit a similar model, the PVL model which is kind of an extended RL model.
> > If I remember correctly, they did not use the beta distribution for the learning rate because they had convergence problems
> > (Though this was likely been with an earlier version of stan. I a writing this from memory, for details it would be best to contact the Helen Steingrove).
> >
> > From my experience with fitting RL models a range of 20 for the temperature of the Luce/soft-max choice rule seems large.
> >
> > An aside about avoiding bimodal learning rate distributions (on the group level): It is not unreasonable to assume a bimodal distribution, because if people learn by slowly accumulating payoff information, you get small learning rates (lets say < .2), but when people simply do win-stay lose-switch this behavior is best captured by high learning rates (close to 1). I have seen data where different participants used both these "strategies".
> >
> > Guido
> >
> > On Thursday, June 4, 2015 at 6:03:45 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > >
> > > > On Jun 3, 2015, at 9:49 AM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hi Bob,
> > > >
> > > > thanks for your comments and suggestions.
> > > >
> > > > As you must have noticed, we were trying to fit a hierarchical model.
> > > >
> > > > First, taking the learning rate (lr) as an example. lr must be between 0 and 1, that's why we chose a beta distribution. lr_mu is the population mean of all the lr(s), lr_kappa is the concentration of the beta distribution.
> > > > Our thought of using something like:
> > > >      transformed parameters {
> > > >         lr_kappa <- 3.0 / (lr_kappa0 * lr_kappa0) - 1.0;
> > > > is to prevent bimodal posterior beta distribution (such as beta(0.5,0.5) ). Or perhaps Stan is clever enough to prevent this case automatically?
> > > > Then, lr_mu and lr_kappa were used to derive lr_a and lr_b for the beta distribution at the individual level.
> > >
> > > You can just declare:
> > >
> > >   parameters {
> > >     real<lower=1> alpha;
> > >     real<lower=1> beta;
> > >
> > > and then if you have
> > >
> > >   y ~ beta(alpha, beta);
> > >
> > > the alpha and beta will be bounded > 1.  The data should pull them
> > > that way anyway if values above 1 make sense.
> > >
> > > You used one that looks like this:
> > >
> > >   real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
> > >   real<lower=0> kappa;
> > >
> > >   y ~ beta(theta * kappa, (1 - theta) * kappa);
> > >
> > > where it's easy to think about theta and kappa, but it's hard to
> > > constrain kappa so that theta * kappa > 1 and (1 - theta) * kappa > 1.
> > > You'd have to do something awkward (from both a readability and
> > > prior specification perspective) like this:
> > >
> > >   real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
> > >   real<lower=(1 / fmin(theta, 1 - theta))> kappa;
> > >
> > > > Second, the idea for the temp parameter is basically the same, with temp could be a between 0 and 20. That's why we used the same procedure for temp0 and multiplied with 20 afterwards.
> > >
> > > You could also just constrain temp0 to be between 0 and 20 and then
> > > give it a truncated prior from another family, but beta's good at
> > > bounding it away from the edges (0 and 20).  I'm curious what Andrew
> > > thinks about this.
> > >
> > > > Based on your experience, would you suggest some other distribution for a positive parameter constrained at (0,n], instead of multiplying n with a beta?
> > >
> > > If you just want something vague or weakly informative, it
> > > probably won't matter much.  If you have real prior knowledge
> > > about what to expect, then you can use that.
> > >
> > > > Third, I've tried to declare v as a vector to avoid transpose, however there is an indexing error.
> > > > Suppose v is now declared as 'vector[2] v[nTrials+1]', how do I put that into the categorical_logit?
> > > > I tried both categorical_logit( temp[s] * v[:,t] )
> > > > and categorical_logit( temp[s] * v[,t] ), but neither worked.
> > > > Perhaps in more general, how could I extract a particular column?
> > >
> > > When you declare
> > >
> > >   vector[2] v[nTrials + 1];
> > >
> > > you have an array of 2-vectors.  So v[n] is a column vector
> > > already.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > P.S.  Here's the original program for reference:
> > >
> > > > > data {
> > > > >   int<lower=1> nSubjects;                            // number of subjects
> > > > >   int<lower=1> nTrials;                              // number of trials
> > > > >   int<lower=1,upper=2> choice[nSubjects,nTrials];    // 2nd choices, 1 or 2
> > > > >   real<lower=-1,upper=1> reward[nSubjects,nTrials];  // outcome, 1 or -1
> > > > > }
> > > > >
> > > > > parameters {
> > > > >   // group-level parameters
> > > > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> lr_mu;
> > > > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> lr_kappa0;
> > > > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> temp0_mu;
> > > > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> temp0_kappa0;
> > > > >
> > > > >   // subject-level parameters
> > > > >   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[nSubjects] lr;
> > > > >   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[nSubjects] temp0;
> > > > > }
> > > > >
> > > > > transformed parameters {
> > > > >   real<lower=0> lr_kappa;
> > > > >   real<lower=0> lr_a;
> > > > >   real<lower=0> lr_b;
> > > > >   real<lower=0> temp0_kappa;
> > > > >   real<lower=0> temp0_a;
> > > > >   real<lower=0> temp0_b;
> > > > >   vector<lower=0,upper=20>[nSubjects] temp;
> > > > >
> > > > >   lr_kappa <- 3.0 / (lr_kappa0 * lr_kappa0) - 1.0;
> > > > >   lr_a <- lr_mu * lr_kappa;
> > > > >   lr_b <- (1-lr_mu) * lr_kappa;
> > > > >
> > > > >   temp0_kappa <- 3.0 / (temp0_kappa0 * temp0_kappa0) - 1.0;
> > > > >   temp0_a <- temp0_mu * temp0_kappa;
> > > > >   temp0_b <- (1-temp0_mu) * temp0_kappa;
> > > > >
> > > > >   temp <- 20.0 * temp0;
> > > > > }
> > > > >
> > > > > model {
> > > > >
> > > > >   row_vector[2] v[nTrials+1]; // values
> > > > >   vector[nTrials] pe;         // prediction errors
> > > > >
> > > > >   // hyperparameters, priors
> > > > >   lr_mu ~ beta(1,1);

messages.body_plain:
Hi All

I've just come across the following and was wondering if its a bug. I'm
using a fairly recent development version of RStan from git and do not
know if the behaviour is the same in the latest official release.

Suppose the data block contains
int n;
int x[n];

one can then sample from R using, for example,
data=list(n=3,x=c(1,2,3))
however one cannot do
data=list(n=1,x=2)
as this gives an error "mismatch in number dimensions declared and
found...".
Instead it is necessary to have
data=list(n=1,x=array(2))

In other words R vectors of length >1 are automatically coerced into
suitable Stan arrays but vectors of length 1 are not coerced. This is
rather inconvenient as its forced me to call the R array function on a
number of vectors in my data just to handle the case that they have
length 1.

Alastair Irving

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] how could I possibly speedup my sampling with a simple reinforcement learning model?
messages.body_plain:
> On Jun 4, 2015, at 12:50 PM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>

> thanks again for your comments and suggestions. They are really helpful.
>
> I just have one more concern at this moment. For the beta(a,b) distribution, though a>1, b>1 does a good constrain to avoid bimodal shape, however is it too rigid? For instance beta(2.5, 0.7) could also yield a good estimate in some cases (and this indeed happens for my current dataset).

> That said, either a or b ought be larger than 1, but not both of them. How could I possibly constrain that? Or does it make much sense to you?

You can just replace the fmin with an fmax, then you're
guaranteed at least one is > 1.  But...

Have you just tried constraining a > 0 and b > 0 and see
what the fit is?  The problem is that constraints can often
lead to boundary behavior;  if the fit with only the natural
constraints of a > 0 and b > 0 lead to a = 1/2 and b = 1/2, then
you may just find yourself estimating on the boundary with a constraint
of min(a,b) > 1.

But if you do what Andrew suggests and inverse-logit transform
an unconstrained parameter (essentially an intercept only logistic
regression), then you won't get bimodal behavior.

But if the modes are interesting rather than right at the boundary
of 0 and 1, then you probably want to fit something like a mixture
model.

- Bob

> btw, an update for other users (if of interest):
> I made two changes that really speed up my sampling speed.
> 1. in the data section, the 'reward' variable was changed as real rather than a two-dimensional vector. Say
>            real reward[s,t];
> rather than
>            row_vector[t] reward[s];
> 2. vectorizing helps a lot. Say
>            lr ~ beta(lr_a, lr_b);
> rather than
>            for (s in 1:S)
>                 lr[s] ~ beta(lr_a, lr_b);
>
> Thanks again.
> Lei
>
>
> On Thu, Jun 4, 2015 at 6:02 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > On Jun 3, 2015, at 9:49 AM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Bob,
> >
> > thanks for your comments and suggestions.
> >
> > As you must have noticed, we were trying to fit a hierarchical model.
> >
> > First, taking the learning rate (lr) as an example. lr must be between 0 and 1, that's why we chose a beta distribution. lr_mu is the population mean of all the lr(s), lr_kappa is the concentration of the beta distribution.
> > Our thought of using something like:
> >      transformed parameters {
> >         lr_kappa <- 3.0 / (lr_kappa0 * lr_kappa0) - 1.0;
> > is to prevent bimodal posterior beta distribution (such as beta(0.5,0.5) ). Or perhaps Stan is clever enough to prevent this case automatically?
> > Then, lr_mu and lr_kappa were used to derive lr_a and lr_b for the beta distribution at the individual level.
>
> You can just declare:
>
>   parameters {
>     real<lower=1> alpha;
>     real<lower=1> beta;
>
> and then if you have
>
>   y ~ beta(alpha, beta);
>
> the alpha and beta will be bounded > 1.  The data should pull them
> that way anyway if values above 1 make sense.
>
> You used one that looks like this:
>
>   real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
>   real<lower=0> kappa;
>
>   y ~ beta(theta * kappa, (1 - theta) * kappa);
>
> where it's easy to think about theta and kappa, but it's hard to
> constrain kappa so that theta * kappa > 1 and (1 - theta) * kappa > 1.
> You'd have to do something awkward (from both a readability and
> prior specification perspective) like this:
>
>   real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
>   real<lower=(1 / fmin(theta, 1 - theta))> kappa;
>
> > Second, the idea for the temp parameter is basically the same, with temp could be a between 0 and 20. That's why we used the same procedure for temp0 and multiplied with 20 afterwards.
>
> You could also just constrain temp0 to be between 0 and 20 and then
> give it a truncated prior from another family, but beta's good at
> bounding it away from the edges (0 and 20).  I'm curious what Andrew
> thinks about this.
>
> > Based on your experience, would you suggest some other distribution for a positive parameter constrained at (0,n], instead of multiplying n with a beta?
>
> If you just want something vague or weakly informative, it
> probably won't matter much.  If you have real prior knowledge
> about what to expect, then you can use that.
>
> > Third, I've tried to declare v as a vector to avoid transpose, however there is an indexing error.
> > Suppose v is now declared as 'vector[2] v[nTrials+1]', how do I put that into the categorical_logit?
> > I tried both categorical_logit( temp[s] * v[:,t] )
> > and categorical_logit( temp[s] * v[,t] ), but neither worked.
> > Perhaps in more general, how could I extract a particular column?
>
> When you declare
>
>   vector[2] v[nTrials + 1];
>
> you have an array of 2-vectors.  So v[n] is a column vector
> already.
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  Here's the original program for reference:
>
> > > data {
> > >   int<lower=1> nSubjects;                            // number of subjects
> > >   int<lower=1> nTrials;                              // number of trials
> > >   int<lower=1,upper=2> choice[nSubjects,nTrials];    // 2nd choices, 1 or 2
> > >   real<lower=-1,upper=1> reward[nSubjects,nTrials];  // outcome, 1 or -1
> > > }
> > >
> > > parameters {
> > >   // group-level parameters
> > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> lr_mu;
> > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> lr_kappa0;
> > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> temp0_mu;
> > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> temp0_kappa0;
> > >
> > >   // subject-level parameters
> > >   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[nSubjects] lr;
> > >   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[nSubjects] temp0;
> > > }
> > >
> > > transformed parameters {
> > >   real<lower=0> lr_kappa;
> > >   real<lower=0> lr_a;
> > >   real<lower=0> lr_b;
> > >   real<lower=0> temp0_kappa;
> > >   real<lower=0> temp0_a;
> > >   real<lower=0> temp0_b;
> > >   vector<lower=0,upper=20>[nSubjects] temp;
> > >
> > >   lr_kappa <- 3.0 / (lr_kappa0 * lr_kappa0) - 1.0;
> > >   lr_a <- lr_mu * lr_kappa;
> > >   lr_b <- (1-lr_mu) * lr_kappa;
> > >
> > >   temp0_kappa <- 3.0 / (temp0_kappa0 * temp0_kappa0) - 1.0;
> > >   temp0_a <- temp0_mu * temp0_kappa;
> > >   temp0_b <- (1-temp0_mu) * temp0_kappa;
> > >
> > >   temp <- 20.0 * temp0;
> > > }
> > >
> > > model {
> > >
> > >   row_vector[2] v[nTrials+1]; // values
> > >   vector[nTrials] pe;         // prediction errors
> > >
> > >   // hyperparameters, priors
> > >   lr_mu ~ beta(1,1);
> > >   lr_kappa0 ~ beta(1,1);
> > >   temp0_mu ~ beta(1,1);
> > >   temp0_kappa0 ~ beta(1,1);
> > >
> > >   // subject loop and trial loop
> > >   for (s in 1:nSubjects) {
> > >     lr[s] ~ beta(lr_a,lr_b);
> > >     temp0[s] ~ beta(temp0_a,temp0_b);
> > >

On Thursday, June 4, 2015 at 10:43:55 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
> Given that I want to place constraints on the matrix such as positive semidefiniteness, is that still possible?

If you were interested in the complex matrix A where

A = B + i * C

and both B and C are real, symmetric, and positive semi-definite, then maybe something could be done with Stan but you would have to deal with the real and imaginary parts separately. See, e.g.,

http://www.maths.manchester.ac.uk/~higham/narep/narep298.pdf

More generally, for any sort of a constrained multivariate unknown, Stan needs a mapping between that space and the real numbers. And Stan doesn't have any such mappings built in for complex variables.

Ben

messages.subject: modeling A -> B -> C & A -> C relationships in a binomial model using Stan
messages.subject_clean: modeling A -> B -> C & A -> C relationships in a binomial model using Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks -

Another modeling question for the list.

I'm working on a model with a single binary exposure (A) a binary diagnostic measure (B) and a binary disease outcome (C). I want to know how much of the effect of A  on C, i.e. the exposure on the development of disease, is detected by the diagnostic test, and how much goes under the radar, i.e. isn't picked up by the diagnostic test, so essentially just the A -> C relationship.

I know a priori that the A -> C relationship is weaker than the  A -> B -> C relationship, i.e. the diagnostic test is a pretty good predictor of disease. Individuals may also have a positive B in the absence of A (i.e they were infected before exposure to B), but those with B not caused by A should be much less likely to develop disease. But this means that A could cause C conceivably without causing B.

I have two ideas about how to model this relationship, one of which I've tried, the other I'm considering:

1) Model the impact of A -> C via B by treating positive results for B among those exposed to A as a mixture of A and non-A causes. So Pr(C | A = 1, B = 1) = rho*Pr(C |A -> B ) + (1-rho)*Pr(C | all other B), where rho is the proportion of B attributable to A when A = 1, where the coefficient for positive values of B resulting from A is represented by A -> B, and the effect of positive B not caused by A is represented by 'all other B'.

The problem with this approach is that it has a lot of moving parts and involves a not terribly well-identified latent variable for A -> B. As a result, when I adjust for the A -> C relationship, the coefficient for C | A -> B blows up and the A -> C shrinks towards zero or becomes negative, even though the C | A -> B relationship is pretty stable in the absence of a covariate for A->C. But this isn't particularly satisfying since it doesn't allow us to explicitly model the A -> C relationship and necessarily tilts the model in the direction of a stronger A -> B -> C relationship.

2) My alternate idea is to take more of a post-stratification approach, in which I model both levels separately, i.e. include  the A -> C and B -> C relationships in a model for C and then estimate the effect of A -> B in its own model, and then predict the proportion of C due to the effect of A via B (i.e. A->B) using an MRP-like approach.

I also know that from a predictive perspective, this model should do a better job of replicating the C data than the A -> B -> C model. My only qualms about this approach relate to being unsure of the best way to induce a correlation between the two levels of the model. In the pre-Stan era, I would have approached this using a parametric or nonparametric bootstrap. My gut instinct using Stan is to just to model the fixed effects for the B & C levels using a single multivariate normal, and to allow any random effects for both levels (in this case just intercepts) to also be correlated. This way, if the A -> B and A -> C effects are strongly correlated, this should be reflected in the MRP results. But before going in this direction I wanted to check to see that this actually made sense.

Apologies if any of the above isn't clear enough; please let me know.

Any ideas/suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

thanks,
Jon

Let me preface this with "I am not an epidemiologist" :-)
And I didn't understand exactly which pieces of data were
observed and what the population was.

Why not just try to set up the joint model

  p(A, B, C) = p(A) * p(C | A) * p(B | C)

so that p(B | C) is the usual diagnostic accuracy model of
sensitivity and specificity?  Then you can do any of the
conditional inferences you want.

I wasn't exactly sure what you wanted to compare, but it
felt like

  P(C | A, B)  vs.  P(C | A)

I'd be inclined to measure this kind of thing via mutual information --- that
is, how much B (diagnostic test) measurement be expected to reduce the uncertainty
about C (disease status), conditioned on exposure (and/or non-exposure
if you have non-exposure data).

- Bob

> > Hi Guido,
> >
> > thanks for your comments and for sharing your experience. I will contact Steingrove for more details.
> >
> > > softmax temperature 20
> > From a not-so-optimal estimate, I do see this parameter doesn't extend that wide on the parameter space. I'll consider to compress it, and this may save some memory.
> >
> > > bimodal beta

> > Cheers,
> > Lei
> >
> >

> > > (Though this was likely been with an earlier version of stan. I a writing this from memory, for details it would be best to contact the Helen Steingrove).

> > >
> > > An aside about avoiding bimodal learning rate distributions (on the group level): It is not unreasonable to assume a bimodal distribution, because if people learn by slowly accumulating payoff information, you get small learning rates (lets say < .2), but when people simply do win-stay lose-switch this behavior is best captured by high learning rates (close to 1). > > >
> > > Guido
> > >
> > > On Thursday, June 4, 2015 at 6:03:45 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > >
> > > > > On Jun 3, 2015, at 9:49 AM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > Hi Bob,
> > > > >
> > > > > thanks for your comments and suggestions.
> > > > >
> > > > > As you must have noticed, we were trying to fit a hierarchical model.
> > > > >
> > > > > First, taking the learning rate (lr) as an example. lr must be between 0 and 1, that's why we chose a beta distribution. lr_mu is the population mean of all the lr(s), lr_kappa is the concentration of the beta distribution.
> > > > > Our thought of using something like:
> > > > >      transformed parameters {
> > > > >         lr_kappa <- 3.0 / (lr_kappa0 * lr_kappa0) - 1.0;
> > > > > is to prevent bimodal posterior beta distribution (such as beta(0.5,0.5) ). Or perhaps Stan is clever enough to prevent this case automatically?
> > > > > Then, lr_mu and lr_kappa were used to derive lr_a and lr_b for the beta distribution at the individual level.
> > > >
> > > > You can just declare:
> > > >
> > > >   parameters {
> > > >     real<lower=1> alpha;
> > > >     real<lower=1> beta;
> > > >
> > > > and then if you have

> > > > You used one that looks like this:
> > > >
> > > >   real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
> > > >   real<lower=0> kappa;
> > > >
> > > >   y ~ beta(theta * kappa, (1 - theta) * kappa);

> > > > where it's easy to think about theta and kappa, but it's hard to

> > > > prior specification perspective) like this:
> > > >
> > > >   real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
> > > >   real<lower=(1 / fmin(theta, 1 - theta))> kappa;
> > > >
> > > > > Second, the idea for the temp parameter is basically the same, with temp could be a between 0 and 20. That's why we used the same procedure for temp0 and multiplied with 20 afterwards.
> > > >
> > > > You could also just constrain temp0 to be between 0 and 20 and then
> > > > give it a truncated prior from another family, but beta's good at
> > > > bounding it away from the edges (0 and 20).  I'm curious what Andrew
> > > > thinks about this.
> > > >
> > > > > Based on your experience, would you suggest some other distribution for a positive parameter constrained at (0,n], instead of multiplying n with a beta?
> > > >
> > > > If you just want something vague or weakly informative, it
> > > > probably won't matter much.  If you have real prior knowledge
> > > > about what to expect, then you can use that.
> > > >
> > > > > Third, I've tried to declare v as a vector to avoid transpose, however there is an indexing error.
> > > > > Suppose v is now declared as 'vector[2] v[nTrials+1]', how do I put that into the categorical_logit?
> > > > > I tried both categorical_logit( temp[s] * v[:,t] )
> > > > > and categorical_logit( temp[s] * v[,t] ), but neither worked.
> > > > > Perhaps in more general, how could I extract a particular column?
> > > >
> > > > When you declare
> > > >
> > > >   vector[2] v[nTrials + 1];
> > > >
> > > > you have an array of 2-vectors.  So v[n] is a column vector
> > > > already.
> > > >
> > > > - Bob
> > > >
> > > > P.S.  Here's the original program for reference:
> > > >
> > > > > > data {
> > > > > >   int<lower=1> nSubjects;                            // number of subjects
> > > > > >   int<lower=1> nTrials;                              // number of trials
> > > > > >   int<lower=1,upper=2> choice[nSubjects,nTrials];    // 2nd choices, 1 or 2
> > > > > >   real<lower=-1,upper=1> reward[nSubjects,nTrials];  // outcome, 1 or -1
> > > > > > }
> > > > > >
> > > > > > parameters {
> > > > > >   // group-level parameters
> > > > > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> lr_mu;
> > > > > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> lr_kappa0;
> > > > > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> temp0_mu;
> > > > > >   real<lower=0,upper=1> temp0_kappa0;
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   // subject-level parameters
> > > > > >   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[nSubjects] lr;
> > > > > >   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[nSubjects] temp0;
> > > > > > }
> > > > > >
> > > > > > transformed parameters {
> > > > > >   real<lower=0> lr_kappa;
> > > > > >   real<lower=0> lr_a;
> > > > > >   real<lower=0> lr_b;
> > > > > >   real<lower=0> temp0_kappa;
> > > > > >   real<lower=0> temp0_a;
> > > > > >   real<lower=0> temp0_b;
> > > > > >   vector<lower=0,upper=20>[nSubjects] temp;
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   lr_kappa <- 3.0 / (lr_kappa0 * lr_kappa0) - 1.0;
> > > > > >   lr_a <- lr_mu * lr_kappa;
> > > > > >   lr_b <- (1-lr_mu) * lr_kappa;
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   temp0_kappa <- 3.0 / (temp0_kappa0 * temp0_kappa0) - 1.0;
> > > > > >   temp0_a <- temp0_mu * temp0_kappa;
> > > > > >   temp0_b <- (1-temp0_mu) * temp0_kappa;
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   temp <- 20.0 * temp0;
> > > > > > }
> > > > > >
> > > > > > model {
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   row_vector[2] v[nTrials+1]; // values
> > > > > >   vector[nTrials] pe;         // prediction errors
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   // hyperparameters, priors
> > > > > >   lr_mu ~ beta(1,1);
> > > > > >   lr_kappa0 ~ beta(1,1);
> > > > > >   temp0_mu ~ beta(1,1);
> > > > > >   temp0_kappa0 ~ beta(1,1);
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   // subject loop and trial loop
> > > > > >   for (s in 1:nSubjects) {
> > > > > >     lr[s] ~ beta(lr_a,lr_b);
> > > > > >     temp0[s] ~ beta(temp0_a,temp0_b);
> > > > > >
> > > > > >     v[1] <- rep_row_vector(0.0,2);
> > > > > >
> > > > > >     for (t in 1:nTrials) {
> > > > > >       //* compute action probs using built-in softmax function and related to choice data */
> > > > > >       choice[s,t] ~ categorical_logit( temp[s] * v[t]' );
> > > > > >
> > > > > >       //* prediction error */
> > > > > >       pe[t] <- reward[s,t] - v[t,choice[s,t]];
> > > > > >
> > > > > >       //* value updating (learning) */
> > > > > >       v[t+1] <- v[t]; // make a copy of current value into t+1
> > > > > >       v[t,choice[s,t]] <- v[t,choice[s,t]] + lr[s] * pe[t]; // overwrite chosen value with pe update
> > > > > >     }
> > > > > >   }
> > > > > > }

messages.subject: Re: modeling A -> B -> C & A -> C relationships in a binomial model using Stan
messages.subject_clean: modeling A -> B -> C & A -> C relationships in a binomial model using Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jon,

It sounds like you're interested in the sensitivity and specificity of test B to pick up a causal link between A and C. However, you also write "the A -> B -> C relationship", suggesting that B is part of the causal chain. Can you clarify please, or describe the context in more detail? As an infectious disease epidemiologist myself, I'm having a hard time grasping what you want to do. I will try to rephrase the problem.

So it's two parameters you are interested in: sensitivity and specificity. From your message, I gather you assume that
sensitivity is <100% as "A could cause C conceivably without causing B", and
specificity is <100% as "individuals may also have a positive B in the absence of A".

Assuming that you observed A and C without measurement error, there are four "outcomes" in the data:

A   C
0   0
0   1
1   0
1   1

And you want to know how well B=1 detects (A=1, C=1):

A   C   B
0   0   0   true negative
0   1   0   true negative
1   0   0   true negative
1   1   0   false negative
0   0   1   false positive
0   1   1   false positive
1   0   1   false positive
1   1   1   true positive

So this is very straightforward, still assuming that you observed A and C without measurement error:

sensitivity = sum(true.positive) / sum(A=1, C=1)
specificity = sum(true.negative) / (N - (sum(A=1, C=1))

Assuming beta-priors for sensitivity and specificity, you can formulate analytical solutions for their marginal posteriors.

When you want to account for measurement error in A and C, you will need to model their joint distribution P(A,C), possibly via some mechanical model, and then again calculate the sensitivity and specificity of B for detecting "true" (A*=1, C*=1), marginalized over the measurement error.

This is something you could do in the generated quantities block. At each iteration, take the model-predicted latent "true" outcomes A* and C* to be data, and produce a draw from the conditional posteriors for sensitivity P(sens | A*, B, C*) and specificity P(spec | A*, B, C*), which you can define analytically if you assume a beta prior for each. Note that these draws for sensitivity and specificity will not be draws from the joint distribution P(sens, spec | A*, B, C*).

To sample from the joint distribution P(sens, spec | A*, B, C*), you would have to do some mixture magic in the model block, allowing for all potential discrete states of A* and C*.

Hope this helps. I may have misunderstood what you want to do. If so, please provide more detail on the context.

Luc

Thanks for the note.  I added a feature request to our issue tracker:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1485

We're working on a lot of core components now and won't have
time to get to this any time soon.  Having said that, it shouldn't
be hard to write given that we already have both student-t and skew
normal --- the one hitch may be that skew student-t would be more
parameters than any of our other distros and the testing framework
may not generalize.

As you found, the best bet is to write a function and use that:

functions {

  real skew_student_t_log(real y, ...) {
    real lp;
    lp <- 0;
    ... increment lp ...
    return lp;
  }
}

Then you'll be able to use it in the language as

  y ~ skew_student_t(...);

- Bob

Thanks a lot for this Bob. Greatly appreciated!

The "+ 0" is just a placeholder because this is the most basic model specification. I've written this for bookkeeping purposes. The full model includes many covariates in each regression and the finite mixture is of beta-binoimal regressions.  This is also the reason for my multiplying some of the parameters by 0 and 1 in the likelihood. Once I have it all specified correctly, I'll cut those out as you've suggested.

The model does indeed get stuck. Traceplots for the model/simulation data that I posted show that they do get stuck unfortunately. There appear also to be a number of sticking points (~6), so I end up with very few chains that show any mixing with others. The chain with the highest lp__ does seem to get the ground truth however. If there's anything on the sampling side that could be done, that would be lovely, but I can try to put more informative priors if that's the only way around this at the moment.

Thanks again,
Greg

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] define a constant probability
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure why you want to do that, but I think I understand
what you want.  You want to use increment_log_prob().  Stan works
on the log scale, so if your likelihood is p1 * p2, your log
likelihood is log p1 + log p2.

So you just want:

  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);

Note that the y on the left of the twiddle is the outcome, not the
log probability --- that gets added implicitly.  Or you can write this
to make it clearer:

  increment_log_prob(normal_log(y, mu, sigma));

which has the same effect.

Then for the conditional, you have:

  if (t == 0)
    increment_log_prob(log(0.823));

You don't need to add log(1), as it's zero.

But either way, it won't do anything to the posterior as
it's just a bunch of constants not involving parameters.

- Bob

constant, it doesn't affect the posterior, so it'll have
no effect.  That's the right thing for Stan to do here --- follow
the math of the posterior.

messages.subject: Define a distribution in PySTAN
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I would like to know if it is possible to define my own distribution using PySTAN. I searched a lot on google but did not get meaningful results. Here's an example:

Consider that my likelihood = p1 * p2

where p1 = 0                                                   if x < 5
                = ( log(x) - log5 ) / (log19 - log5)     if 5 < x < 19
                = 1                                                   if x > 19

and knowing that x = m^2 * n^(-1/3) * o^(-3/2) * p^(-1/6)

and p2 = 0.32 * n^(-2/3) * o * p^(-1/3).

I want to marginalize over m, n, o, and p. Is it possible to implement this in PySTAN?

Thanks !

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Latent variable model/FMM efficiency
messages.body_plain:
Each of the chains gets stuck sampling around a different mode, in a way similar to how in stochastic-EM each run might get stuck jumping around a local maximum and not be able to break out. So not label switching: the model I have has 2 mixtures, each with different predictors, so it's not just a problem of flipping labels, it's about it being difficult to sample from the areas in the posterior with the most mass very quickly (as I understand it).

On Monday, June 8, 2015 at 6:57:25 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Does it get stuck in that it doesn't move or just that each
> chain gets stuck sampling around a different mode?  For
> combinatorially difficult multimodality (as in K-means, latent HMMs,
> or LDA), there's just no hope of doing full Bayes.
>
> If it's just label switching, then you might be OK.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Jun 8, 2015, at 4:47 PM, Gregory <gregor...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Thanks a lot for this Bob. Greatly appreciated!
> >
> > The "+ 0" is just a placeholder because this is the most basic model specification. I've written this for bookkeeping purposes. The full model includes many covariates in each regression and the finite mixture is of beta-binoimal regressions.  This is also the reason for my multiplying some of the parameters by 0 and 1 in the likelihood. Once I have it all specified correctly, I'll cut those out as you've suggested.
> >
> > The model does indeed get stuck. Traceplots for the model/simulation data that I posted show that they do get stuck unfortunately. There appear also to be a number of sticking points (~6), so I end up with very few chains that show any mixing with others. The chain with the highest lp__ does seem to get the ground truth however. If there's anything on the sampling side that could be done, that would be lovely, but I can try to put more informative priors if that's the only way around this at the moment.
> >
> > Thanks again,
> > Greg
> >
> > On Monday, June 8, 2015 at 3:49:32 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> > > On Jun 7, 2015, at 3:39 PM, Gregory <gregor...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hello everyone,
> > >
> > > I've constructed a (partially) latent variable model where the latent variable (Z in {0, 1}) is then used a predictor within a finite mixture of regressions. Mixture membership is naturally also a latent variable.
> >
> > This is likely going to be slow.  You'll need to marginalize
> > out both those variables.
> >
> > > The likelihood is given by p(Z|X) {p(M|X, Z)P(V|X, Z, M)} P(Y|X, Z, M, V), where the mixture of regressions is in braces, Z is the binary latent variable, M is component membership (M in {0, 1}), V is the outcome variable for the mixture of regressions, Y is a response to a survey question used to identify Z, and X are covariates.
> >
> > This is likely going to be slow no matter what you do if you have
> > to marginalize out both Z and M.  Does the Z vary by item?
> >
> >
> > > In any case, I have a model that appears to work with simulated data. The model is slow on its own, but with the actual data (~12,000 observations), the model is extremely slow, which I'm okay with if it's working. But I wonder if there's a way to vectorize it or optimize it otherwise. I can't see to find any example in the mailing list where optimizations are done for a finite mixture model.
> > >
> > > Lastly, because finite mixture models seem to get stuck in lower probability modes of the posterior analogous to getting stuck in local maxima when using EM, I wonder if there's any way to deal with this in a systematic way.
> >
> > Not in what we have now.
> >
> > But are they really getting stuck?  I don't usually see that with
> > mixture models other than the obvious degeneracy of a mixture containing
> > a single comonent and getting a hierarchical variance of 0 and blowing
> > up.
> >
> > > My first thought was simply to run many chains and then use only those chains with the (same) highest lp__. Is this reasonable, or how might one deal with this otherwise in practice?
> >
> > The best thing to do is add a prior that coaxes the model into
> > better behavior.
> >
> > Barring that, good inits can help you explore the good region, but
> > you still won't be able to do proper Bayesian inference.
> >
> > > I have a version of this same model as I coded from scratch using EM, but I get separation, so I figured I'd move to STAN, which I've wanted to do for some time and now have reason to do so thankfully.
> > >
> > > The model is defined as follows, with simulation / model code attached to this message.
> > >
> > > I would really appreciate any help with this. I'd also like to extend my thanks to everyone who has put effort into the STAN project as a whole.
> >
> > Some comments below.
> >
> > >
> > > data {
> > >    int N;
> > >    int J;
> > >    int y[N];
> > >    int b1[N];
> > >    real c1[N];
> > >    real c2[N];
> > >    real c3[N];
> > >    int o[N];
> > >
> > >    int trials;
> > >    int treat[N];
> > > }
> > > transformed data{
> > >
> > >   // Respondent types (observed Z = 1, observed Z = 0, latent Z = 0 or 1)
> > >   vector[N] type0;
> > >   vector[N] type1;
> > >   vector[N] type01;
> > >
> > >   type0 <- rep_vector(0, N);
> > >   type1 <- rep_vector(0, N);
> > >   type01 <- rep_vector(0, N);
> > >
> > >   for(i in 1:N){
> > >     if(treat[i] == 1 && y[i] == 0) type0[i] <- 1;
> > >     if(treat[i] == 1 && y[i] == (J + 1)) type1[i] <- 1;
> > >     if(y[i] > 0 && y[i] < (J + 1)) type01[i] <- 1;
> > >     if(treat[i] == 0) type01[i] <- 1;
> > >   }
> > >
> > You can skip the rep vector and just do this:
> >
> >   for (n in 1:N) {
> >     type0[i] <- treat[i] == 1 && y[i] == 0;
> >     ...
> >   }
> >
> > Whenever you see
> >
> >   if (cond) a <- 1;
> >   else a <- 0;
> >
> > you can replace with:
> >
> >   a <- cond;
> >
> >
> > > }
> > > parameters {
> > >
> > >    real control_beta[3 + 0]; // Control items (intercept, Z, U, ...)
> > >    real sens_beta[1 + 0];    // Sensitive item (intercept, ...)
> > >    real concom_beta[2 + 0];  // Concomitant regression (intercept, Z, ...)
> > >    real outA_beta[2 + 0];    // Outcome regression A (intercept, Z, ...)
> > >    real outB_beta[1 + 0];    // Outcome regression B (intercept, ...)
> > >
> >
> > Why the "+ 0"?  It's not doing anyting for you.
> >
> > > }
> > > model {
> > >
> > >   control_beta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> > >   sens_beta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> > >   concom_beta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> > >   outA_beta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> > >   outB_beta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> > >
> >
> > You may need tighter priors if the computations' still not behaving.
> >
> > >   for(i in 1:N){
> > >
> > >       # IF Z = 0
> > >       if(type0[i] == 1){
> > >         increment_log_prob(
> > >                 log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(0, sens_beta[1]) +
> > >                             bernoulli_logit_log(1,
> > >                                                 concom_beta[1] +
> > >                                                 concom_beta[2] * 0) +
> >
> > You don't ever want to multiply by 0.  Just use this:
> >
> >    bernoulli_logit_log(1, concom_beta[1]);
> >
> >
> > >                             binomial_logit_log(o[i], trials,
> > >                                                outA_beta[1] +
> > >                                                outA_beta[2] * 0) +
> > >                             binomial_logit_log(y[i], J,
> > >                                                control_beta[1] +
> > >                                                control_beta[2] * 0 +
> > >                                                control_beta[3] * 1),
> >
> > Also, just replace (a * 1) with a.  The extra multiplications get
> > the chain rule propagating through them in autodiff and are thus just
> > extra work.
> > >
> > >                             bernoulli_logit_log(0, sens_beta[1]) +
> > >                             bernoulli_logit_log(0,
> > >                                                 concom_beta[1] +
> > >                                                 concom_beta[2] * 0) +
> > >                             binomial_logit_log(o[i], trials, outB_beta[1]) +
> > >                             binomial_logit_log(y[i], J,
> > >                                                control_beta[1] +
> > >                                                control_beta[2] * 0 +
> > >                                                control_beta[3] * 0))
> > >         );
> > >       }
> > >
> > >       # IF Z = 1
> > >       if(type1[i] == 1){
> > >         increment_log_prob(
> > >                 log_sum_exp(bernoulli_logit_log(1, sens_beta[1]) +
> > >                             bernoulli_logit_log(1,
> > >                                                concom_beta[1] +
> > >                                                concom_beta[2] * 1) +
> > >                             binomial_logit_log(o[i], trials,
> > >                                                outA_beta[1] +
> > >                                                outA_beta[2] * 1) +
> > >                             binomial_logit_log(y[i] - treat[i], J,
> > >                                                control_beta[1] +
> > >                                                control_beta[2] * 1 +
> > >                                                control_beta[3] * 1),
> > >
> > >                             bernoulli_logit_log(1, sens_beta[1]) +
> > >                             bernoulli_logit_log(0,
> > >                                                 concom_beta[1] +
> > >                                                 concom_beta[2] * 1) +
> > >                             binomial_logit_log(o[i], trials, outB_beta[1]) +
> > >                             binomial_logit_log(y[i] - treat[i], J,
> > >                                                control_beta[1] +
> > >                                                control_beta[2] * 1 +
> > >                                                control_beta[3] * 0))
> > >         );
> > >       }
> >
> > ...
> >
> > Then if you really want to start optimizing, you'll replace bernoulli_logit(1, alpha);
> > with log_inv_logit(alpha) and cache the log_inv_logit calc for reuse.  Same for the other
> > uses.  The best thing you can do in terms of log prob and gradient evaluation speed is
> > to save computations and reuse them.
> >
> > - Bob

messages.subject_clean: From JAGS to Stan - 2 parameter probit IRT with covariates
messages.body_plain:
Greetings Stan users,

I recently began experimenting with Stan as a tool to simulate two parameter IRT models (probit link) with congressional voting data.  Originally I started with the pscl package in R and then moved on to JAGS via rjags.  The current model I am interested in adds additional covariates to the standard model as in:

P(y_ij = 1) = Phi( beta_j * x_i - alpha_j + gamma * z_ij)

where z_ij represents data (legislator and constituent characteristics).  I have written the code for this model (attached) but after running it a number of times the model doesn't mix well.  It moves to the prior means for the x_i and stays there while all the other parameters remain at their initial values (at least up to 500 iterations which took around 3 hours).

I am certain the code works since I have run it with z_ij equal to all zeros and the output is comparable to using ideal() in pscl which is the exact same model.  I was also successful with a canned example I made for this post (see attached).  So I am thinking this is related to my data.  I have had success using JAGS with this data (code attached) and it does return sensible results.  However it is very slow and so I would really like to get this working in Stan to compare.  I am hoping someone might be able to provide some advice or tips to get things moving.  Better starting values?  Rescaling the data?

As an aside, can someone provide some intuition for the "vanishing density" error?  Either of the following triggers it:
-  Passing initial values for alpha and beta using the coefficients from probit regressions of y_j on the initial x_i and an intercept (one regression per j).  This is a default in ideal().
-  Passing initial values for gamma using the coefficients from a probit regression of y on z (no intercept) with all other initial values at zero

Thanks in advance!

Jake

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob, Andrew & Luc -

Thanks for the replies; lots to chew over, and will come back with an update when I take a swing at these ideas!

Sorry for being vague in the original. The exposure, "A", is an episode of household exposure to tuberculosis that has been documented. The test, "B", is a tuberculin skin test (TST), which is very rough, left-censored measure of tuberculosis infection, and the outcome, "C" is developing TB disease during the year after exposure. A positive TST strongly suggests that an individual was infected with TB at some time before testing positive, but gives no indication of when. Individuals testing positive for TB using the TST are more likely than TST-negative folks to develop disease, but still not terribly likely to do so (< 1%). The caveat is that individuals who might have been TST-negative but for some known source of intensive exposure (either b/c they have relatively few exposure risks or are too young to have had a lot of community exposure) should be much more likely to develop disease. So the idea is to get an estimate of how much of the overall risk of developing TB disease is attributable to that household exposure, both via exposure causing a change in TST status, i.e. the A -> B -> C pathway, or exposure not causing a change in TST status (what I called the A->C pathways), either because it doesn't stimulate a response (i.e. the person remains TST-negative) or they were already TST positive before the exposure.

Andrew - in terms of modeling the joint outcome, are you suggesting something like a multinomial logit for each B/C combination, or just modeling P(C|B)*P(B)?

Thanks!

-Jon

On Sunday, June 7, 2015 at 6:59:10 AM UTC-4, Luc Coffeng wrote:
> About sampling from the joint distribution P(sens, spec | A*, B, C*), I was just thinking that in this particular problem:
>
> P(sens, spec | A*, B, C*) == P(sens | A*, B, C*) . P(spec | A*, B, C*)
>
> This is because the number of observations with (A*=1,C*=1) only determines the posterior uncertainty in sensitivity; posterior uncertainty in specificity is determined by the number of observations with !(A*=1,C*=1).

messages.body_plain:
Those didn't look like at all the same models in Stan and JAGS
given that you give beta a direct multinormal prior in the
JAGS approach.

For speed (and robustness) in Stan, you're better off using

  y ~ bernoulli_logit(beta[rc[r]]*xi[id[r]] - alpha[rc[r]] + zg[r]);

That assumes the parameter's on the logit scale.  It usually doesn't make
much difference in modeling other than scale of coefficients.

I didn't trace through the values for your mu_* and sigma_* constants
or the form of your predictors, but you have to be very careful about
identifiability with these models with independent additive factors.

If the predictors are not standardized, doing that could help.  But
the problem in these models is usually the non-identifiability.

Whatever you do, it would help to generate fake data based on your model
and see if the program can fit it.  That'll test that everything is OK before
moving to real data.

More below.

> I recently began experimenting with Stan as a tool to simulate two parameter IRT models (probit link) with congressional voting data.  Originally I started with the pscl package in R and then moved on to JAGS via rjags.  The current model I am interested in adds additional covariates to the standard model as in:
>
> P(y_ij = 1) = Phi( beta_j * x_i - alpha_j + gamma * z_ij)
>
> where z_ij represents data (legislator and constituent characteristics).  I have written the code for this model (attached) but after running it a number of times the model doesn't mix well.  It moves to the prior means for the x_i and stays there while all the other parameters remain at their initial values (at least up to 500 iterations which took around 3 hours).
>
> I am certain the code works since I have run it with z_ij equal to all zeros and the output is comparable to using ideal() in pscl which is the exact same model.  I was also successful with a canned example I made for this post (see attached).  So I am thinking this is related to my data.  I have had success using JAGS with this data (code attached) and it does return sensible results.  However it is very slow and so I would really like to get this working in Stan to compare.  I am hoping someone might be able to provide some advice or tips to get things moving.  Better starting values?  Rescaling the data?
>
> As an aside, can someone provide some intuition for the "vanishing density" error?

It's triggered when the density is zero (log density negative infinity).
This usually results from a constraint being violated.  A culprit might
be Phi_approx underflowing to 0 or overflowing to 1 with mismatched
data.

> Either of the following triggers it:
> -  Passing initial values for alpha and beta using the coefficients from probit regressions of y_j on the initial x_i and an intercept (one regression per j).  This is a default in ideal().
> -  Passing initial values for gamma using the coefficients from a probit regression of y on z (no intercept) with all other initial values at zero

You can use print statements to track down where the
density goes to zero.  You can use the constant lp__ (not in the
doc and soon to be deprecated and replaced with a function) to inspect
the current value at any point using:

  print("lp==", lp__);

- Bob

"AMC" is adiabatic Monte Carlo, as introduced by Michael Betancourt here:

  http://arxiv.org/abs/1405.3489

That should work to get through multiple modes, but not combinatorially
many of them like you might get in a clustering problem.

But we haven't implemented it in Stan yet.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

The function I implemented is as follows:

real skew_student_t_log(real y, real nu, real mu, real sigma, real skew) {

  real lp;

  lp <- 0;

  if (skew<=0)

    reject("skew has to be positive. Found skew=",skew);

  if (y<mu)

     lp<- student_t_log(y*skew, nu, mu*skew, sigma);

  else

     lp<- student_t_log(y/skew, nu, mu/skew, sigma);

  lp <- lp + log(2*skew)-log(1+skew*skew);

  return lp;

}

and I call it like this:

y ~ skew_student_t(nu, mu, sigma, skew);

It follows Fernandez, C. and Steel definition, also used by R package skewt (except that they do not use sigma or mu).

I did not attempt to code as per newer definition by Azzalini and Capitanio, because it requires multiplying the density by the cumulative distribution, and the latter has reportedly some numerical problems if used in this way: https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!searchin/stan-users/skew$20student/stan-users/j44ipDdQep8/kIx4bC2GsA4J

That’s great, but e.g. I do not know how to efficiently sample from this distribution, and I would like to do it in generated quantities block.

So, looking forward for a full implementation of the Skew Student in Stan, yours :-)

Slawek
