messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Request: Skew Student distribution
messages.body_plain:
Thanks.  Your definition makes it clear how the skew's happening.

I love that you're testing inputs!  You should also test that sigma >= 0.
Of course, if you're estimating skew, then you want to constrain it to
positive, just like sigma.

You could simplify the code a bit by assigning to lp straight off
and then directly returning in the conditionals.  I even wrote
the tests to validate that all return paths end in return statements,
so you can't forget to return.

real skew_student_t_log(real y, real nu, real mu, real sigma, real skew) {
  real lp;

  if (skew <= 0)
    reject("Skew has to be positive. Found skew=", skew);
  if (sigma <= 0)
    reject("Scale has to be positive.  Found sigma=", sigma);
  lp <- log(skew) - log1p(square(skew));
  if (y < mu)
     return lp + student_t_log(y * skew, nu, mu * skew, sigma);
  else
     return lp + student_t_log(y / skew, nu, mu / skew, sigma);
}

Not assigning to 0 and then adding will be more efficient for autodiff.

You can drop the multiplier 2 in the adjustment, because

  log(2 * skew) = log(2) = log(skew)

and Stan only needs densities up to an additive constant.

And you can use the log1p() and square() operations for a bit more
efficiency and in the case of log1p(), robustness for small values of
skew (probably not a problem here if there's a reasonable prior on
skew or if it's fixed).

If you're only using this with constant values of skew, you can do
this:

real skew_student_t_log(real y, real nu, real mu, real sigma, real skew) {

  if (skew <= 0)
    reject("Skew has to be positive. Found skew=", skew);
  if (sigma <= 0)
    reject("Scale has to be positive.  Found sigma=", sigma);
  if (y < mu)
    return student_t_log(y * skew, nu, mu * skew, sigma);
  else
    return student_t_log(y / skew, nu, mu / skew, sigma);
}

because the whole expression is just a constant.  So far, there's no
way to test that in our functions (unlike in C++, where we do it all
the time).

And if sigma is a constant, you can probably get even more efficient
by scaling that rather than y.  But that's getting carried away in
terms of clarity.

- Bob

Just to give some idea of the trace plots for this, I ran 8 chains on simulated data, which I've posted below. As you can see, in this case the chains get to 1 of 2 modes and sample from those areas without moving to explore elsewhere. The chains that have the highest mean lp___ (e.g. that in purple) are the ones that cover the population values for each parameter as I've defined them. I can try to set stronger priors or use "better" starting values so that I'm not moving into the "wrong" area in the posterior. I'm a bit apprehensive to do so because it would be preferable not to have to justify stronger claims (even if they would be reasonable to most).

messages.subject: Mixed models in STAN vs. glmer
messages.subject_clean: Mixed models in STAN vs. glmer
messages.body_plain:
Greetings, STAN-list users.  Another question from a STAN (and Bayesian) neophyte concerning mixed model analysis.

I have been trying to understand better the differences in assumptions and conclusions from fully Bayesian analyses (STAN) and the frequentist analyses (with which I am more familiar) of mixed models.  To be explicit, I have been looking at analyses of the BLOCKER data as in the BUGS, and now the STAN models, and using glmer from the R package nlme4.  The estimates of "d" in the two sets of analyses are virtually identical -- -0.25 using STAN, and -0.26 using glmer.  But the estimates of the SE of d are quite different, about 0.12 for STAN (taking the sqrt of the estimated sigmasqu_delta), but only 0.05 using glmer.  In this case, the conclusions from the two approaches are the same.  But it appears that STAN is estimating a relatively much larger SEM than glmer, and it is easy to see that with a d a bit closer to 0, the conclusions might be quite different.

I am using RSTAN 2.6.0, R version 3.2.0, RStudio 0.99.441, and lme4 1.1-7, on a Windows 8.1 machine with all updates.  I used blocker.stan blocker.dat, and blocker.init, unchanged from the files in the STAN examples.   For the glmer analysis, I restructured blocker.dat so that there was one case per record, with three columns:  death (1 vs 0), study number, and treatment group.  My glmer function was:

m1 <- glmer(death ~ group + (1 | study), data = bldat2, family = binomial)
//group is treated vs. control (1 vs 0);  study is the number of the specific cited study.

I also checked a variant of blocker.stan, using normal distributions instead of t distributions (4 df) for d.  The results of this modified blocker.stan were essentially identical to the results from the original blocker.stan.

My set of questions includes:
a)  What are the differences in assumptions that lead to the different estimates of the SE of d?  Is glmer missing a source of variance that STAN is finding, and if so, where?  Alternatively, is the difference due to error introduced by approximations introduced in the calculations?
b)  Given that the model results are somewhat different, which is more likely to represent "reality"?
c)  My understanding is that the estimates of SE(d) in STAN come directly from sampling the posterior estimates of d, but that with glmer, the SE is estimated as the partial slope of the inverted information matrix, which, as I understand it, is only asymptotically equivalent to a normal distribution.  Does this imply that the STAN estimate is more accurate than the glmer estimate?  If I am correct in my understanding of this, the implication is that one should do most of one's mixed model analysis using STAN rather than glmer.  Am I way off?
d)  If someone could point me to a useful reference that will answer my questions above, I would be deeply grateful to you.  (I am slowly making my way through Gelman's book, "Bayesian Data Analysis.")

Many thanks in advance
.
Larry Hunsicker
L. G. Hunsicker, M.D.
Professor Emeritus, University of Iowa College of Medicine

I used blocker.stan blocker.dat, and blocker.init, unchanged from the files in the STAN examples.   For the glmer analysis, I restructured blocker.dat so that there was one case per record, with three columns:  death (1 vs 0), study number, and treatment group.  My glmer function was:
>
> m1 <- glmer(death ~ group + (1 | study), data = bldat2, family = binomial)
> //group is treated vs. control (1 vs 0);  study is the number of the specific cited study.
>
> I also checked a variant of blocker.stan, using normal distributions instead of t distributions (4 df) for d.  The results of this modified blocker.stan were essentially identical to the results from the original blocker.stan.
>
> My set of questions includes:
> a)  What are the differences in assumptions that lead to the different estimates of the SE of d?  Is glmer missing a source of variance that STAN is finding, and if so, where?

nlme does max marginal likelihood --- marginalizing out low-level
parameters, then optimizing the hierarchical parameters, then plugging
in point estimates for the hierarchical parameters in estimating the
low-level params.  It's not a well-founded process probabilistically.

Andrew or Ben or Rob will know the answer for sure, but my guess is
that the uncertainty in the hierarchical parameters is being missed in
the nlme analysis.

> Alternatively, is the difference due to error introduced by approximations introduced in the calculations?

No.  Neither calculation is "approximate" in the meaningful sense.
nlme's whole approach is an approximation, but the calculation is
not (although it uses an iterative algorithm).  MCMC is only approximate
in that its error goes down with sqrt of number of independent draws.

> b)  Given that the model results are somewhat different, which is more likely to represent "reality"?

That's a loaded question asking whether to do classical point
estimates or full Bayes.

Full Bayes is the way to go.  It captures all the uncertainty
in your estimates and lets you use them downstream for inference.

We think of max marginal likelihood as an approximation procedure.

> c)  My understanding is that the estimates of SE(d) in STAN come directly from sampling the posterior estimates of d, but that with glmer, the SE is estimated as the partial slope of the inverted information matrix, which, as I understand it, is only asymptotically equivalent to a normal distribution.

There is that, too.

>  Does this imply that the STAN estimate is more accurate than the glmer estimate?

They're computing different things;  see above.

> If I am correct in my understanding of this, the implication is that one should do most of one's mixed model analysis using STAN rather than glmer.  Am I way off?

We'd agree, of course.

> d)  If someone could point me to a useful reference that will answer my questions above, I would be deeply grateful to you.  (I am slowly making my way through Gelman's book, "Bayesian Data Analysis.")

I'd recommend the lme4 doc:

  http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lme4/vignettes/lmer.pdf

to actually see what's going on.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Bob, for a very helpful answer.  It is both encouraging and discouraging:  the former in that I have a better sense of where I have to go, and discouraging in that I now have to question the accuracy of my past analyses using glmer.
I would take mild issue with only one of your answers.  "They're computing different things."  I would offer that they are both intended to provide an answer to the same question, in this case "What is the size of the effect of using beta blockers, and how accurately do we know this size?"  (I am a physician, after all.) They are computing the answer to the same question using different methods.  Both are approximations, but one (STAN) appears to be a giving a somewhat more accurate approximation, and the accuracy of the approximation is under my control (by how many chains and iterations I request).
The history of statistics is a record of approximations acceptable because they were tractable.  But with today's computational resources, there is no good excuse for using a less good approximation simply because it runs a bit faster.
I'll spend my free time (after my day job) reading more of Gelman's book rather than trying to digest the innards of glmer.
Again, thanks.
Larry Hunsicker

> On Jun 9, 2015, at 1:48 PM, Larry Hunsicker <lhuns...@mchsi.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks, Bob, for a very helpful answer.  It is both encouraging and discouraging:  the former in that I have a better sense of where I have to go, and discouraging in that I now have to question the accuracy of my past analyses using glmer.
> I would take mild issue with only one of your answers.  "They're computing different things."  I would offer that they are both intended to provide an answer to the same question, in this case "What is the size of the effect of using beta blockers, and how accurately do we know this size?"  (I am a physician, after all.)

The fact that you said "and how accurately" means you're at least
part statistician!

> They are computing the answer to the same question using different methods.

I think I understand what you mean --- it's like saying Newtonian physics
and Einsteinian physics are trying to compute the answer to the same
question using different methods.  They are different mathematical
systems that provide different answers if computed correctly, but they're trying
to get at the same physical phenomenon.

Once you take that view, the world opens up into a huge array of possible
models if you conflate every possible approach to answering the effect of
using beta blockers.  It's almost certainly not linear, for instance, so
all of these approximations to reality using (generalized) linear models are
highly questionable.

What you want to do is get into testing the predictions of your model on
held-out data (or using cross validation).  I think that'll give you the means
you need to properly compare models.

>  Both are approximations, but one (STAN) appears to be a giving a somewhat more accurate approximation, and the accuracy of the approximation is under my control (by how many chains and iterations I request).

Stan computes posterior expectations up to MCMC precision.  All computation
on a computer is approximate in that we have double-precision arithmetic,
not real numbers.  The computer approximation is better for some operations (like
multiplication) than it is for others (like subtraction).

> The history of statistics is a record of approximations acceptable because they were tractable.  But with today's computational resources, there is no good excuse for using a less good approximation simply because it runs a bit faster.

Our point exactly!  Of course, we keep taking on bigger and harder
problems where we can't get the solutions we want using MCMC in
less than a week, which becomes problematic for doing science
again, and forces us to think about approximations like variational
inference and max marginal likelihood.

> I'll spend my free time (after my day job) reading more of Gelman's book rather than trying to digest the innards of glmer.

I'd strongly suggest the Gelman and Hill book for this kind of thing.
It's what convinced me to quit my day job and join the circus :-)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] multiple models
messages.body_plain:
You're right --- you need to declare any variable that's used
in Stan.

The vector type only takes one arg and produces a column vector:

  vector[M] u;

The matrix type takes two args and produces a dense matrix:

  matrix[M,N] v;

There's also arrays:

  real v[M,N];

There's a chapter near the front of the manual about the differences.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Request: Skew Student distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I have just tried the newer definition of skew Student (by A Azzalini, R Arellano-Valle e.g. in  http://arxiv.org/pdf/1203.2376v1, eq.22) . It seems to be working, despite using the CDF, so maybe things improved since 2013 (see above in the thread) or I am using a nice range of inputs? The matching R package is called sn.

Also, I do not understand all the differences between the two formulas, but in my testing this one appears to be working better (the generated forecasts are better).

real skew_student_t_log(real y, real nu, real mu, real sigma, real skew) {

   real z; real zc;

   if (sigma <= 0)

     reject("Scale has to be positive. Found sigma=", sigma);

   z<- (y-mu)/sigma;

   zc<- skew*z*sqrt((nu+1)/(nu+square(z)));

   return -log(sigma) + student_t_log(z, nu, 0, 1) + student_t_cdf_log(zc, nu+1, 0, 1);

}

Regards,

Slawek

prior tighter.  Also, you probably want log(1.0 / K) rather than log(0.25)
if you want it to just be a uniform mixture.  But you don't even need
a constant there, because

  log_sum_exp(a + b, a + c)

    = log(exp(a + b) + exp(a + c))

    = log(exp(a) * exp(b) + exp(a) * exp(c))

    = log(exp(a) * (exp(b) + exp(c))

    = a + log(exp(b) + exp(c))

and the constant term a doesn't do anything for sampling because we only
need the density up to a constant (unless you care about your joint log
probability function f(y, theta | x) [y modeled data, theta params, x predictors]
being normalized as the value of lp__).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I'm going to take a guess that he meant the outcomes
as opposed to means or variances, since he said known covariance
and the example had fixed parameters for the normals.

If you have these marginals

   y[1] ~ normal(-1, 2);

   y[2] ~ normal(3, 1);

and know correlation is rho, then if

  Sigma = | 2   rho |
          | rho   1 |

  mu = | -1 |
       |  3 |

you want

  y ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Jun 10, 2015, at 12:42 PM, Slawek Smyl <slawe...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
> I have just tried the newer definition of skew Student (by A Azzalini, R Arellano-Valle e.g. in  http://arxiv.org/pdf/1203.2376v1, eq.22) . It seems to be working, despite using the CDF, so maybe things improved since 2013 (see above in the thread) or I am using a nice range of inputs? The matching R package is called sn.
>
> Also, I do not understand all the differences between the two formulas,

The algebra's simpler --- it's the numerical properties of the
algorithms that'll get you.  The key thing for efficiency is not to repeat computations
if you can avoid it.  The main think for numerical accuracy is to
make sure that you use the compound functions wherever possible (e.g.,
log1p(x) instead of log(1 + x)), us the parameters with built-in transforms
wherever possible (e.g., bernoulli_logit(alpha) vs. bernoulli(inv_logit(alpha))
and always work on the log scale.

> but in my testing this one appears to be working better (the generated forecasts are better).

Unless there are numerical issues, you should get the same density
value and gradient, so how a function's defined will only matter if
it runs into numerical difficulties.

> real skew_student_t_log(real y, real nu, real mu, real sigma, real skew) {
>
>    real z; real zc;
>
>    if (sigma <= 0)
>
>      reject("Scale has to be positive. Found sigma=", sigma);
>
>
>    z<- (y-mu)/sigma;
>
>    zc<- skew*z*sqrt((nu+1)/(nu+square(z)));
>
>    return -log(sigma) + student_t_log(z, nu, 0, 1) + student_t_cdf_log(zc, nu+1, 0, 1);
>
> }

Thanks for sharing.  That looks great.  What happened to the test
for skew <= 0?

Now we can work on style :-)  I'd add space between operators like *,
remove space between lines, and keep lines to 80 characters max.  At
least those are the guidelines we try to follow ourselves in coding models
and in the C++ for Stan itself.

- Bob

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Puzzling effective sample size values
messages.body_plain:
n_eff is always estimated --- you can't know the "true" effective
sample size unless you set the sampler up analytically.

Stan's been set up to be conservative compared to other methods by
using cross-chain information rather than estimating the n_eff of
each chain separately and then adding.  What are the Rhat values for
those chains --- if it's above 1, you haven't run the chains long enough?
The bigger the Rhat, the more we'll adjust the n_eff
estimates downward.  As Rhat goes to 1, our n_eff estimate should approach
the ones you'd get from running the chains independently and adding.
You can see the formula we use in the manual (MCMC chapter) or in Gelman
et al.'s BDA3 book.

We should make sure that PyStan provides the same answer as CmdStan.
Can we borrow your sample for testing?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Request: Skew Student distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,
In http://www.iew.uzh.ch/static/seminars/downloads/GHSkewTAasHaff05.pdf, in paragraph 3.2 the authors state
" There are several definitions presented in the literature that can be regarded as competing skew Student’s t-distributions" and they follow on showing that e.g. tail behavior is a bit different.
So they look to me like different functions, not just different expressions.
The skew<=0 was removed, because in the Azzalini's formulation, skew is symmetric around 0, and 0 gives you the normal Student distribution. In Fernandez and Steel's formula 1 is central.
I am not sure what is best translation between these two skews.

Regards,
Slawek

On Wed, Jun 10, 2015 at 10:51 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
> > On Jun 10, 2015, at 12:42 PM, Slawek Smyl <slawe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> > I have just tried the newer definition of skew Student (by A Azzalini, R Arellano-Valle e.g. in  http://arxiv.org/pdf/1203.2376v1, eq.22) . It seems to be working, despite using the CDF, so maybe things improved since 2013 (see above in the thread) or I am using a nice range of inputs? The matching R package is called sn.
> >
> > Also, I do not understand all the differences between the two formulas,
>
> The algebra's simpler --- it's the numerical properties of the
> algorithms that'll get you.  The key thing for efficiency is not to repeat computations
> if you can avoid it.  The main think for numerical accuracy is to
> make sure that you use the compound functions wherever possible (e.g.,
> log1p(x) instead of log(1 + x)), us the parameters with built-in transforms
> wherever possible (e.g., bernoulli_logit(alpha) vs. bernoulli(inv_logit(alpha))
> and always work on the log scale.
>
> > but in my testing this one appears to be working better (the generated forecasts are better).
>
> Unless there are numerical issues, you should get the same density
> value and gradient, so how a function's defined will only matter if
> it runs into numerical difficulties.
>
> > real skew_student_t_log(real y, real nu, real mu, real sigma, real skew) {
> >
> >    real z; real zc;
> >
> >    if (sigma <= 0)
> >
> >      reject("Scale has to be positive. Found sigma=", sigma);
> >
> >
> >    z<- (y-mu)/sigma;
> >
> >    zc<- skew*z*sqrt((nu+1)/(nu+square(z)));
> >
> >    return -log(sigma) + student_t_log(z, nu, 0, 1) + student_t_cdf_log(zc, nu+1, 0, 1);
> >
> > }
>
> Thanks for sharing.  That looks great.  What happened to the test
> for skew <= 0?
>
> Now we can work on style :-)  I'd add space between operators like *,
> remove space between lines, and keep lines to 80 characters max.  At
> least those are the guidelines we try to follow ourselves in coding models
> and in the C++ for Stan itself.
>
> - Bob

>
>
>
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Puzzling effective sample size values
messages.body_plain:
It seems to be pretty substantial underestimates to me (factor of 3 to 6). Rhat's are mostly 1.0. (I work on a version of HMC for my PhD thesis, so I am not new to computing ESS.)

I attached the python notebook that can reproduce the result. The burn-in iterations are intentionally large, so that the NUTS will produce more or less independent samples after the burn-in.

On Wednesday, June 10, 2015 at 1:08:08 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> n_eff is always estimated --- you can't know the "true" effective
> sample size unless you set the sampler up analytically.
>
> Stan's been set up to be conservative compared to other methods by
> using cross-chain information rather than estimating the n_eff of
> each chain separately and then adding.  What are the Rhat values for
> those chains --- if it's above 1, you haven't run the chains long enough?
> The bigger the Rhat, the more we'll adjust the n_eff
> estimates downward.  As Rhat goes to 1, our n_eff estimate should approach
> the ones you'd get from running the chains independently and adding.
> You can see the formula we use in the manual (MCMC chapter) or in Gelman
> et al.'s BDA3 book.
>
> We should make sure that PyStan provides the same answer as CmdStan.
> Can we borrow your sample for testing?
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Jun 10, 2015, at 1:58 PM, Akihiko Nishimura <akihiko_...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I am noticing the same issues with the effective sample size outputs as well (using PySTAN).
> >
> > With my simple linear mixed effect model, STAN output consistently underestimates the effective sample sizes of the parameters by a factor of 3 to 6. I tried running 1, 5, and 10 chains, and it made no difference. I tried calculating the "true" effective sample size using Bartlett's spectrograph estimator, Geyer's monotone positive sequence estimator, and spectrum estimate based in AR processes, and they all give more or less the same number. I ran the chains for a fairly long time, so the estimates are not that noisy.
> >
> > On Friday, May 15, 2015 at 4:50:23 PM UTC-5, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> > On Monday, April 20, 2015 at 4:33:53 PM UTC-6, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> > > component with a period on the order of 100 samples, and this should
> >

> >
> > and compare it to
> >
> >     plot((x-mean(x))/sd(x), type='l', ylim=c(-3.5, 3.5))
> >
> > where x is the trace I posted earlier, I can see just as much apparent low-frequency variation in the first plot as in the second.
> >
> > Furthermore, take a look at what happens when we look at the empirical standard deviations of successively larger batch means, and compare that to what we would expect for independent draws (x has length 1500):
> >
> > > sd(x)
> > [1] 0.1406752
> >
> >
> > > sd(x)/sqrt(10)
> > [1] 0.04448542
> > > sd(colMeans(matrix(x, nr=10)))
> > [1] 0.04134681
> >
> >
> > > sd(x)/sqrt(15)
> > [1] 0.03632219
> > > sd(colMeans(matrix(x, nr=15)))
> > [1] 0.03646076
> >
> >
> > > sd(x)/sqrt(20)
> > [1] 0.03145594
> > > sd(colMeans(matrix(x, nr=20)))
> > [1] 0.03124686
> >
> >
> > > sd(x)/sqrt(25)
> > [1] 0.02813505
> > > sd(colMeans(matrix(x, nr=25)))
> > [1] 0.02777601
> >
> >
> > > sd(x)/sqrt(30)
> > [1] 0.02568367
> > > sd(colMeans(matrix(x, nr=30)))
> > [1] 0.02636602
> >
> >
> > > sd(x)/sqrt(50)
> > [1] 0.01989448
> > > sd(colMeans(matrix(x, nr=50)))
> > [1] 0.01958211
> >
> >
> > > sd(x)/sqrt(75)
> > [1] 0.01624378
> > > sd(colMeans(matrix(x, nr=75)))
> > [1] 0.01497145
> >
> >
> > > sd(x)/sqrt(100)
> > [1] 0.01406752
> > > sd(colMeans(matrix(x, nr=100)))
> > [1] 0.01281342
> >
> >
> > If anything, we seem to be getting some negative correlation increasing the effective sample size.
> >
> > On Monday, April 20, 2015 at 4:33:53 PM UTC-6, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > The usual ESS estimators use just one chain — we use a slightly more
> > sophisticated estimators which considers multiple chains and is far
> > more sensitive to poor mixing (which is a good thing).  If you’ve
> > just run one then what happens is that we split the one chain into
> > two and use our multi-chain estimator.
> >
> > Naively looking at your trace plot O(100) seems reasonable to me —
> > although there is high-frequency variation there is a slower low-frequency
> > component with a period on the order of 100 samples, and this should
> > drive the ESS calculation.  I’m guess the coda estimator is just not
> > sensitive enough to catch this lower-frequency component.
> >
> > On Apr 20, 2015, at 11:05 PM, Kevin Van Horn <ke...@ksvanhorn.com> wrote:
> >
> >> The effective sample size calculation requires multiple chains? How is it being computed?
> >>
> >> In this case, one chain is all I have.
> >>
> >> On Monday, April 20, 2015 at 2:13:19 PM UTC-6, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> >> Hi, you need multiple chains but your plot just shows one.  Also I’m surprised that Stan returns a number like 167.4.  We try to round it because it is a noisy estimate in any case.
> >> A
> >>
> >>> On Apr 20, 2015, at 1:31 PM, Kevin Van Horn <ke...@ksvanhorn.com> wrote:
> >>>
> >>>  I am seeing vastly different numbers for effective sample size computed by Stan versus those computed by coda. The attached CSV file and plots are for a trace that Stan says only has an effective sample size of 167.4. Looking at it visually, that number of 167.4 looks very low. Running coda::effectiveSize on it, I get a result of 1616.5. The actual number of sampling iterations is 1500.
> >>>
> >>> Any idea why the large discrepancy? I'm trying to figure out which of these numbers to believe.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks --- I thought some of those looked like different functions!

> On Jun 10, 2015, at 3:05 PM, Slawek Smyl <slawe...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
> In http://www.iew.uzh.ch/static/seminars/downloads/GHSkewTAasHaff05.pdf, in paragraph 3.2 the authors state
> " There are several definitions presented in the literature that can be regarded as competing skew Student’s t-distributions" and they follow on showing that e.g. tail behavior is a bit different.
> So they look to me like different functions, not just different expressions.
> The skew<=0 was removed, because in the Azzalini's formulation, skew is symmetric around 0, and 0 gives you the normal Student distribution. In Fernandez and Steel's formula 1 is central.
> I am not sure what is best translation between these two skews.
>
> Regards,
> Slawek
>
> On Wed, Jun 10, 2015 at 10:51 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > On Jun 10, 2015, at 12:42 PM, Slawek Smyl <slawe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> > I have just tried the newer definition of skew Student (by A Azzalini, R Arellano-Valle e.g. in  http://arxiv.org/pdf/1203.2376v1, eq.22) . It seems to be working, despite using the CDF, so maybe things improved since 2013 (see above in the thread) or I am using a nice range of inputs? The matching R package is called sn.
> >
> > Also, I do not understand all the differences between the two formulas,
>
> The algebra's simpler --- it's the numerical properties of the
> algorithms that'll get you.  The key thing for efficiency is not to repeat computations
> if you can avoid it.  The main think for numerical accuracy is to
> make sure that you use the compound functions wherever possible (e.g.,
> log1p(x) instead of log(1 + x)), us the parameters with built-in transforms
> wherever possible (e.g., bernoulli_logit(alpha) vs. bernoulli(inv_logit(alpha))
> and always work on the log scale.
>
> > but in my testing this one appears to be working better (the generated forecasts are better).
>
> Unless there are numerical issues, you should get the same density
> value and gradient, so how a function's defined will only matter if
> it runs into numerical difficulties.
>
> > real skew_student_t_log(real y, real nu, real mu, real sigma, real skew) {
> >
> >    real z; real zc;
> >
> >    if (sigma <= 0)
> >
> >      reject("Scale has to be positive. Found sigma=", sigma);
> >
> >
> >    z<- (y-mu)/sigma;
> >
> >    zc<- skew*z*sqrt((nu+1)/(nu+square(z)));
> >
> >    return -log(sigma) + student_t_log(z, nu, 0, 1) + student_t_cdf_log(zc, nu+1, 0, 1);
> >
> > }
>
> Thanks for sharing.  That looks great.  What happened to the test
> for skew <= 0?
>
> Now we can work on style :-)  I'd add space between operators like *,
> remove space between lines, and keep lines to 80 characters max.  At
> least those are the guidelines we try to follow ourselves in coding models
> and in the C++ for Stan itself.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
I narrowed the normal prior but still no luck.  Same warning message and big rhat.  Very surprising and discouraging.

# simulated data
N=1000
K=4
sigma = .25
c <- sample(1:K, N, replace=TRUE)

mu=c(-10.,0.,10.,20.)
s = 1:N
for (i in 1:N){

  s[i] = rnorm(1, mu[c[i]], sigma)
}
myData = list(N=N,K = K, y = s, sigma=sigma)

data {
  int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
  int<lower=1> N; // number of data points
  real y[N]; // observations

  real<lower=0> sigma;

}
parameters {
  ordered[K] mu; // locations of mixture components
}
model {
  real ps[K]; // temp for log component densities

  mu ~ normal(0,10);

  for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K) {

      ps[k] <- log(1.0/K) + normal_log(y[n],mu[k], sigma);
    }
    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
    }
}

On Wednesday, June 10, 2015 at 1:07:09 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> That's surprising given the normal prior.   I'd try making the
> prior tighter.  Also, you probably want log(1.0 / K) rather than log(0.25)
> if you want it to just be a uniform mixture.  But you don't even need
> a constant there, because
>
>   log_sum_exp(a + b, a + c)
>
>     = log(exp(a + b) + exp(a + c))
>
>     = log(exp(a) * exp(b) + exp(a) * exp(c))
>
>     = log(exp(a) * (exp(b) + exp(c))
>
>     = a + log(exp(b) + exp(c))
>
> and the constant term a doesn't do anything for sampling because we only
> need the density up to a constant (unless you care about your joint log
> probability function f(y, theta | x) [y modeled data, theta params, x predictors]
> being normalized as the value of lp__).
>
> - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
I just had to play with this myself --- I should've done
that before putting the example in the manual.  Bottom line
is that Seth's absolutely right --- it's a multimodality and
local optimum problem.  I'll add some hedges to the manual for the
next release:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1420#issuecomment-111238073

I think the problem you're going to run into is with random inits or
initial steps getting too close to each other, so reasonable inits with
a smaller initial step size will probably help things settle down.

The deeper problem is that there's not going to be enough properly
directed energy in HMC's random momenta to get out of a local
optimum (Metropolis will have the same problem, and there will not be
enough freedom in the conditional samples to move in Gibbs, either).

So if you can do meaningful inits, that'd be a huge help in
this case where there are local optima to fall into.  Of course,
you won't get complete mixing in your posterior if you don't consider
the degenerate solutions, but I'm guessing their mass will be negligible
compared to the "correct" solution, so it probably won't matter.

One approach is to use many more mixture components than you think your
data needs --- if two go to the same place, it's probably no big deal in
terms of the overall posterior density.

You get another problem when you estimate sd in that there
are degenerate unbounded likelihood solutions when one of the
sigma goes to 0 and the mean for that cluster approaches the value
of a single item in the data set.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Jun 11, 2015, at 3:07 PM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> But it should be small for mu[4]--in the output I posted from chains
> 1-3, where everything worked, the mean is 3.98, sd 0.01. And if you
> just look at chain 4 which I posted the mean and sd are basically the
> same as well. So combining them does what I'd expect, mean 3.99, sd
> 0.01--but why is n_eff so low? Does the calculation of n_eff for some
> parameter take into account other parameters somehow?

No, it doesn't.  It's calculated param by param, but does
use cross-chain information and it does split each chain in
half, which is why it's more conservative than what you get in
say Coda.  The definition's in BDA3 and in the Stan manual.

- Bob

I think this'll do it:

Centered:

  parameters {
    vector<lower=0> a[K];
    real mu_a;
    real<lower=0> sigma_a;

  model {
    a ~ lognormal(mu_a, sigma_a);

Non-Centered:

  parameters {
    vector<lower=0> log_a_raw[K];
    real mu_a;
    real<lower=0> sigma_a;

  transformed_parameters {
    vector<lower=0> a[K];
    a <- exp(mu_a + sigma_a * log_a_raw);

  model {
    log_a_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

I've never tried it on the log scale, so I'm curious how well

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] From JAGS to Stan - 2 parameter probit IRT with covariates
messages.body_plain:
Bob: Just wanted to provide an update.

Things are mixing well now on account of standardizing the data I think.  I was able to track down the "vanishing density" error as well using print().  The issue was related to the initial values I was trying to use.  Specifically, they were pushing the value of the link (xb) to such extremes that Phi_approx() was essentially returning zero's and one's.  Same error occurred using Phi().  Hence the "vanishing density."

Regarding identification, I realized my code did not include any of my priors.  I think identification won't be an issue by specifying priors for the xi of N(-1,1) and N(1,1) with the means being based on political party (democrats are -1, republicans are 1).  The xi are most definitely bimodal so this prevents sampling from values that are equivalent via rotation.  This should also provide the scale for the other parameters, etc.  Do you agree with that?

In any case, I am now seeing comparable results with JAGS and really nice performance running parallel in Windows 7.

Thanks again for your help.

Jake

On Monday, June 8, 2015 at 9:43:37 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Jun 8, 2015, at 11:41 PM, Jake Johnson <jak...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Thanks for the the fast reply.  It isn't evident in the code I sent but the sigma's in the dmnrom() in JAGS are diagonal.  I read that this could improve performance versus a loop statement.  My impression is the same is not true for Stan - i.e. the loop is better than using multi_normal().
>
>
> Absolutely --- and vectorizing is better still.
>
> > I am not too concerned with identifiability per se since I am mainly interested in the rankings of the x_i.
>
> It's important for Stan --- if the model's not identifiable,
> Stan will run all over the posterior and the results won't make
> sense.  There's a discussion in the manual chapter on problematic
> posteriors.
>
> Specifically, you can't define an improper posterior and then
> hope to standardize it back.
>
> > I will also be placing a restriction on the distribution of the posterior means of the x_i and then
> > transforming alpha_j and beta_j.  In fact, the magnitudes of gamma are not that important either since I am mainly interested in their sign.
>
> You need to make it at least weakly identifiable as the
> density is defined in the parameters.  If it isn't,
> there will be problems for sampling with both HMC and Gibbs.
>
> > I'll try standardizing the data and see what happens.  From there I will try fitting some simulated data.
>
> Let us know how it goes.  A model along the lines of what you're
> doing should be estimable.
>

Thanks to all for looking into this.  I'm not an expert in MCMC, just trying to use Stan, so I'm not sure I understand the subtleties here.  Is it correct to say that the conclusion is that this is still an identifiability problem?  If so, why isn't the problem resolved by declaring the means to be an ordered data type?  Should this not eliminate multimodality?

On Thursday, June 11, 2015 at 3:32:21 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Jun 11, 2015, at 3:07 PM, Seth Flaxman <fla...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > But it should be small for mu[4]--in the output I posted from chains
> > 1-3, where everything worked, the mean is 3.98, sd 0.01. And if you
> > just look at chain 4 which I posted the mean and sd are basically the
> > same as well. So combining them does what I'd expect, mean 3.99, sd
> > 0.01--but why is n_eff so low? Does the calculation of n_eff for some
> > parameter take into account other parameters somehow?
>
> No, it doesn't.  It's calculated param by param, but does
> use cross-chain information and it does split each chain in
> half, which is why it's more conservative than what you get in
> say Coda.  The definition's in BDA3 and in the Stan manual.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
What ever came of this? I'm trying to solve a similar problem and would love to know the recommended solution.

Thanks!

- Avi

On Sunday, May 10, 2015 at 5:11:19 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hmm, this is tough because I fear that it destroys some simplicity in the code.
>
> Bob,
>
> Let me explain.  First I’ll show you the linear model:
>
> data {
>   int J;                         // #people in y
>   int T;                         // #time points in y
>   int K;                         // #parameters in delta
>   int K_phi;                     // #parameters in phi
>   matrix[J,T] y;
>   vector[T] x;
>   vector[K_phi] mu_phi_g;        // pseudo-prior mean
>   cov_matrix[K_phi] Sigma_phi_g; // pseudo-prior variance
> }
> parameters {
>   matrix[J,K] eta_a;
>   real<lower=0> sigma_y;
>   vector[K] mu_a;
>   vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_a;    // Now assuming indep
>   real b;                        // Shared parameter
> }
> transformed parameters {
>   matrix[J,K] a;
>   vector[K_phi] phi;
>   for (j in 1:J)
>     for (k in 1:K)
>       a[j,k] <- mu_a[k] + sigma_a[k]*eta_a[j,k];
>   phi[1] <- mu_a[1];
>   phi[2] <- mu_a[2];
>   phi[3] <- b;
>   phi[4] <- log(sigma_a[1]);
>   phi[5] <- log(sigma_a[2]);
>   phi[6] <- log(sigma_y);
> }
> model {
>   matrix[J,T] y_pred;
>   for (j in 1:J)
>     for (t in 1:T)
>       y_pred[j,t] <- a[j,1] + a[j,2]*x[t] + b*x[t]^2;
>   to_vector(y) ~ normal(to_vector(y_pred), sigma_y);
>   to_vector(eta_a) ~ normal(0,1);
>   phi ~ multi_normal(mu_phi_g, Sigma_phi_g);
> }
>
> You don’t really have to worry about phi here; I just included it to remind you of my desire to be able to access the concatenated transformed parameter vector directly (I need to do this because I’m running an EP-like algorithm).
>
> Here’s the point.  What I want to do is get rid of sigma_y, change the real data matrix y to an integer data array y, and replace normal by bernoulli_logit.  And from your previous message it looks like I need to change to_vector to to_array_1d.  But then I have a horrible feeling that the indexes will get flipped.
>
> So maybe the best solution is to change my model and make “a” and “y_pred” into 2-way arrays instead of matrices?
>
> This array/matrix thing is always tripping me up!
>
> Thanks
> A
>
>
> > On May 10, 2015, at 2:34 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > Key concept is the five basic types of Stan:
> >
> >  real-valued:
> >    real, vector, row_vector, matrix
> >
> >  integer-valued:
> >    int
> >
> > Then you can have an array of any dimensionality of
> > any basic type.
> >
> > So when you declare y as
> >
> >  int y[I,J];
> >
> > you get a 2D integer array.
> >
> > So assuming you want this:
> >
> > ...
> >
> >  for (i in 1:I)
> >    for (j in 1:J)
> >      y[i,j] ~ bernoulli_logit(theta);
> >
> > for a fixed theta, you can do this:
> >
> >  to_array_1d(y) ~ bernoulli_logit(theta);
> >
> > They go in column-major order (or last-index order
> > if the argument is more than 2D).  And then theta
> > has to be either a single real value or an array or
> > vector of I*J real values.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> >> On May 9, 2015, at 4:11 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >>
> >> Hmm, how I’m confused.  What I want to do is have y be an array (as you have it, “int y[I,j]”; is fine) and then give it a bernoulli_logit distribution.  Can I do this using to_vector?
> >> A
> >>
> >>
> >>> On May 9, 2015, at 12:51 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >>>
> >>> For a 2D array of integers, that's:
> >>>
> >>> int y[I,J];
> >>>
> >>> But you can't use it in matrix operations.  If you want
> >>> to do that you need to have
> >>>
> >>> matrix[I,J] y;
> >>>
> >>> But then you can't use it on the LHS of binomial or bernoulli.
> >>> If you need the binomial or bernoulli, then you are going to
> >>> need to convert the int array to a matrix in the transformed
> >>> data block.
> >>>
> >>> transformed data {
> >>>  matrix[I,J] y_mat;
> >>>
> >>>  y_mat <- to_matrix(y);
> >>> }
> >>>
> >>> It's more efficient defining it once as transformed data than to
> >>> reconvert it using to_matrix() each time you need it.
> >>>
> >>> - Bob
> >>>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] simple mixture model puzzle
messages.body_plain:
> On Jun 12, 2015, at 7:18 AM, Mark Ettinger <jetti...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Thanks to all for looking into this.  I'm not an expert in MCMC, just trying to use Stan, so I'm not sure I understand the subtleties here.  Is it correct to say that the conclusion is that this is still an identifiability problem?  If so, why isn't the problem resolved by declaring the means to be an ordered data type?  Should this not eliminate multimodality?

It eliminates the label swapping, but not the more degenerate multimodality
you get when two components collapse onto each other.

For instance, consider what happens if you really have two mixture components
but fit it with a model with five.  It's likely that a bunch of those mixture
components are going to be close to each other.

But even in the case where the model matches the generative process, you
get local optima of the likelihood with collapsed modes.

Suppose I have two components that are (near) identical and at the same
mixture component:

  mu[1] ~=~ mu[2]
  sigma[1] ~=~ sigma[2]

Then if you look at the derivative of the log likelihood, it goes down
as mu[1] moves away from mu[2].  You can do the log likelihood plot if you want with
everything fixed other than mu[1] to see the problem.

Now if the valleys are steep enough, as they are in your very well
separated example, the problem is that if you initialize or initially
jump randomly to a place where mu[1] is close to mu[2], there's not enough
energy to get away in the algorithm.  Same problem that you run into using
classical optimization techniques looking for a maximum likelihood estimate.

In higher dimensions, the normal mixture turns into K-means clustering,
which is very multimodal and combinatorially impossible to optimize
properly.  So it's not just MCMC, it's the fundamental nature of computing :-)

- Bob

>
> On Thursday, June 11, 2015 at 3:32:21 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

messages.subject: Optimizing the posterior and warmup sampling
messages.subject_clean: Optimizing the posterior and warmup sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am a PhD student in Civil Engineering at the University of Colorado at Boulder.  Last semester I fulfilled my final coursework credit by taking a spatial statistics course.  For the final project in this class, I had built a Bayesian stochastic weather generator in Stan (and RStan).  A quick description of this model is as follows:

I have daily weather (precipitation, temperature) data for 15 stations in Argentina.  I am using probit regression for the precipitation occurrence, and gamma for the intensity; the temperature processes (minimum and maximum) are conditioned on precipitation occurrence, previous day's temperature, and are modeled using linear regression.  What I have done is set up the model so each location has spatially-correlated coefficients for their respective regressions, each coefficient with respective kriging parameters (assumed no nugget [they are latent processes], variable sill, and variable range).  In the model file, the errors for each of the models are not assumed to be spatially correlated.

For my class, I ran eight chains of the model in parallel, each with 1400 iterations; the warmup period for each chain is 1000.  The results looked very good -- the model converged well before the end of the warmup period, and I had 3200 samples making up the posterior distributions, which had properties consistent with convergence.  I did not simulate daily weather on a grid, so did not use the spatial parameters to simulate the regression coefficients on a grid.  My multisite simulations looked very good.

Now this model has become a potential chapter of my dissertation, and I have begun using conditional simulation (sim.Krig in the fields package) to simulate the regression coefficients on a regular grid.  These daily weather sequences will be used by scientists and agronomists in Argentina to drive hydrologic and crop simulation models for better estimates of risk on the seasonal scale.  Naturally, I used the model I built and subsequently ran for my spatial statistics class as a first go for simulating these gridded weather sequences.  It turns out the estimation of sill and range (which, unfortunately, are inconsistently estimable) are wrong, which was due to the fact that I set a maximum limit on the range to be the maximum distance between stations.  This in turn lead to incorrect estimates of both sill and range, and produced wildly (spatially) variable coefficients.

I have met with a colleague, who thinks it is physically unrealistic to set this maximum bound on the range parameter.  After going back through my model and setting a very large maximum limit (1000x the maximum distance between stations), I was able to optimize the posterior and obtain the mode for each parameter.  Indeed, the optimal range values are more than 2x the maximum distance between stations (this is a small basin, and the range parameter is for unobserved processes -- the coefficients).  Using these optimized parameters to simulate gridded weather sequences yields reasonable results.  However, using the modes for these parameters as initial guesses in my updated Stan model, and inflating the max_treedepth value to 20 (as is suggested for big models), my model simply sits at the first iteration during warmup.  I figured I would let it run for a while to see if it ever got past the first iteration, to no avail.  It was still on the first iteration after nearly 2 days, at which point I had to kill the job.

Can you advise on the situation?  I have attached my model, R script, and data files (NOTE: the .RData file needed to load setup information would not attach to this post.  You may access this through my ftp site at http://civil.colorado.edu/~verdina/20140930-gridSim-setup-oneyear-oneTempCov.RData )

Thanks!
Andrew Verdin

> For instance, if my correlation matrices are never more than 7x7, do I

The overhead of correlation matrices that are of order 7 is going to be small relative to the cost (time, memory, imprecision) of autodiffing linear predictors that are 50000 x 7. >>
>> I think that the mean and sd for the parameter "d" are what I need.  "d" is a scalar, not a vector.  What does the "se_mean" measure?  Is this just a value that is routinely returned and is not meaningful for estimation of a scalar?

“se_mean” refers to the Markov Chain Monte Carlo Standard Error, which quantifies
the error in the estimate of the mean assuming certain regularity conditions between
your posterior and the HMC sampler.  Under those conditions it is given by

se_mean[f] = sqrt{ Var[f] / n_eff[f] }

In practice we estimate Var[f] using the MCMC samples.

>> I do understand that n_eff is less than the 4000 draws because the draws aren't independent.  How is this number estimated?  Maybe you can just point me to where in Gelman et al, edition 3, that this is explained.

See Section 54.4 in the Stan manual.

messages.body_plain:
In your R script, it looks like you're transforming your initial values:

pars = function()constrain_pars(stan_model,o$par)

But if o$par contains the true parameter values in unlogged space, I think you can pass those directly to Stan, i.e.:

sflist <- stan(fit = stan_model, data = lm_data,
                chains = 1, iter=iterations, init=list(o$par),
                seed = rng_seed, warmup = warmup, refresh = 1, control=list(max_treedepth=20))

(Another thing I'd try is rerunning with 4 chains rather than just 1, but maybe you've tried that already.)

Next thing I'd do is to try a non-zero nugget. This may not be correct for your setting theoretically, but it helps in practice with numerical stability. You could replace all the calls to exp_cov_matrix(..., 0) with, e.g. exp_cov_matrix(..., 0.0001).

Other suggestions that won't necessarily help with your issue but aren't a bad idea in any case (and might uncover a bug):

        c_max <- exp_cov_matrix(x, sill, range, nugget)

can be replaced with

       c_max <- sill * exp(-1.0 / range * x);
       for(i in 1:M)
             c_max[i,i] <- sill + nugget;

Another quick thing to try is that I've had more success using an inverse sqrt length-scale specification:

c_max <- sill * exp(- invrange * x[i,j])

I'm having trouble getting your code to run, perhaps because I'm missing some libraries. If you can simplify things a bit--trying fixing some of the parameters, using fewer weather stations, conditioning on fewer variables, etc.--and also send code that's easier to run, i.e. if possible the R code should just load an RData file and then compile and run the model, that'll help us give you more ideas...

Seth
P.S. Here's what happens when I try to run your code:

> o$par$sigma2_max  # did it load correctly?

I am currently trying to run stan on eye-movement models, which require some calculations on a grids and the computation time and memory demands are quite high (seconds per sample + 20-40 Gig memory). On the other hand parallel chains are very limited by the memory constrains here and help very little, compared to the 50-100 cores I could have for these calculations easily.

So is there any way to code in stan to run in parallel? Or will there be in near future?

And in case this is not possible: Are there rules to keep the memory requirements of stan / it's autodiff algorithm low? (simply to run more parallel chains)

all the best
Heiko

> >
> > I have daily weather (precipitation, temperature) data for 15 stations in Argentina.  I am using probit regression for the precipitation occurrence, and gamma for the intensity; the temperature processes (minimum and maximum) are conditioned on precipitation occurrence, previous day's temperature, and are modeled using linear regression.  What I have done is set up the model so each location has spatially-correlated coefficients for their respective regressions, each coefficient with respective kriging parameters (assumed no nugget [they are latent processes], variable sill, and variable range).  In the model file, the errors for each of the models are not assumed to be spatially correlated.
> >
> > For my class, I ran eight chains of the model in parallel, each with 1400 iterations; the warmup period for each chain is 1000.  The results looked very good -- the model converged well before the end of the warmup period, and I had 3200 samples making up the posterior distributions, which had properties consistent with convergence.  I did not simulate daily weather on a grid, so did not use the spatial parameters to simulate the regression coefficients on a grid.  My multisite simulations looked very good.
> >
> > Now this model has become a potential chapter of my dissertation, and I have begun using conditional simulation (sim.Krig in the fields package) to simulate the regression coefficients on a regular grid. > On Jun 15, 2015, at 6:57 AM, 'Heiko Schütt' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

On the other hand parallel chains are very limited by the memory constrains here and help very little, compared to the 50-100 cores I could have for these calculations easily.
>

Not within a chain.

> Or will there be in near future?

We haven't even tried to get the multicore
matrix operations working, but it's on our to-do list.
At that point, some matrix ops will be much faster.

Our math library's getting more factored to the point
where it'd be possible to drop in replacements that
ran on GPUs, but that's a ways off because none of us
know how to do it.

> And in case this is not possible: Are there rules to keep the memory requirements of stan / it's autodiff algorithm low? (simply to run more parallel chains)

Vectorize whatever you can, use as many of the compound operations as
you can, and precompute results and reuse them rather than recomputing.
That is, don't doo foo(exp(x)) + bar(exp(x)) --- store that exp(x) and
use it twice.

In terms of writing out results, you can move parameters from transformed
params to locals in the model block.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Greetings, folks:  Back for more help.  I am having difficulty visualizing how the vectorized commands are working in the epil example (Book 1 of the old BUGS examples).  This is a mixed Poisson model.  (Ancient history, I know.  But the great masters tried to understand historical models before doing something "original.")

In this example, there are N (59) subjects, each seen T (4) times.  The dependent variable  y is declared in a 59 x 4 matrix.  Other covariates (constant within subject) are given in length 59 vectors.  There is an indicator variable for the fourth visit (all other visits are treated the same).  So visit number is given as a length four vector (0,0,0,1).  The data are eventually all centered, but that is, I think, irrelevant to my question.  b and b1 are two variance variables to be estimated for the patient and the patient * visit levels.  a0 and Alphas are all parameters to be fitted.  After various declarations and data manipulation, the final model is given as:

for(n in 1:N) {
    b[n] ~ normal(0, sigma_b);
    y[n] ~ poisson_log(a0 + alpha_Base * log_Base4_c[n]
                          + alpha_Trt * Trt_c[n]
                          + alpha_BT  * BT_c[n]   //log(Base) * trt
                          + alpha_Age * log_Age_c[n]
                          + b1[n] + alpha_V4 * V4_c + b[n]);
  }

My confusion comes in the last line.  There are 59 * 4 observations, with no missing values, and I am assuming that a (perhaps virtual) 59 * 4 matrix of predictors for each subject is being created.  I assume that a 59 * 4 length y vector is being created for each patient and each visit.  Since R and STAN go by column major order, the y vector holds the value for the first visit for each patient, then for the second visit for each patient, and so forth.  No problem with the vectors for the various columns of of patient level data.  Each column is just repeated four times, lining up correctly with the y's.  But the V4_c  variable is only length 4.  It should be repeated 59 times, but with as "rep(V4_c, each = 59), rather than as "rep(V4_c, 59) which would assign the indicators for the V4 visit incorrectly.  Since "V4_c" is referenced in the last line without any indices, how does the code know to create a column of "rep(v4_c, each = 59)" rather than rep(V4_c, 59), i.e., the length four V4c vector repeated 59 times?

And am I visualizing correctly how the final design matrix and dependent variable vector are being created?

Thanks in advance for your help with my confusion.

Larry Hunsicker

Dear Bob:

Thanks for your helpful and detailed feedback.

Especially, the following change made a huge difference:

    covY <- quad_form(zmat, covMat)

and

    for (k in 1:nobs)
      covY[k,k] <- covY[k,k] + stdErr;

I did not notice any significant change by changing to the cholesky-factor parameterization; however, this may be due to the structure of my problem.

Much appreciated.

On Wed, Jun 10, 2015 at 2:02 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Our advice for coding covariance priors for random effects is
> in the regression chapter of the manual.  Short answer is that you
> want to move to a Cholesky-factor parameterization for both speed
> and stability.
>
> You can also just use 0 for meanFixef rather than making a vector
> of copies of 0 --- Stan will broadcast the 0 for you automatically.
>
> You don't need to define mu or covRanef as transformed params --- you
> can move those into the model block as local variables because you
> probably don't want to save them separately.
>
> There's not much you can do about Stan's clunky block and segment
> functions if you're coding up ragged arrays.
>
> You can increase the regularization of correlations by upping the
> parameter to the LKJ density --- that can help condition correlation
> matrices (e.g., avoiding correlation 1 answers).
>
> You can also look at what happens with sclRanef --- if those are
> getting crazy big values, you can swap the Cauchy out for a normal
> to keep things better controlled.
>
> Finally, this line's very inefficient:
>
>     covY <- (zmat * covMat) * zmat' + stdErr * diag_matrix(rep_vector(1.0, rows(zmat)));
>
> What you want (assuming zmat is symmetric) is
>
>     covY <- quad_form(zmat, covMat)
>
> and
>
>     for (k in 1:nobs)
>       covY[k,k] <- covY[k,k] + stdErr;
>
> The former does the gradients much more efficiently and the latter
> avoids constructing a huge matrix and adding a bunch of zeroes (which
> isn't itself so expensive, but it sucks up time in the gradient calcs,
> which are more costly).
>
> - Bob

Bob:
My apologies for being unclear in my last post.  Let me try to ask my question in a way that I hope is closer to correct.  b1 is intended to be the patient level residual and b the residual patient * visit residual, to account for extra Poisson variability.  Neither of these is an input value.  They are both declared to be draws from normal 0 mean distributions with sd's = sigma_b1 and sigma_b, respectively.
My question is not how these values are fit by STAN, but only about how STAN knows that b1 is the patient level residual and b the patient by visit residual.  My guess is that this is because b1 is declared OUTSIDE of the do-loop, so that it sees that it has N levels, whereas b is declared INSIDE of the do-loop, so that it sees that, at each level of N, there are four (visit) levels.  I think that this is corroborated by the fact that at each draw, STAN draws N sample values for b1, but N * 4 values for b.
At this point of my STAN learning curve, I don't need to know how STAN figures out the densities.  That comes later after I have made more progress through Gelman et al.  All I need to understand better today is how to code this sort of nested mixed model correctly.
Again, thanks for your help, your availability, and (I hope) your patience with me.
Larry

On Tuesday, June 16, 2015 at 7:28:02 PM UTC-4, Larry Hunsicker wrote:
> My question is not how these values are fit by STAN, but only about how STAN knows that b1 is the patient level residual and b the patient by visit residual.  My guess is that this is because b1 is declared OUTSIDE of the do-loop, so that it sees that it has N levels, whereas b is declared INSIDE of the do-loop, so that it sees that, at each level of N, there are four (visit) levels.  I think that this is corroborated by the fact that at each draw, STAN draws N sample values for b1, but N * 4 values for b.

What Bob was saying is that Stan (unlike BUGS) does not infer the number of elements in b and b1 from whether they are outside or inside some loop but simply accepts the dimensions that the user declares in the Stan program. In the epil example,

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stan-dev/example-models/master/bugs_examples/vol1/epil/epil.stan

we have in the parameters block

...
real  b1[N];
vector[T] b[N];
...

so b1 has N elements and b has T * N elements regardless of what goes on in the subsequent blocks.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Dear list:

My question is about using Laplace approximation of the GLMM likelihood in user-defined function.

My question is very similar to the problem/solution posed/answered here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Max-Marginal-Optimization-(lmer)-Design

Following Bob's convention, if I assume 'alpha' to be the random effect, 'phi' to be the fixed effect, 'p(y | phi, alpha)' to be a member of the exponential family in

p(phi | y) = INTEGRAL p(phi,alpha | y) d.alpha,

then I can interpret 'log p(phi | y)' as the contribution of an individual to the log-likelihood in GLMMs.  Bob proposes a very general approach to solve this problem in Stan, but my problem is very structured.  To make the discussion concrete, in my case (with notational abuse)
p(phi,alpha | y)  = p1(y | alpha, phi) p2(alpha | Sigma),

where p1 is the Bernoulli likelihood with

prob_success = 1 / [1 + exp{ - (x_t' * phi + z_t' * alpha)}]

and p2 is Multivariate Normal density with mean 0 and covariance matrix Sigma.  If I was in R, then for a given value of 'phi', 'Sigma', and 'y' I know how to find the Laplace approximation for the INTEGRAL p(phi,alpha | y) d.alpha:
(based on McCulloch & Searle 2001; pp 282)
1. calculate the gradient
2. calculate the Hessian
3. use Fisher scoring or optim
4. plug the optimum in the expression for Laplace approximation, which is analytically tractable.

I can also do this in Rstan by using the 'optimizing' function; however, my needs are a bit different.

I want to generate random variables with the likelihood obtained after Laplace approximation. Specifically, I want define a function

functions {
  // takes care of the modified likelihood for one individual; assume I have sample size 1 currently.
  real laplace_approx_log (vector y, vector phi, matrix Sigma, vector startVal) {
        // return the result of 4. (i.e., analytic expression for Laplace approximation evaluated at the optimum with 'startVal' as starting value)
  }

and use it later as

model {
   ...
   y ~ laplace_approx(phi, Sigma, startVal)  // I would like this function to be free of startVal, but this would work.
}

I see that the 'Point Estimation' section in the manual deals with general optimization problems.

Question: I was wondering if there is a way to use the 'optimizing' function to solve my special problem using Hessians and gradients?  Unless I am missing something obvious, I could not find any documentation related to 'optimizing' in the manual. (I could also implement my own Newton-Raphson in the functions, but it would be amazing if I can use Stan's function.)

Thanks for your time and patience,

B.

On Wednesday, June 17, 2015 at 6:56:10 PM UTC-4, Larry Hunsicker wrote:
> Based on yesterday's discussion, I thought that I understood that the prior for b: "b[n] ~ normal(0, sigma_b);" could be put pretty much anywhere, since the shape of b had been set by its earlier declaration in the parameters section.

It is true that the dimensions of b are declared in the parameters section, but a for-loop in Stan

  for(n in 1:N) {

    b[n] ~ normal(0, sigma_b);

    ...

works like a for-loop in any other language. Here it indicates that the n-th element of b --- which happens to be a vector of length T in this case --- has a prior on its elements that is iid normal with mean zero and standard deviation sigma_b.
If you put anything involving b[n] outside the for loop, Stan wouldn't know what n refers to.
b[N][K] ~ normal(0, sigma_b) does not make much sense because it puts the normal(0, sigma_b) prior only on the N,K element and does not put a proper prior on any of the other elements (which is why it took a long time to sample)

There are some ways that this could be improved upon:
Delete the line that says b[n] ~ normal(0, sigma_b); and add (outside the for loop) the line to_array_1d(b) ~ normal(0, sigma_b);. This concatenates all the elements of b into a one-dimensional array and asserts the prior is iid normal with mean 0 and standard deviation sigma_b.
Delete the line that says b[n] ~ normal(0, sigma_b); and the line that says b1 ~ normal(0, sigma_b1); Add (outside the for loop) the line to_array_1d(b) ~ normal(0, 1); and the line b1 ~ normal(0,1). Finally, change the last line of the likelihood to say + b1[n] * sigma_b1 + alpha_V4 * V4_c + b[n] * sigma_b); . This basically redefines b[n] and b1 to be standard normal shifts that are scaled by the unknowns sigma_b and sigma_b1 respectively, which often improves the efficiency of the sampling by reducing the dependence between these unknown parameters.

You can always print things to the screen if you are having trouble understanding the structure:

print("b is");
for(n in 1:N) print(b[n]);
but something like that is best called in diagnostic mode (in R with test_grad = TRUE and chains = 1) so that you only see it once rather than millions of times.

Ben

Another STAN newbie question.
I was looking at the documentation for the parameter list for STAN and finally read the init information carefully.  In BUGS you have to supply your inits, and for better or for worse, many times the inits for all of the chains are the same.  But one should really want a variety of (credible) inits to be sure that one is not finding only a local maximum.  I saw that with STAN, if the init is not defined, the default is "random," defined as "randomly generated by STAN," presumably on "the unconstrained support."
This sounds exactly like what one would want to use as differing inits for multiple chains.  Does this imply that, barring a special situation, one would do better to invoke STAN without a specified init?  Sounds pretty neat to me.
Larry Hunsicker

Hi Bob:

Sorry to be unclear.

"What's the statistical operation you want to perform where
you need a Laplace approximation?  Is it just because
you want a max marginal likelihood estimate?  If so, you're probably
better of sticking with lme4 until we get all that working in Stan."

I would like to find the likelihood of 'phi' (fixed effects) and 'Sigma' (the covariance matrix for random effects).  As you correctly point, this is just the likelihood after marginalizing the random effects; however, unlike Lme4, I am not interested in maximizing the likelihood of 'phi' and 'Sigma'.  I am interested in sampling when the likelihood is modified as

myLogLikelihood = nrep * marginalLogLikelihood // marginal LogLikelihood is what lme4 maximizes and would use with a usual GLMM...

In a Gaussian LMM, the marginaLogLikelihood is also a normal, so I was able to get this to work with Stan [very nicely actually; see code below].  For the non-Gaussian case, one needs to approximate the integral and I chose laplace approximation as quadrature would be slow. The laplace approx. part was attached in the stan file earlier. I think it works correctly, but I am not sure how to increase the speed.

May be I am doing something ridiculously stupid and I am not able to catch my error.

Thanks again for your time.

Best,
B.

functions {
  // takes care of the modified likelihood

  real marg_approx_log (vector y, vector mu, real stdErr, matrix covMat, matrix zmat, real nrep) {
    matrix[num_elements(y), num_elements(y)] covY;
    int tmp1; int tmp2;

    covY <- (zmat * covMat) * zmat' + stdErr * diag_matrix(rep_vector(1.0, rows(zmat)));

    return (nrep * multi_normal_log(y, mu, covY));
  }
}

....

model {

  // handle prior for rand. eff. prior and fixed eff.

  for (ii in 1:ngroup) {
    segment(yvec, pos1[ii], pos2[ii] - pos1[ii] + 1) ~ marg_approx(segment(mu, pos1[ii], pos2[ii] - pos1[ii] + 1),
                                                                   stdErr, covRanef,
                                                                   block(zmat, pos1[ii], 1, pos2[ii] - pos1[ii] + 1, nranef),
                                                                   nrep);
  }
}

messages.body_plain:
For speed:

1.  move to Cholesky factorization of the covariance matrix,

2.  compute each study's covariance matrix once and group the
calls to multi_normal by study.

These two steps should provide a substantial speedup.

You also want to replace

   if_else(x - y, 1, 0)

with just

   (x > y)

in Stan.  Similarly for the step() functions.  This isn't a big
deal for efficiency, just clarity.  But what you really want is to use
conditionals:

  mu[n] <- delta[xstudy[n]];
  if (x > y)
    mu[n] <- mu[n] + 1;

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I don't know about these models, but if y's likelihood is
expressed as a normal mixture with latent boolean (discrete --- don't
try in Stan) indicator:

  z[n] ~ bernoulli(theta);

  y[n] ~ normal(mu[z[n]], sigma[z[n]]);

then the likelihood is usually just p(y | mu, z) and it needs to
integrate (sum) out the z[n], to get:

  p(y[n] | mu, z) = theta * normal(y[n] | mu[1], sigma[1])
                  + (1 - theta) * normal(y[n] | mu[2], sigma[2])

So if you have latent parameters per item, they should be marginalized
out for the likelihood.

- Bob

messages.subject: Is there a simple way to query a Graphical Model in Stan?
messages.subject_clean: Is there a simple way to query a Graphical Model in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan users,

I've been playing around with the 'abn' R package for DAG strutcture discovery using GLM and GLMM parametrization. Simply put, the package has algorithms for discovering directed graph structures where each node is either gaussian, binomial or poisson variables and each arc represents a regression between variables (more information here <http://www.r-bayesian-networks.org/>).

It's easy to represent the discovered DAG in Stan and fit it to the data. My problem now is: having a fitted model, how can I query it? Meaning, how can I use the model to retrieve the marginals of a node in the light of some evidence, as classical expert systems (like Nettica, BayesNet, Bayesia, etc)? I know Stan is not build for this kind of query, but is there a simple way to do it?

How I am doing it now with a simple classifier:

Using the Iris dataset and the discovered DAG as a classifier, I exploited the DAG structure and used the sum-product rule to compute the marginals directly in Stan (in 'generated quantities'). The results are fine for this data set: in a random 2/3 train 1/3 test fit, the classifier hardly ever misses.

The attached code should give a rough idea how to discover the model with abn and fit it with Stan. Warning: the code in 'generated quantities' is ugly. Any suggestions on how to improve it?

Thanks!
Erikson

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is there a simple way to query a Graphical Model in Stan?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is there a simple way to query a Graphical Model in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
> On Jun 18, 2015, at 5:28 PM, Erikson Kaszubowski <erik...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Stan users,
>
> I've been playing around with the 'abn' R package for DAG strutcture discovery using GLM and GLMM parametrization. Simply put, the package has algorithms for discovering directed graph structures where each node is either gaussian, binomial or poisson variables and each arc represents a regression between variables (more information here).
>
> It's easy to represent the discovered DAG in Stan and fit it to the data. My problem now is: having a fitted model, how can I query it? Meaning, how can I use the model to retrieve the marginals of a node in the light of some evidence, as classical expert systems (like Nettica, BayesNet, Bayesia, etc)? I know Stan is not build for this kind of query, but is there a simple way to do it?

Actually, that's all Stan is built for:

  Specify a joint log probability function p(theta, y),
  observe y, and take a sample from the posterior p(theta | y).

(We can also do optimization, but I don't think that's relevant here.)

So I'm not quite sure what you're asking because the language
isn't familiar.

The best way to simplify your code would be with functions for
common operations.

But you should never ever use things like

 exp(log(1-inv_logit(sVir_Intercept))

Just replace exp(log(...)) with (...)!

There's also a log_inv_logit function.  and a log1m_inv_logit
for log(1 - inv_logit(x)).

Also, you probably don't want priors as wide as normal(0, 100),
depending on the scale --- but if that's the scale, then you probably
don't want cauchy(0, 5) on the sd.

> How I am doing it now with a simple classifier:
>
> Using the Iris dataset and the discovered DAG as a classifier, I exploited the DAG structure and used the sum-product rule to compute the marginals directly in Stan (in 'generated quantities').

Which marginals are you trying to compute?  It's hard to tell
from the code.

> The results are fine for this data set: in a random 2/3 train 1/3 test fit, the classifier hardly ever misses.

Is there a reason you can't just code the classifier up
in Stan directly?

> The attached code should give a rough idea how to discover the model with abn and fit it with Stan. Warning: the code in 'generated quantities' is ugly. Any suggestions on how to improve it?

Functions.  But I think the whole thing could probably be
rewritten much more straightforwardly if you're just
trying to do classification.  I think what you're doing is the
same as assigning responsibilities in a mixture model --- at least
if you're doing the usual trick of turning a mixture model into
a classifier.

- Bob
