messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is there a simple way to query a Graphical Model in Stan?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is there a simple way to query a Graphical Model in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Bob,

I'm interested in making a query in the sense of the use of Bayesian Networks in expert systems (like the 'Asia' BUGS model, HUGIN-style, or the classical Sprinkler-Rain graphical model), as discussed in Koller and Friedman's "Probabilistic Graphical Models", chapter 9.
In my case, instead of using conditional distribution tables, as usual in those models, I'm modeling conditional distributions as GLMs, as suggested by the 'additive bayesian network' package.

I'm using Stan to represent and fit the parameters of the DAG discovered by the 'abn' package. I want to use the fitted parameters to query the marginal probabilities of specific nodes, given the evidence in other nodes. E.g., using a sug-graph from the attached model:

Speciesversicolor(SVE) -> Petal.Width(PW) <- Speciesvirginica(SVI)

In this simple sub-graph, the joint distribution is given by:

P(SVE, PW, SVI) = P(SVE)P(SVI)P(PW|SVE,SVI)

If a have a piece of evidence about petal width, I would like to know the updated probabilities of the parent nodes. Suppose I have the information that the petal width with mean value (0 for standardized data). What is the prob. it's an Iris Versicolor?

The priors on SVE and SVI are given by the first level logistic regression. As parent nodes, those regression have just an intercept: -.49 and -.72 in one version of the fitted model, or P(SVI=1) = inv_logit(-.49) = 0.38; P(SVE=0) = 1 - inv_logit(-.72) = 0.67.
The conditional probability for the child node is given by the linear regression PW = Intercept + B1*SVE + B2*SVI + error, so: P(PW=0|SVE=0,SVI=1) = dnorm(0, mean=-1.26 + 2.37*1 + 1.44*0, sd=0.27). So the joint is:

P(SVE=1, SVI, PW=0) = (0.38 * 0.67 * 0.00031) + (0.38 * 0.33 * 0) ### Marginalizing over SVI, normalize for P(SVE=1|PW=0)

I don't know if I made it clerarer now.

Thanks for the modeling tips! I'm using exp(log ()) because I'm summing over various log-probabilities and only then exponentiating. I want to compute the marginals for the nodes that represent the species, using the evidence from the other nodes.

I understand that it would be easier to just use a classifier for this purpose (in this example, a simple linear discriminant analysis or a naive bayes), but I'm doing it this way to understand the 'additional bayesian networks' better.

Erikson

Em quinta-feira, 18 de junho de 2015 20:17:04 UTC-3, Bob Carpenter escreveu:
>
> > On Jun 18, 2015, at 5:28 PM, Erikson Kaszubowski <erik...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear Stan users,
> >
> > I've been playing around with the 'abn' R package for DAG strutcture discovery using GLM and GLMM parametrization. Simply put, the package has algorithms for discovering directed graph structures where each node is either gaussian, binomial or poisson variables and each arc represents a regression between variables (more information here).
> >
> > It's easy to represent the discovered DAG in Stan and fit it to the data. My problem now is: having a fitted model, how can I query it? Meaning, how can I use the model to retrieve the marginals of a node in the light of some evidence, as classical expert systems (like Nettica, BayesNet, Bayesia, etc)? I know Stan is not build for this kind of query, but is there a simple way to do it?
>
> Actually, that's all Stan is built for:
>
>   Specify a joint log probability function p(theta, y),
>   observe y, and take a sample from the posterior p(theta | y).
>
> (We can also do optimization, but I don't think that's relevant here.)
>
> So I'm not quite sure what you're asking because the language
> isn't familiar.
>
> The best way to simplify your code would be with functions for
> common operations.
>
> But you should never ever use things like
>
>  exp(log(1-inv_logit(sVir_Intercept))
>
> Just replace exp(log(...)) with (...)!
>
> There's also a log_inv_logit function.  and a log1m_inv_logit
> for log(1 - inv_logit(x)).
>
> Also, you probably don't want priors as wide as normal(0, 100),
> depending on the scale --- but if that's the scale, then you probably
> don't want cauchy(0, 5) on the sd.
>
> > How I am doing it now with a simple classifier:
> >
> > Using the Iris dataset and the discovered DAG as a classifier, I exploited the DAG structure and used the sum-product rule to compute the marginals directly in Stan (in 'generated quantities').
>
> Which marginals are you trying to compute?  It's hard to tell
> from the code.
>
> > The results are fine for this data set: in a random 2/3 train 1/3 test fit, the classifier hardly ever misses.
>
> Is there a reason you can't just code the classifier up
> in Stan directly?
>
> > The attached code should give a rough idea how to discover the model with abn and fit it with Stan. Warning: the code in 'generated quantities' is ugly. Any suggestions on how to improve it?
>
> Functions.  But I think the whole thing could probably be
> rewritten much more straightforwardly if you're just
> trying to do classification.  I think what you're doing is the
> same as assigning responsibilities in a mixture model --- at least
> if you're doing the usual trick of turning a mixture model into
> a classifier.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it better to invoke STAN with no defined set of inits?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is it better to invoke STAN with no defined set of inits?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I am very often in the situation that the priors limits the sensible range in which to initialize - would be possible to let Stan choose inits based on quantiles of the prior? That is I would love to specify that I want random inits out of the 99.9% prob mass region on the constrained scale (whatever that means on the unconstrained one).

This would be very useful for  complex non-linear models which are only locally defined and simply need sane inits.

Best,
Sebastian

On Thursday, June 18, 2015 at 10:09:49 PM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Supplying inits can also help when a model has strong priors.  For example if you have a parameter theta whose prior is concentrated between -0.1 and +0.1, it can be a problem to start it with uniform inits on (-2,2).
>
> > On Jun 18, 2015, at 1:15 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > Yes.  Because we can map unconstrained params back to constrained,
> > we can do init uniformly on (-2,2) on the unconstrained scale for
> > each chain and then map back to constrained.  The description of how
> > all those transforms work is a chapter in the manual.
> >
> > If models are really complex, it can help to give it inits.
> >
> > I believe BUGS will do automatic inits for you, as will JAGS, but
> > JAGS does them the same deterministic way for each chain --- I don't
> > know what BUGS does.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >> On Jun 18, 2015, at 11:41 AM, Larry Hunsicker <lhuns...@mchsi.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> Another STAN newbie question.
> >> I was looking at the documentation for the parameter list for STAN and finally read the init information carefully.  In BUGS you have to supply your inits, and for better or for worse, many times the inits for all of the chains are the same.  But one should really want a variety of (credible) inits to be sure that one is not finding only a local maximum.  I saw that with STAN, if the init is not defined, the default is "random," defined as "randomly generated by STAN," presumably on "the unconstrained support."
> >> This sounds exactly like what one would want to use as differing inits for multiple chains.  Does this imply that, barring a special situation, one would do better to invoke STAN without a specified init?  Sounds pretty neat to me.
> >> Larry Hunsicker

> Hi!

> I am very often in the situation that the priors limits the sensible range in which to initialize - would be possible to let Stan choose inits based on quantiles of the prior? That is I would love to specify that I want random inits out of the 99.9% prob mass region on the constrained scale (whatever that means on the unconstrained one).
>
> This would be very useful for  complex non-linear models which are only locally defined and simply need sane inits.
>
> Best,
> Sebastian
>
> On Thursday, June 18, 2015 at 10:09:49 PM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Supplying inits can also help when a model has strong priors.  For example if you have a parameter theta whose prior is concentrated between -0.1 and +0.1, it can be a problem to start it with uniform inits on (-2,2).
>
> > On Jun 18, 2015, at 1:15 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > Yes.  Because we can map unconstrained params back to constrained,
> > we can do init uniformly on (-2,2) on the unconstrained scale for

> > If models are really complex, it can help to give it inits.

> On Jun 18, 2015, at 10:03 PM, Erikson Kaszubowski <erik...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Bob,
>
> I'm interested in making a query in the sense of the use of Bayesian Networks in expert systems (like the 'Asia' BUGS model, HUGIN-style, or the classical Sprinkler-Rain graphical model), as discussed in Koller and Friedman's "Probabilistic Graphical Models", chapter 9.
> In my case, instead of using conditional distribution tables, as usual in those models, I'm modeling conditional distributions as GLMs, as suggested by the 'additive bayesian network' package.

I'm afraid I don't know any of this material.

> I'm using Stan to represent and fit the parameters of the DAG discovered by the 'abn' package. I want to use the fitted parameters to query the marginal probabilities of specific nodes, given the evidence in other nodes.

> E.g., using a sug-graph from the attached model:
>
> Speciesversicolor(SVE) -> Petal.Width(PW) <- Speciesvirginica(SVI)

I don't understand this notation.  What is Speciesversicolor() do
as a wrapper?

> In this simple sub-graph, the joint distribution is given by:
>
> P(SVE, PW, SVI) = P(SVE)P(SVI)P(PW|SVE,SVI)

> If a have a piece of evidence about petal width, I would like to know the updated probabilities of the parent nodes. Suppose I have the information that the petal width with mean value (0 for standardized data). What is the prob. it's an Iris Versicolor?

I'm a bit confused, though, because SVE and SVI look like
species indicators.  How can they both be variables?

I'd think there'd be one boolean variable z[i] that would
indicate with z[i] = 0 if item i is plant type 1 and z[i] = 1
if item i is plant type 2.  Then you'd condition things like
the observables on the type of plant.  Then the problem's
a simple classification.

> The priors on SVE and SVI

I don't know what that means, either.

> are given by the first level logistic regression. As parent nodes, those regression have just an intercept: -.49 and -.72 in one version of the fitted model, or P(SVI=1) = inv_logit(-.49) = 0.38; P(SVE=0) = 1 - inv_logit(-.72) = 0.67.
> The conditional probability for the child node is given by the linear regression PW = Intercept + B1*SVE + B2*SVI + error, so: P(PW=0|SVE=0,SVI=1) = dnorm(0, mean=-1.26 + 2.37*1 + 1.44*0, sd=0.27). So the joint is:
>
> P(SVE=1, SVI, PW=0) = (0.38 * 0.67 * 0.00031) + (0.38 * 0.33 * 0) ### Marginalizing over SVI, normalize for P(SVE=1|PW=0)

> I don't know if I made it clerarer now.

A bit, but I'm still very confused.  Is it consistent to have
SVE=1 and SVI=1?  or SVE=0 and SVI=0?  And what's this B1 and B2 variable
that gets introduced?

> Thanks for the modeling tips! I'm using exp(log ()) because I'm summing over various log-probabilities and only then exponentiating. I want to compute the marginals for the nodes that represent the species, using the evidence from the other nodes.

No matter what your intent, you never ever ever want to use exp(log())
or log(exp()) or any other pair of inverse functions applied to each other.
It'll only hurt your speed and arithmetic precision and robustness.

> I understand that it would be easier to just use a classifier for this purpose (in this example, a simple linear discriminant analysis or a naive bayes), but I'm doing it this way to understand the 'additional bayesian networks' better.

I just meant build the classifier in Stan.  I think that's
what you're trying to do, we're just not communicating notationally.

What I want to see is:

  data y:  variable types and dimensions and constraints

  parameters theta:  ditto

  joint probablity function: p(y, theta)

At that point, all the inference you want to do is turn-the-crank.

- Bob

> I totally agree with you, but may be I am trying to do this because I don't know how to use Stan well.  This is what I want to do:
>
> 1. Generate random error:  stdErr ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> 2. Generate random effect covariance matrix:
>      matrix[nranef, nranef] covRanef;
>       sclRanef ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
>       corrRanef ~ lkj_corr(2);
>        covRanef <- quad_form_diag(corrRanef, sclRanef);
> 3. Generate random effects:
>   for (ii in 1:ngroup) {
>     ranef[ii] ~ multi_normal(meanRanef, covRanef);
>   }
>
> 4. Generate fixed effects:
>   stdErrFixef ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
>   fixef ~ normal(meanFixef, stdErrFixef);
>
> Steps 1-4 are usual GLMM steps, but the last step that samples data is different.
>
> 5. I want to draw data 'y' from a normal / bernoulli distribution raised to the power 'nrep'. For normal everything is tractable, so I can compare the results of Stan
>
>   real yHat[nobs];
>   for (ii in 1:nobs) {
>     yHat[ii] <- xmat[ii] * fixef + zmat[ii] * ranef[group[ii]]; // individual level mean
>   }
>
>   // sample data
>   yvec ~ normal(yHat, stdErr / nrep)  // is dividing by nrep correct (?) if my likelihood is normal likelihood raised to a power .. This seems to be true for the conditional

Dividing by nrep is not correct.  If you want to raise the normal
density to a power, you have to multiply on the log scale,
as in:

  increment_log_prob(nrep * normal_log(yvec, yHat, stderr)

If some of the values yvec, yHat, or stderr are unknown, just
declare them as parameters.

In this way, we can do any kind of weighted regression (or other
model) you want, right in Stan.

Not quite sure why you'd want to do this other than if you're doing
something like EM or have importance weights or something from the
outside.

- Bob

Just to emphasize this:  In a Stan model, there’s just the log-posterior.  There’s no “prior.”  If we do the graphical models wrapper, that’s another story.
But setting inits isn’t so hard!

Bob:  I assume that the user can set inits for some parameters and Stan will set inits for the others?  Or is it all or nothing?

> On Jun 19, 2015, at 2:43 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> There's no way of marking (at least yet and probably not
> in the foreseeable future) what the prior is.
>
> What we'd like to do (again, not going to happen soon) is
> have an init block written in the Stan language.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Jun 19, 2015, at 6:38 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Hi!
>>
>> I am very often in the situation that the priors limits the sensible range in which to initialize - would be possible to let Stan choose inits based on quantiles of the prior? That is I would love to specify that I want random inits out of the 99.9% prob mass region on the constrained scale (whatever that means on the unconstrained one).
>>
>> This would be very useful for  complex non-linear models which are only locally defined and simply need sane inits.
>>
>> Best,
>> Sebastian
>>
>> On Thursday, June 18, 2015 at 10:09:49 PM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>> Supplying inits can also help when a model has strong priors.  For example if you have a parameter theta whose prior is concentrated between -0.1 and +0.1, it can be a problem to start it with uniform inits on (-2,2).
>>
>>> On Jun 18, 2015, at 1:15 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> Yes.  Because we can map unconstrained params back to constrained,
>>> we can do init uniformly on (-2,2) on the unconstrained scale for
>>> each chain and then map back to constrained.  The description of how
>>> all those transforms work is a chapter in the manual.
>>>
>>> If models are really complex, it can help to give it inits.
>>>
>>> I believe BUGS will do automatic inits for you, as will JAGS, but
>>> JAGS does them the same deterministic way for each chain --- I don't
>>> know what BUGS does.
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>> On Jun 18, 2015, at 11:41 AM, Larry Hunsicker <lhuns...@mchsi.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> Another STAN newbie question.
>>>> I was looking at the documentation for the parameter list for STAN and finally read the init information carefully.  In BUGS you have to supply your inits, and for better or for worse, many times the inits for all of the chains are the same.  But one should really want a variety of (credible) inits to be sure that one is not finding only a local maximum.  I saw that with STAN, if the init is not defined, the default is "random," defined as "randomly generated by STAN," presumably on "the unconstrained support."
>>>> This sounds exactly like what one would want to use as differing inits for multiple chains.  Does this imply that, barring a special situation, one would do better to invoke STAN without a specified init?  Sounds pretty neat to me.
>>>> Larry Hunsicker

messages.subject: Permutation of posterior draws and autocorrelation
messages.subject_clean: Permutation of posterior draws and autocorrelation
messages.body_plain:
Back again.
I want to be sure that I understand a sentence from Gelman, Carlin, et al, Appendix 3:
"...and they are permuted so that they can be analyzed directly without concerns of autocorrelation."
But if the draws in their original order are autocorrelated (which they are likely to be), then permuting them won't change the fact that the draws aren't independent.  Unless we are actually looking for autocorrelation (or, equivalently, plotting results against "draw N"), the results of most statistical analyses won't care what the order of the posterior draws was.   Autocorrelation is taken into account in estimation of the effective sample size, and this, in turn, is used to assess MCMC error.  What about the actual parameter estimates themselves?  I imagine that, given a long enough chain, the draws do ultimately cover the distribution in a representative fashion.  That is, even if close up there is autocorrelation, the paths, broken down into pieces, are effectively random paths through the distribution space.
Am I close to correct in the above?
Larry Hunsicker

messages.body_plain:
I see. Would it be possible to, let's say, run the optimizer on a model for a limited number of iteration steps, then add some random noise to the result and use that?

To make this happen from the interfaces is control over the iteration steps in the optimizers, but certainly this is better done internally inside Stan as it can more easily operate on the unconstrained scale. Maybe this is worth a ticket to track for the future?

The downside is that this approach is that it assumes roughly equal scales of all variables, but this is anyway a recommended way of writing models...

Sebastian

On Jun 21, 2015, at 4:15 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I see. Would it be possible to, let's say, run the optimizer on a model for a limited number of iteration steps, then add some random noise to the result and use that?

Yes.  You want the noise for diffuse inits?  Because you've
probably already lost the ability to detect multimodality unless
the whole operation of optimization plus sampling gets replicated
from differing optimization inits.

I'm hoping that the variational inference will be better for
inits like this --- it won't get tripped up by models with no posterior
mode (hence no MLE), like most clustering or hierarchical models.

> To make this happen from the interfaces is control over the iteration steps in the optimizers,

What kind of control are you looking for?  You can set the max
number of steps externally.

> but certainly this is better done internally inside Stan as it can more easily operate on the unconstrained scale.

You mean avoiding the roundtrip of constraining for the answer
of optimization and then unconstraining to form the init in Stan?
I think that cost will be negligible compared to everything else and
will also be something we want to inspect on the constrained scale.

> Maybe this is worth a ticket to track for the future?

If you have a concrete behavior to suggest, it should be
a feature request issue.  If it's a more general line of inquiry
that requires more research, it should go in our wiki of future
to-do items (I can give you editing permission if you don't have it).

> The downside is that this approach is that it assumes roughly equal scales of all variables, but this is anyway a recommended way of writing models...

What assumes equal scales?

- Bob

Hello All,

I have recently implemented an unsupervised HMM in Stan very successfully.  In the manual a fully unsupervised HMM is not discussed except to say that the posterior is typically very multi-modal.  Having read this I am surprised I got it to work so well.  I am writing this post for three reasons:

1) If anyone is interested in the model then an example is attached
2) To get feedback on whether other more experienced Stan users and better statisticians than myself are surprised I got it to work - is there something about my case that makes it work?
3) To get feedback on the model in general - is there anything I could do to make it more efficient

I ran my model using rstan in R.  I attach the R script.  The script is completely self-contained.  The model is running on simulated data.

My data is a large number (1000) of short timeseries (length=10).  I have two latent groups.  The data emitted at each timestep is normal with different parameters for the two groups.  I have specified time invariant transition probabilities.  I am interested in estimates of the model parameters (likelihood parameters, transition probabilities and prior for the first timestep) and group membership for each timestep of each timeseries.

My strategy is to embed the forward-backward algorithm in the transformed parameters block.  From this block I keep the estimates of group membership (because I am interested in them) and the one-step prediction probabilities from the forward algorithm (which I need to increment the log_probability).

Hopefully this is clear.  I suspect my coding of the forward-backward algorithm might be a bit non-standard.  It certainly could be made more general (e.g. I have hard-coded in two groups which is all I will ever need for this project).

Thanks,

Jon.

messages.body_plain:
Andrew --- do you have any general guidelines
on starting points?  I see lots of examples around where people
use some kind of rough point estimate to intialize.

Our uniform(-2,2) unconstrained was just pulled out of
thin air, though if you started at the mean of a unit
normal, it'd give you a uniform draw from the marginal 95%
interval.

But correlation and dimensionality will kill you quickly.
A multivariate normal with high correlation means that
marginal uniform(-2,2) thing puts you way out in the tails.

If you knew what the posterior was, would it matter where
you started in the typical set?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it better to invoke STAN with no defined set of inits?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is it better to invoke STAN with no defined set of inits?
messages.body_plain:
I believe the original Gelman-Rubin (1992) paper on R-hat suggests a heuristic which is similar in spirit to what Sebastian describes. That is, you find “all” of the local optima using something such as EM, then build a mixture of t-distributions where each is centered at the local optima and whose variance is given by an approximation of the inverse Fisher information evaluated at that point. To run M chains, you sample N>M points from the mixture of t’s, and then apply sequential importance resampling to refine the N points to get M of them.

This was in fact a point Don was interested in hearing more about, because I recall Andrew mentioned something about this no longer being necessary when I was presenting the paper in Don’s missing data seminar. My guess is that the problem is the time it takes to find “all” of the local optima.

Slightly related: there is also work by Chuanhai Liu and Don (1996, 2002) on Markov normal-based analysis in order to define “restarting distributions”, which propose a better distribution to restart one’s chains as they run. It’s also computationally efficient because it’s just MLE on normal approximations.

Dustin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it better to invoke STAN with no defined set of inits?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is it better to invoke STAN with no defined set of inits?
messages.body_plain:
Let’s all step back and review the basics.  We want to compute expectations
with respect to the posterior, which means finding neighborhoods in parameter space
which dominate the contribution to the respective integrals.  We colloquially call
these neighborhoods components of the “typical set”.  Markov Chain Monte Carlo
is essentially a method for discovering (convergence) and then exploring (mixing)
the typical set of a complicated posterior distribution.

Convergence to a component of the typical set is made difficult when the tails of
the posterior of pathological.  For example, the posterior density can be expensive
to compute (a la stiff ODEs) or the tails can be so heavy that the chains simply
don’t have enough information to find the typical set in any finite time (a la Cauchy
tails).  The immediate solution is to not start in the tails, which amounts to starting
in the typical set which is exactly what we do not know how to do.

What about trying to seed from a mode?  Well modes are tricky because of the
parameterization dependence — in some parameterizations they can be closer
to the typical set than in others — but in general there’s no guarantee they offer
better initial conditions.  In fact, a good Markov chain will find the typical set in about
the same time that the optimizer will find a mode — subject to the usual regularity
conditions (which we need for finite-time MCMC estimators anyways) the convergence
time is on the order of the mixing time.  This ignores parameter-dependent transition
costs (i.e. ODEs becoming stiff in the tails), but those costs affect optimization just
as much as they affect the chains.

Our adaptation can mess up this intuition a bit, but that’s why I included an initial
convergence window in the adaptation — we converge for a few iterations with a
unit metric before beginning to learn a diagonal/dense one.  If there are serious
convergence issues it may very well be prescient to increase the size of this
initial window.

To summarize, convergence shouldn’t take much longer than optimization.  Similarly,
any “restarting distribution” will be fundamentally limited because by the time you’ve
constructed a good one you already have enough information to construct your MCMC
estimators.  For example, if you want to initialize with EM then what initial conditions
do you choose for the EM algorithm?  You’re not solving the problem, just sweeping
it under the rug of another step.  Moreover, a good initialization or restarting distribution
won’t be all that helpful for multimodal posteriors given that finding all of the modes
will be incredibly difficult and even if you could find them all then you still have to be
able to weight them appropriately in order to construct a valid MCMC transition
(which means computing local evidences which means you need more than a
simple Markov chain).

Thanks Bob, I'll have a look.
Though the negative binomial (and hence the dispersion parameter) may not be the issue here. As Aki mentioned  the ZINB seems to produce 'reasonable' estimates of p_waic and p_loo but the zero inflate poisson - the model with no over dispersion parameter has very large values.

I'm really not sure why the WAIC calculations are off in the ZIP. but phi in the negative binomial appears to be important so the ZINB is probably the better model to use.

On Friday, 19 June 2015 05:10:04 UTC+10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I don't know about these models, but if y's likelihood is
> expressed as a normal mixture with latent boolean (discrete --- don't
> try in Stan) indicator:
>
>   z[n] ~ bernoulli(theta);
>
>   y[n] ~ normal(mu[z[n]], sigma[z[n]]);
>
> then the likelihood is usually just p(y | mu, z) and it needs to
> integrate (sum) out the z[n], to get:
>
>   p(y[n] | mu, z) = theta * normal(y[n] | mu[1], sigma[1])
>                   + (1 - theta) * normal(y[n] | mu[2], sigma[2])
>
> So if you have latent parameters per item, they should be marginalized
> out for the likelihood.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: Mixture model & priors
messages.body_plain:
I think this is a case of label switching. In the second model, theta (approximately) equals 1-theta from the first model. Also, the order of magnitude of the standard errors of the two mixture components have switched. The cause is the use of rather wide priors in the second model (relative to the first model), which allow for multimodality in the posterior (and thus, label switching).

It may or may not be coincidence that in the second model, all three chains explored the area around the same mode.

Anyway, in the second model I would adopt more informative priors for sda, sdb, and SD2 that reflect your knowledge about the second source of error being larger than the first (a Cauchy prior is rather vague). E.g.:
sda ~ normal(0, 3)
sdb ~  normal(0, 0.1)
SD2 ~ normal(0, 10)

By the way, you can drop the truncation terms in the second model ("T[,]"), as the parameters of the prior are fixed (and thus also is the adjustment of the posterior, which we can therefore ignore).

messages.body_plain:
In general, you can use print statements to debug where things
go wrong.  I don't see how the normal could fail, but you
could underflow or overflow and run into problems with softmax.

Could you try init=0 and see if that works?  It will initialize
the matrix of coefficients to 0 and should prevent initial overflow.

Also, it's more stable to write this:

 for (n in 1:numData)
    y[n] ~ categorical(softmax(beta[label[n]] * x[n]));

as

 for (n in 1:numData)

    y[n] ~ categorical_logit(beta[label[n]] * x[n]);

We can save a round trip exp and log in the middle that helps
prevent some overflow/underflow.

I don't see anywhere your program could get tripped up by
indexing.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it better to invoke STAN with no defined set of inits?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is it better to invoke STAN with no defined set of inits?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks.  I'm embarassed to say I've never read the original papers.

The problem is that we have so many models that don't have
local optima.  I think that's why Sebastian was suggesting "early
stopping" as it's known in the machine learning world (a procedural
approximation of a kind of regularization).  That is, stop before
convergence to avoid params getting extreme values.

Assuming we approximate the Fisher info matrix somehow (say by
a smoothed Hessian as in Betancourt's SoftAbs metric), then we
still have the problem of O(N^2) entries for N dimensions, which
quickly becomes problematic for problems with thousands of parameters.

But the problem for me is that I don't see how to deal with correlation
without doing something like this.

Low rank approximations, perhaps?  It's something we have to think about
for Riemannian HMC, too --- whether we can get somethin in between a diagonal
and dense metric that's more useful than diagonal but easier to compute
than the dense metric.

- Bob

> On Jun 22, 2015, at 1:56 AM, Dustin Tran <dustinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I believe the original Gelman-Rubin (1992) paper on R-hat suggests a heuristic which is similar in spirit to what Sebastian describes. That is, you find “all” of the local optima using something such as EM, then build a mixture of t-distributions where each is centered at the local optima and whose variance is given by an approximation of the inverse Fisher information evaluated at that point. To run M chains, you sample N>M points from the mixture of t’s, and then apply sequential importance resampling to refine the N points to get M of them.
>
> This was in fact a point Don was interested in hearing more about, because I recall Andrew mentioned something about this no longer being necessary when I was presenting the paper in Don’s missing data seminar. My guess is that the problem is the time it takes to find “all” of the local optima.
>
> Slightly related: there is also work by Chuanhai Liu and Don (1996, 2002) on Markov normal-based analysis in order to define “restarting distributions”, which propose a better distribution to restart one’s chains as they run. It’s also computationally efficient because it’s just MLE on normal approximations.
>
> Dustin

messages.body_plain:
Better to have init’d and lost than to never have init’d at all.

More seriously, I think we can often get reasonable starting points based on priors.  This is something we should think more about when we do the graphical-models wrapper.

> On Jun 22, 2015, at 3:34 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Let’s all step back and review the basics.  We want to compute expectations
> with respect to the posterior, which means finding neighborhoods in parameter space
> which dominate the contribution to the respective integrals.  We colloquially call
> these neighborhoods components of the “typical set”.  Markov Chain Monte Carlo
> is essentially a method for discovering (convergence) and then exploring (mixing)
> the typical set of a complicated posterior distribution.
>
> Convergence to a component of the typical set is made difficult when the tails of
> the posterior of pathological.  For example, the posterior density can be expensive
> to compute (a la stiff ODEs) or the tails can be so heavy that the chains simply
> don’t have enough information to find the typical set in any finite time (a la Cauchy
> tails).  The immediate solution is to not start in the tails, which amounts to starting
> in the typical set which is exactly what we do not know how to do.
>
> What about trying to seed from a mode?  Well modes are tricky because of the
> parameterization dependence — in some parameterizations they can be closer
> to the typical set than in others — but in general there’s no guarantee they offer
> better initial conditions.  In fact, a good Markov chain will find the typical set in about
> the same time that the optimizer will find a mode — subject to the usual regularity
> conditions (which we need for finite-time MCMC estimators anyways) the convergence
> time is on the order of the mixing time.  This ignores parameter-dependent transition
> costs (i.e. ODEs becoming stiff in the tails), but those costs affect optimization just
> as much as they affect the chains.
>
> Our adaptation can mess up this intuition a bit, but that’s why I included an initial
> convergence window in the adaptation — we converge for a few iterations with a
> unit metric before beginning to learn a diagonal/dense one.  If there are serious
> convergence issues it may very well be prescient to increase the size of this
> initial window.
>
> To summarize, convergence shouldn’t take much longer than optimization.  Similarly,
> any “restarting distribution” will be fundamentally limited because by the time you’ve
> constructed a good one you already have enough information to construct your MCMC
> estimators.  For example, if you want to initialize with EM then what initial conditions
> do you choose for the EM algorithm?  You’re not solving the problem, just sweeping
> it under the rug of another step.  Moreover, a good initialization or restarting distribution
> won’t be all that helpful for multimodal posteriors given that finding all of the modes
> will be incredibly difficult and even if you could find them all then you still have to be
> able to weight them appropriately in order to construct a valid MCMC transition
> (which means computing local evidences which means you need more than a
> simple Markov chain).
>
>
> On Jun 22, 2015, at 6:56 AM, Dustin Tran <dustinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> I believe the original Gelman-Rubin (1992) paper on R-hat suggests a heuristic which is similar in spirit to what Sebastian describes. That is, you find “all” of the local optima using something such as EM, then build a mixture of t-distributions where each is centered at the local optima and whose variance is given by an approximation of the inverse Fisher information evaluated at that point. To run M chains, you sample N>M points from the mixture of t’s, and then apply sequential importance resampling to refine the N points to get M of them.
>>
>> This was in fact a point Don was interested in hearing more about, because I recall Andrew mentioned something about this no longer being necessary when I was presenting the paper in Don’s missing data seminar. My guess is that the problem is the time it takes to find “all” of the local optima.
>>
>> Slightly related: there is also work by Chuanhai Liu and Don (1996, 2002) on Markov normal-based analysis in order to define “restarting distributions”, which propose a better distribution to restart one’s chains as they run. It’s also computationally efficient because it’s just MLE on normal approximations.
>>
>> Dustin

messages.body_plain:
Cool..what a great discussion here!

@ Bob: Yes, your are right, I was suggesting an early stopping scheme. The idea is to a have cheap way to get close to the typical set - I do not care about the mode at all. All I want is to be close to the typical set (and somehow add noise coherent to some extent, the Fisher matrix sounds good, but is likely expensive to get ).

@ Michael: I am not sure if doing full blown MCMC is really so efficient here to find the starting points. You are right in that I would also need starting points for the more "simple minded" method, but I think that using a cheap method first should help in many instances to get a practical solution to the problem of getting sane inits.

@ Andrew: The graphical model thing sounds exciting and maybe this is a better approach to do these kind of things in a smart way as you have a lot more structural information at hand in that case.

In short: Complex models need clever initialization and if something smart can be done here, then this will be good for many, i.e. there are a number of users out there using very complex models to deal with their (complex) systems, but these users need good methods or guidance to handle those complex models the right way.

Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luc,
I think you meant sdb > sda > SD2.
I tried to fit the model the way you described. But I still had problems with it recovering the simulated parameters. I've tried it with informative priors, stan's improper priors, bounded uniform priors, lognormal priors, truncated normals etc. No avail.

dbh <- rlnorm(n_obs, 3.443309, 0.9253412) #mock data

sda <- 0.927
sdb <- 0.0038
SD2 <- 25.6
theta <- 0.028

sim <- c(rnorm(n_obs*(1-theta), 0, sda + sdb * dbh), rnorm(n_obs*theta, 0, SD2))

model <- '
data {
int<lower=1> n_obs;
vector[n_obs] sim;
vector[n_obs] dbh;
}
parameters {

real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
positive_ordered[3] sigma; # sort sigmas from smallest to largest - helps with switching issues
}
model {

 for (i in 1:n_obs) {

   increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log1m(theta) + normal_log(sim[i], 0, sigma[2] + sigma[1] * dbh[i]), #most of data
                                  log(theta) + normal_log(sim[i], 0, sigma[3])));  #few data
 }
}'

mod <- stan(model_code = model, data = list(n_obs=n_obs, dbh=dbh, sim=sim),

            pars = c('sigma','theta'), chains = 1, iter = 500, control=list(adapt_delta=0.9))

messages.body_plain:
Hi. If I understand this correctly, you have a graphical model with
edges parameterizing using logistic regressions. And you want to know
how to calculate the marginal probabilities: P(Sprinkler), P(Rain),
P(Grass wet)? Recall that the whole idea of using MCMC is that we're
going to get a full probability distribution for each of these, by
generating draws.

To accomplish that, I think you should just be able to take the code
you wrote above and add it to the full model (i.e. the dag.stan code
you sent) in a generated quantities block. Instead of hardcoding in
those point estimates, you'd simply use the current draw of the
parameters, transforming them as needed as you've done in the code you
sent...

But maybe I'm missing something...can you say exactly what
P(Sprinkler) is in terms of the variables in your model? Once you have
that, we should be able to help you calculate it given the current
draws of the model parameters...

Seth

> already have a 'fit' model for the dependecies between variables in the form

> parent nodes). The Wikipedia article shows an example of query on this

> probability that it rained? Using the information from the CDT and the

> 'Sprinkler' variable.

> Nothing new here, just simple application of Bayes Rule over a graph.

> BUT! Suppose I don't have CDT for my variables; let's say I want to
> represent this information using GLMs. So, e.g., the 'Rain' node could be
> represented using a logistic regression with an intercept only. The variable

messages.subject: How to get Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of Nonsymmetric Matrices?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a nonsymmetric matrix Q, which is actually what's called a generator
matrix in continuous-time markov chain theory (see:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous-time_Markov_chain). I need to get
the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of Q so that I can find probabilities of
state transitions computationally efficiently.

It seems like the Stan users removed the eigenvector() and eigenvalue()
functions. Why is this? Is there still a way to get the eigenvectors and
eigenvalues of a nonsymmetric matrix?

Best Regards,
Arya

On Tuesday, June 23, 2015 at 8:26:43 PM UTC-4, apourz...@evidation.com wrote:
> It seems like the Stan users removed the eigenvector() and eigenvalue()
> functions. Why is this?

In general, we can't guarantee that the eigenvalues are real and can't autodiff complex numbers.

> Is there still a way to get the eigenvectors and
> eigenvalues of a nonsymmetric matrix?

I have a branch that partially implements what Eigen calls a pseudo-eigendecomposition

http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/classEigen_1_1EigenSolver.html#a4140972e2b45343d1ef1793c2824159c

that could be used in a wider variety of circumstances, including those where a nonsymmetric matrix happened to have all real eigenvalues.

Ben

>>>>
>>>> A bit, but I'm still very confused.  Is it consistent to have
>>>> SVE=1 and SVI=1?  or SVE=0 and SVI=0?  And what's this B1 and B2 variable
>>>> that gets introduced?
>>>>
>>>
>>> OK, I'll use the 'Sprinkler-Rain-Grass' example now. In this example, we
>>> already have a 'fit' model for the dependecies between variables in the form
>>> of conditional distribution tables (or just prior probabilities for the
>>> parent nodes). The Wikipedia article shows an example of query on this
>>> simple model: given the evidence that the grass is wet, what is the
>>> probability that it rained? Using the information from the CDT and the
>>> sum-product rule, we can compute the query as P(R=T|G=W) summing out the
>>> 'Sprinkler' variable.
>>>
>>> Nothing new here, just simple application of Bayes Rule over a graph.
>>>
>>> BUT! Suppose I don't have CDT for my variables; let's say I want to
>>> represent this information using GLMs. So, e.g., the 'Rain' node could be
>>> represented using a logistic regression with an intercept only. The variable
>>> probability table is simply (0.8, 0.2); so the model for this variable could
>>> be: Pr(Rain=T) = inv_logit(-1.38). The same thing could be done for the
>>> Sprinkler variable, but now we must condition on the value of 'Rain':
>>> Pr(Sprinkler=T | Rain) = inv_logit(-0.4 - 4.1 * Rain). The information is
>>> (almost) exactly the same, but I'm encoding it using GLMs instead of the
>>> traditional CDT. The main advantage is that, by using a parameterized model,
>>> I can represent any probability distribution I want, e.g. a conditional
>>> gaussian for continuous variables.
>>>
>>> I hope I made it clearer! In this case, the 'B1', 'B2' parameter introduced
>>> in my example are the regression parameters that allow me to compute P(X |
>>> Y), as explained above. And you are right, it's not consistent to have both
>>> indicator varibles == 1, but this knowledge is not encoded in the graph (OK,
>>> I know it's dumb, but please bear with me!)
>>>
>>> So, I'm using Stan to fit the GLMs that represent the (conditional)
>>> probability distributions of the variables of my full model. But what I
>>> truly want is to use the fitted model to make a query, in the sense of the
>>> above example. My question is: is there a way to do this directly in Stan?
>>>
>>> As I said, right now I'm using the sum-product rule over the fitted model to
>>> find the marginal probabilities of each indicator variable. But I could
>>> query the network using MCMC, if I could fix the evidence and sample from
>>> the queried node. But I'm lost in how to do this directly in Stan. Maybe if
>>> I encode the fitted model using custom probability functions, like this (for
>>> the Wikipedia example)?
>>>
>>> functions {
>>> real rain_log(real y) {
>>>   return if_else(y > 0.5, log_inv_logit(-1.38), log1m_inv_logit(-1.38));
>>> }
>>> real sprinkler_log(real y, real rain) {
>>>   return if_else(y > 0.5, log_inv_logit(-0.4 - 4.1 * round(rain)),
>>> log1m_inv_logit(-0.4 - 4.1 * round(rain)));
>>> }
>>> real grass_log(real y, real sprinkler, real rain) {
>>>   return if_else(y > 0.5, log_inv_logit(-10 + 12.2 * round(sprinkler) +
>>> 11.39 * round(rain) - 8.99 * round(rain) * round(sprinkler)),
>>>   log1m_inv_logit(-10 + 12.2 * round(sprinkler) + 11.39 * round(rain) -
>>> 8.99 * round(rain) * round(sprinkler)));
>>> }
>>> }
>>>
>>> transformed data {
>>> real g;
>>> g <- 1.0;
>>> }
>>>
>>> parameters {
>>> real<lower=0, upper=1> s;
>>> real<lower=0, upper=1> r;
>>> }
>>>
>>> model {
>>> g ~ grass(s, r);
>>> s ~ sprinkler(r);
>>> r ~ rain();
>>> }
>>>
>>> generated quantities {
>>> real truSpr;
>>> real truRain;
>>>
>>> truSpr <- round(s);
>>> truRain <- round(r);
>>> }
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> (well, it feels like using a cannon to kill a fly -- and it takes too many
>>> iterations for a good estimate! And I'm using a point estimates for the
>>> user-defined priors and likelihoods))
>>>
>>>
>>>>
>>>>> I understand that it would be easier to just use a classifier for this
>>>>> purpose (in this example, a simple linear discriminant analysis or a naive
>>>>> bayes), but I'm doing it this way to understand the 'additional bayesian
>>>>> networks' better.
>>>>

>>>> what you're trying to do, we're just not communicating notationally.
>>>>
>>>> What I want to see is:
>>>>

>>>>
>>>> parameters theta:  ditto
>>>>
>>>> joint probablity function: p(y, theta)

>>>>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Is there a simple way to query a Graphical Model in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Bob, Seth and Andrew,

Seth is spot on! My problem is: to simulate draws from the queried node, conditional on the evidence, I need to compute the node's markov blanket, right? This should be done manually in the 'generated quantities' block, then, e.g. using a bernoulli rng with parameter equal to the probability of a success given the blanket.

Seth, I'm using a general bayesian network for classification (an example comparing Naïve Bayes, TAN, BAN and general Bayesian Networks here <http://arxiv.org/pdf/1301.6684v1.pdf>). I want to evaluate the network performance for predicting the class of held-out data. Each class is a separate discrete node in the network.

In summary:

1) I have a large dataset with many variables;
2) I'm doing DAG structure discovery using exact search based on topological ordering, as implemented in the 'abn' R package;
3) I implement the DAG in Stan to estimate its parameters using a training dataset (the discovered DAG structure is, in fact, just a set of generalized linear models);
4) I want to evaluate the network performance for a held-out test dataset, considering uncertainty in the parameter estimates.

I want to use Stan for two different steps: a) estimate de model parameters for a given network structure and training dataset (easy); b) use the fitted DAG to compute the probability of each class for held-out data (my question). I have seen the code for Naïve Bayes Classification in Stan manual, but my network is not of the naïve kind and the class variable is split in various nodes with different edges. I will try to implement simulating variable value using markov blanket information; I will post it here later.

Andrew, I understand how you feel about those silly examples of bayesian reasoning. My statistics classes only taught 'Bayesian Statistics' up to those simple examples, and we all had the impression that Bayes seemed like a nice trick without practical research applications. But Bob pointed the reason behind bringing the example to this discussion -- to help us arrive at some mutual understanding! The data I'm interested in modeling is much more complex; the 'abn' package, in fact, has been used for modeling complex observational data in Epidemiology (like this <http://aje.oxfordjournals.org/content/176/11/1051.abstract>), allowing complex dependency structures between variables.

Erikson

> On Jun 24, 2015, at 10:05 AM, Erikson Kaszubowski <erik...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Bob, Seth and Andrew,
>
> Seth is spot on! My problem is: to simulate draws from the queried node, conditional on the evidence, I need to compute the node's markov blanket, right?

For continuous nodes, this is automatic.  Check out the MCMC section
of the manual.

For discrete nodes, you have to compute the conditional (Stan
doesn't require models to be graphical, but if it is a directed graphical
model, that will indeed correspond to the Markov blanket).

>  This should be done manually in the 'generated quantities' block, then, e.g. using a bernoulli rng with parameter equal to the probability of a success given the blanket.

No reason to simulate.  You can just straight up compute expectations
for anything you want.  There's a chapter in the manual on latent
discrete parameters that provides some examples.

The naive Bayes implementation in the manual has an example, as do
the models in the latent discrete paramters chapter of the manual.

> Seth, I'm using a general bayesian network for classification (an example comparing Naïve Bayes, TAN, BAN and general Bayesian Networks here). I want to evaluate the network performance for predicting the class of held-out data. Each class is a separate discrete node in the network.
>
> In summary:
>
> 1) I have a large dataset with many variables;
> 2) I'm doing DAG structure discovery using exact search based on topological ordering, as implemented in the 'abn' R package;
> 3) I implement the DAG in Stan to estimate its parameters using a training dataset (the discovered DAG structure is, in fact, just a set of generalized linear models);
> 4) I want to evaluate the network performance for a held-out test dataset, considering uncertainty in the parameter estimates.
>
> I want to use Stan for two different steps: a) estimate de model parameters for a given network structure and training dataset (easy); b) use the fitted DAG to compute the probability of each class for held-out data (my question). I have seen the code for Naïve Bayes Classification in Stan manual, but my network is not of the naïve kind and the class variable is split in various nodes with different edges. I will try to implement simulating variable value using markov blanket information; I will post it here later.

If you can write out the probability function, it can probably
be coded in Stan, unless it's one of those connected discrete
examples that Andrew so dislikes (like the Asia model in BUGS, for
example, if I'm recalling the right one).  Those Stan isn't going to
help with at all.

> Andrew, I understand how you feel about those silly examples of bayesian reasoning. My statistics classes only taught 'Bayesian Statistics' up to those simple examples, and we all had the impression that Bayes seemed like a nice trick without practical research applications. But Bob pointed the reason behind bringing the example to this discussion -- to help us arrive at some mutual understanding! The data I'm interested in modeling is much more complex; the 'abn' package, in fact, has been used for modeling complex observational data in Epidemiology (like this), allowing complex dependency structures between variables.

There's already a very deep Bayesian epidemiology literature.
As an example, Dawid and Skene's (1979!) diagnostic accuracy and population
prevalence model is presented in the latent discrete parameters chapter.

- Bob

don't have at that point, but it may introduce some redundancy.

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, June 24, 2015 at 3:44:10 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
> I'm not sure if this would work as a constraint mechanism but my plan is to create a new parameter in the transformed parameter section, and in that transformed parameter (a matrix), I'll set <lower, upper> close to zero so that it will have elements close to 0. Does that sound feasible?

No, but this is not explained so well in the manual. Any lower=a, upper=b constraints in the parameters block are "substantive" in the sense that they preclude any proposal for the parameters from violating those constraints. But any lower=c, upper=d constraints in the transformed parameters block are only useful to catch mistakes on the part of the user who intended for the lower=c, upper=d constraints on the transformed parameters to be satisfied for every admissible proposal for the objects in the parameters block.

If 0 < p < 1 is the proportion of the posterior distribution where all the constraints in the transformed parameters block are simultaneously satisfied, then in principle, you should divide the posterior distribution by p to account for the truncation. But if p < 1, then in general we do not know what value p is (there are some univariate exceptions where you can use the T[,] notation to enforce the truncation). So, if you are using the lower=c, upper=d constraints in the transformed parameters block "substantively" (the same holds for reject() statements), then the posterior distribution Stan is drawing from does not correspond the posterior distribution in your mind.

Also, Stan will have a very difficult time sampling efficiently from the (wrong) posterior distribution unless p is very close to 1 (in which case it is not that wrong). But I doubt that would hold in your case or most cases.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] equality constraints
messages.body_plain:
As Ben notes the right answer is to reparameterize your model.

When you have a holonomic constraint of the form f(x_1, …, x_n) = 0
then you don’t have n degrees of freedom but rather (n - 1).  If you
try to sample from the over constrained space, (x_1, …, x_n), directly
then you’ll spend an infinite amount of time trying to perturb your initial
state into one that satisfies the constraint*.

So what you really want to do is find (n - 1) parameters, (y_1, …, y_{n-1}),
and a map g : x -> y, such that g \circ f(y_1, …., y_{n-1}) = 0 exactly.
This is what Bob was recommending when he suggested taking any

y_1, …, y_{n - 1}

and define the map

x_{i} = y_{i}, i < n
x_{n} = - sum_{j = 1}^{n} x_{j}.

By construction you always satisfy the constraint.

The only tricky bit that you’d a have to worry about is that if you want to
assign a prior on x space then you’ll have to keep the Jacobian in mind,
as

p(y) = p(x(y)) | dx / dy |.

* There’s a clever geometric way to handle such constraints, which
is what the Shake and Rattle integrators exploit to simulate non-Hamiltonian
systems, but we don’t do anything like this in Stan at the moment.

where you are essentially putting positive prior density on proposals for the parameters that are not admissible if Q having real eigenvalues is a constraint. (If complex eigenvalues are admissible, then you have the more manageable problem of handling the real and complex parts separately).

But then the question remains if you had V and D such that QV = VD where D has (some) 2x2 blocks along its diagonal, could you write your log-posterior handling the real and imaginary parts of the eigenvalues separately?

Eigen doesn't seem to provide a reference for it other than it being real matrices V and D where D may have 2x2 blocks along its diagonal such that QV = VD and the eigenvalues of Q are the eigenvalues of D. It is a function of the real Schur decomposition.

But a pseudo-eigendecomposition (if it were modified to only use real operations internally) may be adequate in your case because the matrix exponential of a block diagonal matrix is a block diagonal matrix of matrix exponentials and the matrix exponential of a 2x2 matrix is known.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, June 25, 2015 at 1:53:04 AM UTC-4, bee wrote:
> This code adds negative infinity to log posterior when constraint violates. I'm just wondering what differences are...

The differences are more fundamental than this particular toy example. BUGS is (primarily) a Gibbs sampler that draws from the full-conditional distribution of each parameter given all the other parameters. That BUGS code is sufficient to characterize the distributions of a | b and b | a.

The default algorithm in Stan is a lot more complicated but entails a mechanism to generate proposals for the joint distribution of the parameters a and b. So, you have to be able to express something proportional to the joint posterior density. If your prior density does not integrate to 1 over the parameter space because there is some hole in the middle, then you generally don't have something proportional to the joint posterior density. In your case, I think the hole has a constant size so it is actually proportional to a joint posterior density.

But the complicated mechanism to generate proposals for the joint distribution will not work well because it will often leapfrog through the high density region just outside the hole and land in the hole. It works much better when the parameter space is differentiable everywhere. Mike did a Stan example like this BUGS one starting at about 1 hour and 12 minutes in

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pHsuIaPbNbY

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parameter constraint a^2 + b^2 > 1
messages.body_plain:
Actually that example didn’t have any hard constraint, so there wasn’t any real hole.

The problem with a hole like this is that it changes the shape of parameter space
and Stan can’t handle that directly (formally for the math junkies — you’re trying to
sample from a distribution defined on R^{2} / D, with D a disc centered at zero, where
as Stan can sample from only R^{n}).  The easiest thing to do is reject sample as
Andrew suggested.  There are two strategies for this.

Sample as usual and compute r = a^{2} + b^{2} in generated quantities.  Then take
your Stan output and remove any samples with r < 1.

Add a reject statement to your model black,

model {
  …
  if (a^{2} + b^{2} < 1)
    reject();
  ...
}

which will immediately throw the current sample away.

As Bob notes this can be inefficient if most of your posterior mass is near the disk
but there aren’t many other options given the wacky topology of this space.

Oh, and changing to polar coordinates won’t work!  We’ve talked about this before,
but the ultimately problem is that the Jacobian you need to add is an infinite sum
that can’t be computed in closed form.  Reparameterizations only work when you’re
mapping between spaces with the same shape (topology)!

messages.subject: Feature request: easy R-like construction of diagonal and identity matrices
messages.subject_clean: Feature request: easy R-like construction of diagonal and identity matrices
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've got what's perhaps an very minor feature request, but I would find it convenient. In R, one can create a diagonal n by n matrix from an n-length vector x via diag(x). The output has the elements of x on the diagonal, and 0 on the off-diagonal elements.

Likewise, one can make an identity n by n matrix by supplying an integer n, so diag(n) is the identity matrix of dimension n by n.

Currently, I implement these by initializing a matrix and then writing loops over them and assigning values as needed. It's not at all hard to do, but it's slightly inconvenient.

Thanks for your time.

David

On Thursday, June 25, 2015 at 3:35:58 PM UTC-4, Arya Pourzanjani wrote:
> > If having eigenvalues with non-zero imaginary parts is admissible, then what I wrote in my previous post is not quite sufficient because Eigen utilizes a few unnecessary operations on complex numbers when it does a pseudo-eigendecomposition.
>
> Are you saying that Eigen is too inefficient at pseudo-eigendecomposition involving complex numbers or that Eigen simply can't do it for some reason?

It uses complex numbers internally when it doesn't need to, even though the input matrix is real and the output matrices are real. So, we need to avoid that to make it not segfault with Stan.

> > I do have some local C++ code that reimplemented that in Stan with only real operations, but it would probably be better if I proposed that in a patch to the Eigen developers. But then the question remains if you had V and D such that QV = VD where D has (some) 2x2 blocks along its diagonal, could you write your log-posterior handling the real and imaginary parts of the eigenvalues separately?
>
> What do you mean by handling the real and imaginary parts of the log-posterior separately?

You don't really need the eigenvalues to calculate exp(D) but if you did, then for any complex number

c = a + i * b

you only get the real (a) and imaginary (b) parts. So, you can manually do some things like abs(c) = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) by handling the real and imaginary parts separately.

Ben

messages.subject: Hierarchical model and positive posterior probabilities near the boundaries
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical model and positive posterior probabilities near the boundaries
messages.body_plain:
I know it is mentioned in the manual that Stan won't sample well near the boundaries of constrained parameters, but I just wanted to suggest more explicit warnings about this perhaps somewhere in the manual or in Google group FAQ, given the popularity of Bayesian hierarchical models and potentially substantial impact (overestimates of scale parameters) on the inference caused by this "boundary effect."

To help me explain the issue, let me briefly provide the context. I have been hired by a data consulting company to speed up the Bayesian hierarchical model they have been using for a while. I decided to use an approach similar to INLA (except that everything was conjugate in the model, so no approximation errors from Laplace approximation) and analytically integrated out all the latent parameters to get the marginal likelihood for the scale parameters. Then I computed the posterior mean of the latent parameters using a numerical integration and discovered that my estimates and Stan's estimates were similar but quite noticeably different (and I ran Stan for very long time to ensure the convergence).

Here is what I eventually discovered (using simulated data) and I will speak in terms of a simple random effect model as in Gelman 2006 to be concrete. With a uniform (or half-Cauchy) prior on the scale parameter of group effects, there can be substantial posterior probabilities near the boundary (scale = 0). But Stan does not sample very well near the boundary and this leads to an overestimate of the scale of the group effects. Since the scale parameter is overestimated, the resulting estimates of the group effects are less "shrunk" toward the overall mean.

A Bayesian hierarchical model is a popular way to obtain a shrinkage estimator and I bet many people try to fit such models with Stan, so I think the boundary effect and potential overestimates of scale parameters warrant more explicit warnings. In one of the simulated data I cooked up, the estimates of the latent parameters from Stan had 50% larger MSE than the MSE I obtained using the numerical integration.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchical model and positive posterior probabilities near the boundaries
messages.body_plain:
Yes, Stan did poor job of reconstructing the true parameter values. The model has two scale parameters in addition to the one for observation noise and they were set to zero so that the posterior concentrates near the boundary, and Stan did not generate samples near the boundaries.

I will check with my boss if it is OK to share the example (the data is fake, but the model is not, so there may be issues with non-disclosure agreements). If not, I will see if I can replicate the issue with another model.

On Thursday, June 25, 2015 at 5:16:11 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, since you did simulated-data examples, let me just ask to make sure:  did you simulate the true values of the parameter from the prior?  And, if so, did Stan do a poor job of reconstructing the true parameter values?  If you have a fake-data simulation setup, this would be the natural thing to check.  In your description below, when you talk about MSE, it’s not clear whether Stan is mischaracterizing the posterior, or maybe it’s just that your numerical integration method is doing some smoothing.
>
> Can you share your example with us?  Fake data is fine.
>
> > On Jun 25, 2015, at 6:09 PM, Akihiko Nishimura <akihiko_...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I know it is mentioned in the manual that Stan won't sample well near the boundaries of constrained parameters, but I just wanted to suggest more explicit warnings about this perhaps somewhere in the manual or in Google group FAQ, given the popularity of Bayesian hierarchical models and potentially substantial impact (overestimates of scale parameters) on the inference caused by this "boundary effect."
> >
> > To help me explain the issue, let me briefly provide the context. I have been hired by a data consulting company to speed up the Bayesian hierarchical model they have been using for a while. I decided to use an approach similar to INLA (except that everything was conjugate in the model, so no approximation errors from Laplace approximation) and analytically integrated out all the latent parameters to get the marginal likelihood for the scale parameters. Then I computed the posterior mean of the latent parameters using a numerical integration and discovered that my estimates and Stan's estimates were similar but quite noticeably different (and I ran Stan for very long time to ensure the convergence).
> >
> > Here is what I eventually discovered (using simulated data) and I will speak in terms of a simple random effect model as in Gelman 2006 to be concrete. With a uniform (or half-Cauchy) prior on the scale parameter of group effects, there can be substantial posterior probabilities near the boundary (scale = 0). But Stan does not sample very well near the boundary and this leads to an overestimate of the scale of the group effects. Since the scale parameter is overestimated, the resulting estimates of the group effects are less "shrunk" toward the overall mean.
> >
> > A Bayesian hierarchical model is a popular way to obtain a shrinkage estimator and I bet many people try to fit such models with Stan, so I think the boundary effect and potential overestimates of scale parameters warrant more explicit warnings. In one of the simulated data I cooked up, the estimates of the latent parameters from Stan had 50% larger MSE than the MSE I obtained using the numerical integration.
> >
> >

messages.body_plain:
There is a Bayesian thing going on here.  If the true value of the parameter is zero, but the prior is not centered at zero (which it can’t be, since the parameter is restricted to be nonnegative), then Bayes will necessarily “shrink” the estimate toward the prior, and you’ll get a positive, nonzero parameter estimate.

What I’m getting at is, I think it’s still not clear whether the problem is with Stan not converging to the posterior, or maybe Stan’s giving the right answer given the model you’re supplying.

A

messages.body_plain:
I am not looking at the posterior mean of the hyper parameters, but the posterior distributions. The model is a type of a Gaussian process regression and I have an analytical expression (up to constant) for the posterior distributions of the three scale parameters, so I can easily and accurately estimate the marginal distributions of the scale parameters via numerical integration. This clearly shows that the mode is at (or very close to) scale = 0, but the samples from Stan are clearly bounded away from zero.

To ensure that my own code is right, I also tried putting an informative prior so that the posterior distribution vanishes at scale = 0, and in this case the numerically approximated posterior distribution and histogram from a long Stan run coincide almost exactly.

I think this phenomenon also makes sense theoretically; as I understand, Stan transformed a bounded interval into an infinite interval when given constraints, right? If there were indeed positive probability density at the boundary, this transformation results in a heavy tailed distribution with substantial mass close to infinity. It may well take impractically long time for HMC or NUTS to the tail of such distributions. Given that the geometric ergodicity of MALA is violated for such a heavy tailed distribution (Roberts and Tweedie 1996), I would not be surprised if HMC and NUTS also are not geometrically ergodic either for a heavy tailed distribution.

messages.body_plain:
> On Jun 25, 2015, at 6:09 PM, Akihiko Nishimura <akihiko_...@hotmail.com> wrote:
>

> I know it is mentioned in the manual that Stan won't sample well near the boundaries of constrained parameters, but I just wanted to suggest more explicit warnings about this perhaps somewhere in the manual or in Google group FAQ, given the popularity of Bayesian hierarchical models and potentially substantial impact (overestimates of scale parameters) on the inference caused by this "boundary effect."

Will do:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1508#issuecomment-115430800

> To help me explain the issue, let me briefly provide the context. I have been hired by a data consulting company to speed up the Bayesian hierarchical model they have been using for a while. I decided to use an approach similar to INLA (except that everything was conjugate in the model, so no approximation errors from Laplace approximation) and analytically integrated out all the latent parameters to get the marginal likelihood for the scale parameters. Then I computed the posterior mean of the latent parameters using a numerical integration and discovered that my estimates and Stan's estimates were similar but quite noticeably different (and I ran Stan for very long time to ensure the convergence).

You need to run long enough that all the R-hat values from
multiple chains are near 1.

> Here is what I eventually discovered (using simulated data) and I will speak in terms of a simple random effect model as in Gelman 2006 to be concrete. With a uniform (or half-Cauchy) prior on the scale parameter of group effects, there can be substantial posterior probabilities near the boundary (scale = 0). But Stan does not sample very well near the boundary and this leads to an overestimate of the scale of the group effects.

How near the boundary are we talking?  Stan does Bayesian inference,
so it's never going to push the posterior mean to zero.

> Since the scale parameter is overestimated, the resulting estimates of the group effects are less "shrunk" toward the overall mean.

How do you know the scale parameter is overestimated?

> A Bayesian hierarchical model is a popular way to obtain a shrinkage estimator and I bet many people try to fit such models with Stan,

:-)  We're well aware of this, though we call it "pooling"
rather than "shrinkage" because the posterior mean is not
always zero.

> so I think the boundary effect and potential overestimates of scale parameters warrant more explicit warnings. In one of the simulated data I cooked up, the estimates of the latent parameters from Stan had 50% larger MSE than the MSE I obtained using the numerical integration.

I take it you're talking about using the posterior mean as
an estimate?  It's set up to minimize expected square error of
the estimators *relative to the model*.  When you add priors, that's
not the same as the MLE, which will literally minimize square error
on the training data for straight-up linear regression.

If you can send us a fake data example and model, we can try to understand
what's going on.

- Bob

But those aren't points.  How do you estimate square error with
a distribution?  In expectation?

> The model is a type of a Gaussian process regression and I have an analytical expression (up to constant) for the posterior distributions of the three scale parameters, so I can easily and accurately estimate the marginal distributions of the scale parameters via numerical integration. This clearly shows that the mode is at (or very close to) scale = 0, but the samples from Stan are clearly bounded away from zero.

But Bayesian inference doesn't care about the mode.  But it
will correspond to the mean in a symmetric distribution, but
your posterior for a scale parameter can't be symmetric, because
it's bounded below at 0 and has support on (0, inf).  (Actually,
I'm just guessing here.)

> To ensure that my own code is right, I also tried putting an informative prior so that the posterior distribution vanishes at scale = 0, and in this case the numerically approximated posterior distribution and histogram from a long Stan run coincide almost exactly.
>
> I think this phenomenon also makes sense theoretically; as I understand, Stan transformed a bounded interval into an infinite interval when given constraints, right?

Right --- if you supply <lower=0>, we log transform
the parameter for sampling, and apply the appropriate Jacobian
adjustment.  And you only need to get to -700 or so to
underflow to 0 using the inverse transform, exp().

> If there were indeed positive probability density at the boundary, this transformation results in a heavy tailed distribution with substantial mass close to infinity.

Not quite.  There's a positive *density* at the boundary, but
that doesn't translate into heavy mass near infinity because things
get very stretched out under the log transform.

And then there's the Jacobian.

Of course, it depends where you start, because log transforming
an improper uniform on (0, inf) to (-inf, inf) produces an improper
result.

Here's a histogram of the log transformed half Cauchy(0, 2.5),
produced in R with:

hist(log(abs(rt(1000000, 1, 2.5))), breaks=50)

> It may well take impractically long time for HMC or NUTS to the tail of such distributions. Given that the geometric ergodicity of MALA is violated for such a heavy tailed distribution (Roberts and Tweedie 1996), I would not be surprised if HMC and NUTS also are not geometrically ergodic either for a heavy tailed distribution.

You're right that if the distribution's heavy tailed enough (as in
a Cauchy) or light tailed enough (in an untransformed triangle distribution,
say), then you can run into problems.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm new to Bayesian things and STAN, so please don't kill me.

I used the attached R code to obtain summaries on posterior distributions for parameters in the attached stan file (a simple model with only 3 levels). A call to stan() yielded a warning of the following type, 36 times in 1000 samples and again 39 times in 1000 samples:

# Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
# stan::prob::beta_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Random variable is 4.23105:0, but must be less than or equal to 1
# If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
# but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

I don't actually know why this warning is occurring. I guess it has something to do with the parameter p1 being drawn near 1 some of the time, which somehow leads to the parameter p1tilde being drawn to be out of bounds [0,1]? Does it have something to do with underflow or overflow when a computer stores numbers?

I'm getting the underflow/overflow idea from the STAN reference manual, which mentions "arithmetic stability" in what it says about informational messages:

"In cases where the message persists, it is worth investigating the arithmetic stability of the Stan program. There are several tips in this manual and in the user group about how to rewrite problematic programs."

Thanks!
Qian

P.S. I'll read Chapters 10 and 11 of BDA so I actually know what is going on under the hood, if that has anything to do with this warning.

There's a chapter in the manual that goes over the transforms
and the Jacobians.  For upper and lower bounds we use a scaled
and translated inverse-logit transform, which produces a logistic
distribution once the Jacobian's applied.  (Basically, the logistic
is the CDF.)

> Given that the log transform does not result in a heavy tailed distribution, I am not too sure why Stan is not sampling near scale = 0 at all in my example.

OK --- these terms all have pretty clear definitions, so I hope
we're not miscommunicating about them.

This is helpful for my understanding, too.  Here's what Stan does
with a very simple model:

  data { int<lower=0> N; vector[N] y; }
  parameters { real mu; real<lower=0> sigma; }
  model { y ~ normal(mu, sigma); }

given data y that is 10 copies of the value 1 (equivalent to
y being a random effect with complete pooling [variance=0]):

            mean  se_mean        sd        2.5%       97.5% n_eff      Rhat
mu      1.0000000 0.000000 0.0000001   0.9999998   1.0000002  3087 0.9995303
sigma   0.0000002 0.000000 0.0000001   0.0000001   0.0000005     3 2.8025187
lp__  137.4845920 1.918341 3.0348166 130.8990197 142.8267866     3 2.8581082

And that's using an improper prior, which is fatter tailed
than any proper density.  So you can see that Stan can get very
close to 0.  But the problem is that it's not converging well
by the R-hat values.  A better math stats person than me can
probably work out the posterior.

You get roughly the same result with a Cauchy(0, 2.5) prior.

- Bob
