messages.body_plain:
The problem is that you declare

  real<lower=0> p1tilde[J];

which allows any value for p1tilde > 0, and then have
a model statement:

    p1tilde[j] ~ beta(10*p1, 10*(1-p1));

which requires p1tilde[j] < 1.  So what you want is:

  real<lower=0, upper=1> p1tilde[J];

So what Stan does is jump outside of (0,1), then rejects
with an error.

You also want to vectorize, and rewrite as:

  ptilde ~ beta(10 * pi, 10 * (1 - pi));

and

  a ~ binomial(n, p1tilde);

It'll run a lot faster.  But you can probably just reformulate
using the beta-binomial and cut out estimating that p1tilde
altogether:

  a ~ beta_binomial(n, 10 * p1, 10 * (1 - p1))

I'm also not sure why you're pegging the prior count to 8 (the parameters
add 1 to the prior counts), but the above should give you much more
efficient inference for p1, which is presumably what you care about.

- Bob

You started with the process we recommend, so it's great
you've already figured out it's not a bug in the model.

The Stan code's very tight, but I can make a couple
suggestions.

First, move the declaration and definition of
Sigma_beta to the generated_quantities block because you
don't use them in the model.  This will be a big savings
if the matrix is large.

Second, the expression

  exp(-exp(lrc[jj[n]])

is just an underflow waiting to happen.  It'll basically underflow
if lrc > 6.5 or so.  Is there a way to express this not on
the exp(-exp()) scale?

It's odd that there'd be a stack overflow.  That indicates
recursion going beyond the max depth that C++ can handle.  We
wrote everything in Stan iteratively to avoid this issue.

We can run in CmdStan to see if it's an R or Stan issue.  Daniel
and I are both on the road now, so I don't have anywhere I can
try a long-running model.

- Bob

> Both reject("in hole") and increment_log_prob(negative_infinity()) will result in the proposal being rejected. In principle, using reject("in hole") is a bit more efficient because it abandons the proposal immediately whereas doing increment_log_prob(negative_infinity()) will keep evaluating subsequent sampling statements that add or subtract to negative . messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feature request: easy R-like construction of diagonal and identity matrices
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Feature request: easy R-like construction of diagonal and identity matrices
messages.body_plain:
You almost never want to be explicitly building up
a diagonal matrix.  May I ask what do you do with it once it's
constructed?

We have some diagonal multiplication routines such as

  diag_pre_multiply(a, b) = diag(a) * b

that are much more efficient for diagonal matrices.

And you don't want to be calling multi_normal unless absolutely
necessary --- it should never be called with a diagonal covariance
matrix.  That is, instead of

  y ~ multi_normal(mu, diag(a))

you just want to use the vectorized univariate form to get the
same result:

  y ~ normal(mu, a);

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Bob. Very helpful. I moved Sigma_beta to the generated quantities but it only improved speed on a smaller data (1K individuals, 6K observations) set by about 3%. This isn't too surprising I think since that's only a 3x3 matrix. But still very useful for me to note for future work.

As for exp(- exp(lrc) * time) and underflow issues, I'd prefer to keep lrc (log rate of change) to be sampled on a log scale since, as a rate, that is the more meaningful scale to sample it from a normal distribution (it's multinormally distributed with the other parameters). I plotted the model for lrc =seq(-3, 3, len=9) on both scales to double check that the spacing is indeed problematic on the un-logged scale. As you can see from the attached figure, indeed it is.

But in thinking about this I realized that I have ridiculous priors right now and I wonder if that's part of the problem. I kept
to_vector(gamma) ~ Normal(0,5)
from the manual code. But the first row of my gamma matrix are intercepts for each of the non-linear model parameters. And I know a priori that R0 should be in the range of of 2-6 and Asym should be 5-7. lrc is probably in the range of -2 to 2. So I changed the priors to:
  gamma[1,1] ~ normal(6, 5);
  gamma[1,2] ~ normal(4, 5);
  gamma[1,3] ~ normal(0, 2);
  gamma[2] ~ normal(0,5);
This did not speed up the HMC iterations at all on the smaller test set (1K indiv). But I'm hoping that by narrowing the prior on lrc to normal(0,2) it would reduce the chance of underflow, though I'm not sure if I'm thinking about this clearly.

I'll rerun it on a full-sized (ie size of the eventual real data) data set tonight & report what happens in the morning.

>
> and
>
>   a ~ binomial(n, p1tilde);
>

> using the beta-binomial and cut out estimating that p1tilde
> altogether:
>
>   a ~ beta_binomial(n, 10 * p1, 10 * (1 - p1))
>
> I'm also not sure why you're pegging the prior count to 8 (the parameters
> add 1 to the prior counts), but the above should give you much more
> efficient inference for p1, which is presumably what you care about.

The exponential family priors act like data.
So you can think of beta(alpha, beta) as the posterior of
a Bernoulli (or binomial) model starting with a uniform prior
and observing alpha-1 successes and beta-1 failures.
So (alpha + beta - 2) is how many data points the prior is
equivalent to, so your prior beta(10*p1, 10*(1-p1)) with p1 in (0,1)
is defined so that it's equivalent to 8 prior observations.

- Bob

> On Jun 26, 2015, at 12:24 AM, Qian Zhang <qian.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks!
>
> I understand everything in your post except this comment:
>
> "you're pegging the prior count to 8 (the parameters add 1 to the prior counts)"
>
> What's this "prior count," and why is it 8, and which particular parameters are adding 1 to the prior counts?
>
> On Thursday, June 25, 2015 at 7:56:39 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The problem is that you declare
>
>   real<lower=0> p1tilde[J];
>
> which allows any value for p1tilde > 0, and then have
> a model statement:
>
>     p1tilde[j] ~ beta(10*p1, 10*(1-p1));
>
> which requires p1tilde[j] < 1.  So what you want is:
>
>   real<lower=0, upper=1> p1tilde[J];
>
> So what Stan does is jump outside of (0,1), then rejects
> with an error.
>
> You also want to vectorize, and rewrite as:
>
>   ptilde ~ beta(10 * pi, 10 * (1 - pi));
>
> and
>
>   a ~ binomial(n, p1tilde);
>
> It'll run a lot faster.  But you can probably just reformulate
> using the beta-binomial and cut out estimating that p1tilde
> altogether:
>
>   a ~ beta_binomial(n, 10 * p1, 10 * (1 - p1))
>
> I'm also not sure why you're pegging the prior count to 8 (the parameters
> add 1 to the prior counts), but the above should give you much more
> efficient inference for p1, which is presumably what you care about.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: way of fixing parameters?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I often tend to pack my model parameters into vectors like

vector[10] theta;

Now, sometimes I want to fix a subset of the parameters to fixed values. How could I achieve this? I mean I would like to have some special prior here which fixes a value to a certain value. I know I can use a normal with an almost 0 sd, but this does not sound to be a good idea efficiency wise - and I anyway really just want to fix the parameter. Suggestions? Rewriting my program would be an option, yes; but this is time-consuming and error-prone.

So a construct like

theta[2] ~ fixed_prior(3);

would do the job, but maybe there is a more clever way to do it. As I recall doing theta[2] = 3 in the model block is a no go for obvious reasons.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] problems estimating generalized (non-parallel) ordered logit models
messages.body_plain:
Indeed, you don’t want negative probabilities!  From a Bayesian perspective, you no longer have a generative model.
Regarding Waic etc.:  Aki and Jonah and I will be posting a paper on this very soon.
A

> On Jun 25, 2015, at 10:33 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> I'll let Andrew or Aki answer the WAIC/DIC, etc questions.
> You may need to repost with WAIC in the title to get their
> attention.
>
> Almost all the posts on this list are problem-oriented.   We
> wish more people would write in with success stories and to
> share models.  We hear them from people in person and via
> off-list e-mail, but not so much on-list.  It gives a very skewed
> perspective!
>
> Whatever you do, a model generating negative probabilities is
> ill posed.  The usual thing to do to convert unbounded values into
> probabilities is to use softmax (exp-transform before normalizing).
> It's the link for multi-logit.
>
> As to (1), I don't know if Martyn Plummer updated rjags to
> use split-R-hat the way we do in Stan.  The split-R-hat (aka
> split-"psrf") defined in our manual and in the latest Gelman
> et al. Bayesian Data Analysis book is more conservative,
> as is our n_eff calculation, which also uses cross-chain information.
> You can pull the JAGS output into Stan this way, assuming you can
> get the same kind of output out of rjags as out of R2jags.
>
> fit_jags <- jags(model.file = "irt_hier.jags",
>                 data = list(I=I, J=J, y=y),
>                 init = init_list,
>                 parameters.to.save = c("mu_a", "sigma_a", "a",
>                                        "mu_b", "sigma_b", "b",
>                                        "theta"),
>                 n.chains = num_chains,
>                 n.iter = 20000,
>                 n.thin = 2,
>                 jags.seed = init_seed);
>
> print(c("jags", elapsed_time_jags));
>
> fit_jags_mcmc <- as.mcmc(fit_jags);
> arr <- as.array(fit_jags_mcmc);
> arr <- aperm(arr, c(1,3,2));
> mon <- monitor(arr, inc_warmup = FALSE);
>
> The mon object should everything you need in it.
>
> Some comments on the model below.
>
>> On Jun 25, 2015, at 8:39 PM, jun...@gmail.com wrote:
>>
>> My question actually can be rephrased as whether there is way to estimate generalized ordered logit/probit models, in which we can get negative predicted probabilities (so if we replace those negative predicted probabilities with zero, we might have sums greater than one). Thanks!
>>
>> On Thursday, June 25, 2015 at 8:05:38 PM UTC-4, jun...@gmail.com wrote:
>> Dear rstanians,
>>
>> This is a bit problems loaded post since I ran into couple of problems estimating a generalized ordered logit model, which is an extension to ordered logit/probit model discussed in p.50 of the Stan Modeling Language User's Guide v2.6.2. Instead of assuming that slopes (for the same independent variables) are the same across different cut-point equations (hence the proportional odds assumption), the generalized ordered logit model allows slopes to vary across equations. Because simple ordered logit model assumes the equivalence of coefficients, stan uses the ordered_logistic() function to set up the likelihood; but to set up a generalized ordered logit model, one may have to some modified version of of the stan codes on p.51 for an ordered probit regression model. Here are my questions (from the most to least straightforward):

I do have a couple of arithmetic and efficiency tips.

For efficiency and arithmetic stability, you should
define log_mu instead of mu, so that

  mu[2] <- exp(c+ e[2] + 2*d*u*e[1]);

becomes

  log_mu[2] <- + e[2] + 2*d*u*e[1];

and then you can use

  y ~ poisson_log(mu);

which is the Poisson with log-scale parameter.

Second, you want to only evaluate any given subexpression once
if at all possible.  So rather than this:

for (i in 4:N)

  log_mu[i] <- c
               + e[i]

               + 2*d*u*e[i-1]
               + (2*u*((d-1)/2+1)*2*d*u
               - (2*(d-1/2)+1)*1)*e[i-2]
               + (2*u*((d-1)/3+1)*(2*u*((d-1)/2+1)*2*d*u
               - (2*(d-1/2)+1)*1)

               - (2*(d-1/3)+1)*2*d*u)*e[i-3];

you can define variables to store terms like
(2 * d * u) and (2*(d-1/2)+1)*1) that'd don't depend on the
loop variable once and then reuse them.  It'll make a huge
difference in speed, especially for the N=167 you're using.

If you get it coded and it doesn't work, let us know and
we might be able to help.

- Bob

P.S.  And can you send us a link if you get it working and write
      about it?  We'd love to add "quantum mechanics" to our list
      of applications!

On Thursday, June 25, 2015 at 9:48:40 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Jun 25, 2015, at 10:28 PM, Akihiko Nishimura <akihiko_...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Oh, I see that the transformation does not result in a very heavy tail; thanks for the clarification. Btw, how do you handle a parameter with both a lower and upper bound? I am using a proper uniform prior with an upper bound.
>
> There's a chapter in the manual that goes over the transforms
> and the Jacobians.  For upper and lower bounds we use a scaled
> and translated inverse-logit transform, which produces a logistic
> distribution once the Jacobian's applied.  (Basically, the logistic
> is the CDF.)
>
> > Given that the log transform does not result in a heavy tailed distribution, I am not too sure why Stan is not sampling near scale = 0 at all in my example.
> >
> > I think there are miscommunication (mode, mean, MSE, Bayesian & MLE, and etc), so I will just send the example as soon as I get a permission from the company.
>
> OK --- these terms all have pretty clear definitions, so I hope
> we're not miscommunicating about them.
>
> This is helpful for my understanding, too.  Here's what Stan does
> with a very simple model:
>
>   data { int<lower=0> N; vector[N] y; }
>   parameters { real mu; real<lower=0> sigma; }
>   model { y ~ normal(mu, sigma); }
>
> given data y that is 10 copies of the value 1 (equivalent to
> y being a random effect with complete pooling [variance=0]):
>
>             mean  se_mean        sd        2.5%       97.5% n_eff      Rhat
> mu      1.0000000 0.000000 0.0000001   0.9999998   1.0000002  3087 0.9995303
> sigma   0.0000002 0.000000 0.0000001   0.0000001   0.0000005     3 2.8025187
> lp__  137.4845920 1.918341 3.0348166 130.8990197 142.8267866     3 2.8581082
>
> And that's using an improper prior, which is fatter tailed
> than any proper density.  So you can see that Stan can get very
> close to 0.  But the problem is that it's not converging well
> by the R-hat values.  A better math stats person than me can
> probably work out the posterior.
>
> You get roughly the same result with a Cauchy(0, 2.5) prior.
>
> - Bob
>
> >
> > On Thursday, June 25, 2015 at 9:05:39 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> >> On Jun 25, 2015, at 9:41 PM, Akihiko Nishimura <akihiko_...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> I am not looking at the posterior mean of the hyper parameters, but the posterior distributions.
> >
> > But those aren't points.  How do you estimate square error with
> > a distribution?  In expectation?
> >
> >> The model is a type of a Gaussian process regression and I have an analytical expression (up to constant) for the posterior distributions of the three scale parameters, so I can easily and accurately estimate the marginal distributions of the scale parameters via numerical integration. This clearly shows that the mode is at (or very close to) scale = 0, but the samples from Stan are clearly bounded away from zero.
> >
> > But Bayesian inference doesn't care about the mode.  But it
> > will correspond to the mean in a symmetric distribution, but
> > your posterior for a scale parameter can't be symmetric, because
> > it's bounded below at 0 and has support on (0, inf).  (Actually,
> > I'm just guessing here.)
> >
> >> To ensure that my own code is right, I also tried putting an informative prior so that the posterior distribution vanishes at scale = 0, and in this case the numerically approximated posterior distribution and histogram from a long Stan run coincide almost exactly.
> >>
> >> I think this phenomenon also makes sense theoretically; as I understand, Stan transformed a bounded interval into an infinite interval when given constraints, right?
> >
> > Right --- if you supply <lower=0>, we log transform
> > the parameter for sampling, and apply the appropriate Jacobian
> > adjustment.  And you only need to get to -700 or so to
> > underflow to 0 using the inverse transform, exp().
> >
> >> If there were indeed positive probability density at the boundary, this transformation results in a heavy tailed distribution with substantial mass close to infinity.
> >
> > Not quite.  There's a positive *density* at the boundary, but
> > that doesn't translate into heavy mass near infinity because things
> > get very stretched out under the log transform.
> >
> > And then there's the Jacobian.
> >
> > Of course, it depends where you start, because log transforming
> > an improper uniform on (0, inf) to (-inf, inf) produces an improper
> > result.
> >
> > Here's a histogram of the log transformed half Cauchy(0, 2.5),

> >> It may well take impractically long time for HMC or NUTS to the tail of such distributions. Given that the geometric ergodicity of MALA is violated for such a heavy tailed distribution (Roberts and Tweedie 1996), I would not be surprised if HMC and NUTS also are not geometrically ergodic either for a heavy tailed distribution.
> >
> > You're right that if the distribution's heavy tailed enough (as in
> > a Cauchy) or light tailed enough (in an untransformed triangle distribution,

messages.body_plain:
Well, those clearly haven't converged.  Are the chains close
and just not mixing, or are they clearly stuck in different
modes?  That is, does it look like running longer might help?

I don't know if you're getting any divergences here (typically
indicated by warmup messages, but you can also pull them out
of the fit in RStan and they're printed in CmdStan), but if you
are, you probably want to start with a smaller step size and
up the adapt_delta target above its default of 0.8 (perhaps as
high as 0.99).  That'll keep step size down and allow the gradients
to do a better job of mimicking the curvature.  But it'll slow
down the iterations (at the benefit of getting higher n_eff per
iteration).

The problem with increasing data is that it can increase posterior
curvature along narrow ridges, making it harder for the Hamiltonian
simulation to find a large step size to make large moves.  Sometimes
this is good and you actually get sublinear growth with data.  Sometimes
it's bad and constrains the parameters and makes them correlated in
a way that makes it much harder to move in Euclidean space with just
a gradient.  So you'll probably see the number of leapfrog steps going up and
the step size going down as you get more data to try to compensate.

- Bob

>
> I don't know if you're getting any divergences here (typically
> indicated by warmup messages, but you can also pull them out
> of the fit in RStan and they're printed in CmdStan), but if you
> are, you probably want to start with a smaller step size and
> up the adapt_delta target above its default of 0.8 (perhaps as
> high as 0.99).  That'll keep step size down and allow the gradients
> to do a better job of mimicking the curvature.  But it'll slow
> down the iterations (at the benefit of getting higher n_eff per
> iteration).
>
> The problem with increasing data is that it can increase posterior
> curvature along narrow ridges, making it harder for the Hamiltonian
> simulation to find a large step size to make large moves.  Sometimes
> this is good and you actually get sublinear growth with data.  Sometimes
> it's bad and constrains the parameters and makes them correlated in
> a way that makes it much harder to move in Euclidean space with just
> a gradient.  So you'll probably see the number of leapfrog steps going up and
> the step size going down as you get more data to try to compensate.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Sampler diagnostic parameter questions
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to understand how to use the sampler diagnostic parameters returned by get_sampler_params() to identify and fix possible problems with my models. I've found and read several relevant threads on this list, but I have a few questions:

First, I am confused about the relationship between treedepth__ and  max_treedepth that indicates a failed NUTS step. The Stan manual says (p. 453) that if treedepth__ equals the maximum, NUTS gives up and terminates that step prematurely. But when I look at the diagnostics from some model runs, sometimes treedepth__ == max_treedepth + 1 and that suggests that the steps with treedepth__ == max_treedepth were successful and it's the ones with treedepth__ > max_treedepth that were unsuccessful.

Second, should I worry if I get a few instances of excessive treedepth__ or nonzero n_divergent__ during warmup, or is it only a sign of trouble if it happens during the post-warmup sampling?

Third, is there a simpler way than the following code to get max_treedepth from a stanfit object in Rstan?

lapply(my_stanfit_obj@sim$samples, function(x) attr(x, 'args')$control$max_treedepth)

Finally, I'm not finding much documentation on how to interpret the sampler diagnostic parameters. I can get a feel for what treedepth__ is telling me from the section of the Stan manual that describes the NUTS algorithm, but I don't know whether I should be looking for anything other than checking that treedepth__ <= max_treedepth. And I can't find anything about what I should be learning from the other parameters, such as n_divergent__. I've looked in the Stan manual (but it's big and I might not have looked in the right places or searched on the right terms), the RStan manual, and Appendix C of BDA3 with no success.  Is there something else a basic stan user should read to understand these diagnostic parameters?

On Monday, June 29, 2015 at 10:15:46 PM UTC-4, Jonathan Gilligan wrote:
> First, I am confused about the relationship between treedepth__ and  max_treedepth that indicates a failed NUTS step. The Stan manual says (p. 453) that if treedepth__ equals the maximum, NUTS gives up and terminates that step prematurely. But when I look at the diagnostics from some model runs, sometimes treedepth__ == max_treedepth + 1 and that suggests that the steps with treedepth__ == max_treedepth were successful and it's the ones with treedepth__ > max_treedepth that were unsuccessful.

Treedepth starts counting at zero. So, if max_treedepth is 10 (the default) and treedepth goes to 11, then it terminated prematurely.

> Second, should I worry if I get a few instances of excessive treedepth__ or nonzero n_divergent__ during warmup, or is it only a sign of trouble if it happens during the post-warmup sampling?

There are almost always some divergent transitions during the warmup phase but we don't really worry about them. It is trying to find a stepsize during the warmup phase that achieves the target acceptance probability without diverging and without hitting the max_treedepth.

> Third, is there a simpler way than the following code to get max_treedepth from a stanfit object in Rstan?
>
> lapply(my_stanfit_obj@sim$samples, function(x) attr(x, 'args')$control$max_treedepth)

No.

> Finally, I'm not finding much documentation on how to interpret the sampler diagnostic parameters.

Unfortunately, these things are better explained in the CmdStan manual

https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/releases/download/v2.6.2/cmdstan-guide-2.6.2.pdf

Ben

On Monday, June 29, 2015 at 11:56:25 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> If someone could write the solver and the gradients, it should
> be very easy to put in the language.  I don't even understand
> what we'd need to do it --- if it's just an ode integrator, then
> it'd be great if we could isolate the integrator from the function
> because Daniel's currently plugging and playing some alternatives.

There's at least 3 similarish things we could potentially do with a user-defined function in Stan:
integrate it, which we can sort of do already with the ODE stuff but we don't have other quadrature algos
optimize it, which we can't do now but it basically just entails passing a user-defined function to our LBFGS algorithm instead of the log_prob()
solve it (within an interval) for the parameters that cause it to be zero, which we can't do now but there is stuff in Boost and Eigen for that
Ideally, these would all have similar semantics to ODEs in Stan with the functors and all that.

This particular thread is referring to 2). The "likelihood" function involves weights and you have to find the optimal weights given the parameters to evaluate the log-likelihood. There is a review paper about ideas like this here

http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com.ezproxy.cul.columbia.edu/doi/10.1002/9781118771051.ch11/pdf

As for 1), some PDFs involve intractable integrals. For example, equation 4 in

http://academic2.american.edu/~jpnolan/stable/density.ps

I had some C++ code that yields a good numerical approximation of that particular integral but we need a more general framework.

For 3), we can solve some linear systems of equations but have nothing for the nonlinear ones. A simple example where this is needed is (most) inverse CDFs, given 0 < p < 1 and theta, you have to numerically choose x such that F(x|theta) - p = 0. And once you get that x*(p, theta), you have utilize implicit differentiation to ultimately get the derivatives of the log-posterior wrt p and / or theta.

There's more applications, but it is really more of a deal where we need to build on the syntactic framework we used for ODEs.

Ben

how they couple with the sampler performance.

hesitant to offer any quadrature that isn’t super robust.

(2) This one is somewhat more straightforward but I think more
subtle than people realize.  Aside from identifiability problems,
there are various regularity conditions required for the derivative
and the optimization criterion to commute, which we need to
compute the derivative of the optimum (as is done the in MML
derivation).  I’m not sure how we can guarantee these conditions
or warn the user if they’re not satisfied.

Somewhat straightforward to implement but would require a
pretty serious amount of work to make robust methodologically.
A good masters/PhD project.

(3) This is probably the most straightforward theoretically given
the guarantees of the Implicit Function Theorem.  We already
have gradients so we can put together a slick root finder
pretty easily (again, there are always identifiability issues at hand)
and the derivatives of the solution will then be relatively straightforward.

Another relatively self-contained project ideal for students.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sampler diagnostic parameter questions
messages.body_plain:
Unfortunately we’re overdo for a serious rewrite of the manual,
especially given our rapidly evolving understanding of subtle
theoretical MCMC issues.  I have everything collected into
slides, but turning it into text will have to wait until I have some
free time.  But I’ll summarize the results here.

MCMC is just a method for numerically estimating integrals,
which is hard in high dimensions because of something called
concentration of measure.  Essentially the only parameters
that contribute to integrals lie on a hyper surface in parameter
space and if we want to estimate integrals then we need to
find that hyper surface and then explore it.  That’s exactly
what a Markov chain does — eventually we have a series
of states distributed across the hyper surface, { y_{n} }, that
we can use as a grid for doing really simple quadrature,

\int dy p(y) f(y) ~ 1/N sum_{n = 1}^{N} f(y_{n})

Everything relies on our being able to find and then explore
the _entire_ hyper surface (which we call the typical set).
This is incredibly hard to determine theoretically so we’re
left with a bunch of necessary but not sufficient diagnostics
to identify when we’re not exploring everything.

All of these apply only to samples — because we dynamically
adapt sampling parameters in warmup those samples will
behave very differently.  Again, ignore anything you see
in warmup.

Traceplots:

The characteristic way pathologies manifest is the Markov
chain getting stuck in the boundary of a pathological region
of parameter space.  If you run long enough you’ll literally
see the chain get stuck for long periods of time.  You can
also compare chains to identify multi modality and other
problems.

R-hat:

If our Markov chain can explore the entire target distribution
then any realization of it should look the same.  R-hat
essentially performs an analysis of variance on a bunch of
chains (and subsets of chains) looking for any deviations.
The more chains you use the more sensitive you’ll be to
potential pathologies.

n-divergent:

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo has a unique diagnostic — regions
of the typical set that are hard to explore induce particular
numerical divergences that we can capture and report.  This
is much more sensitive then looking at trace plots! If
you see any divergences in sampling then you have to be
careful.  For a few divergences you can increase the target
acceptance probability, but for any nontrivial number of
divergences you’ll probably have to consider tweaking your
model to use stronger priors or different parameterizations.

In RStan you can grab the divergences with

fit <- stan(file='model_name.stan', data=input_data,
            iter=2000, chains=1, seed=4938483)

count_divergences <- function(fit) {
  sampler_params <- get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)
  sum(sapply(sampler_params, function(x) c(x[,'n_divergent__']))[,1])
}

Finally the treedepth issue is not so much a diagnostic of a
bad Markov chain but rather a safeguard we’ve built in to
avoid infinite loops caused by ill-formed posteriors which
require the sampler to explore all the way to infinity in back
(requiring an infinite tree depth an infinite time).  Sometimes
your sampler will need to explore beyond our default safeguard
value, in which case you have to increase it manually — this
doesn’t effect the validity of your results, just the performance
of the algorithm.

I like looking at a histogram of the treedepths,

hist_treedepth <- function(fit) {
  sampler_params <- get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)
  hist(sapply(sampler_params, function(x) c(x[,'treedepth__']))[,1], breaks=0:20, main="", xlab="Treedepth")
  abline(v=10, col=2, lty=1)
}

Technically the sampler tries one more step after maxdepth
which is why you might see it exceed that value by one.  I
can never remember the indexing and ordering to state whether
you should see maxdepth or maxdepth + 1 but in the end it
doesn’t really matter as the bad behavior (histogram saturating
at a large value) is pretty obvious.

>
> I don't know if you're getting any divergences here (typically
> indicated by warmup messages, but you can also pull them out
> of the fit in RStan and they're printed in CmdStan), but if you
> are, you probably want to start with a smaller step size and
> up the adapt_delta target above its default of 0.8 (perhaps as
> high as 0.99).  That'll keep step size down and allow the gradients
> to do a better job of mimicking the curvature.  But it'll slow
> down the iterations (at the benefit of getting higher n_eff per
> iteration).
>
> The problem with increasing data is that it can increase posterior
> curvature along narrow ridges, making it harder for the Hamiltonian
> simulation to find a large step size to make large moves.  Sometimes
> this is good and you actually get sublinear growth with data.  Sometimes
> it's bad and constrains the parameters and makes them correlated in
> a way that makes it much harder to move in Euclidean space with just
> a gradient.  So you'll probably see the number of leapfrog steps going up and
> the step size going down as you get more data to try to compensate.

I've also seen this lead to non-convergence when some chains find the narrow ridges and others never do (and explore a much broader parameter space).  You can ususally tell that from trace plots or just looking at means/variances for multiple chains.

Krzysztof

messages.body_plain:
No, I know.

Let’s say we have parameters theta and there is some
component of the likelihood of the form

\hat{f} (theta) = max_{phi} g(theta, phi)

We can run an optimizer to get a point value of \hat{f} (theta),
but then what is the derivative, d \hat{f} / d theta that we need
to run our algorithms?

The regularity conditions to which I was referring are those
that ensure that we can do

d/dtheta \hat{f} (theta)
= d/dtheta max_{phi} g(theta, phi)
= max_{phi} d / dtheta g(theta, phi)

which gives another optimization that we can run.  This is
one way to derive the MML updates, but here has a more
general use.

But the OP is referring to something else, where the user is going to do MCMC with informative priors but evaluating the "log-likelihood" entails constrained optimization of a user-defined function. The "likelihood" for observation i is $\frac{w_{i}^{\ast}\left(\theta\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}w_{j}^{\ast}\left(\theta\right)}$.  So the .stan program would be like

messages.subject: Modeling of multimodal data distributions
messages.body_plain:
Can anyone offer advice for an analysis problem I'm working on.  I want to apply a partial-pooling approach like the radon examples in chapter 12 of ARM to analyzing a database of arsenic concentration in well-water. I have a measured arsenic concentrations in roughly 465,000 wells distrtibuted among roughly 3700 sites with the number or wells per site  ranging from 1 to roughly 2300 (the median is 82).

Right now, I'm getting started by trying a partially pooled analysis of mean arsenic and uncertainty at each site, similar to figure 12.1 in ARM. Once I'm confident this is working, I plan to build on this to add parameters that account for the effect of well depth, stratigraphic characteristics, and ultimately to consider spatial effects (e.g., draw inferences from the nearest neighbor sites).

The precision of arsenic measurements is sufficiently poor that it's reasonable for me to add 1 part per billion to every measurement (to deal with the measurements that are nominally zero parts per billion) and then take the log (base 10 to make it easier for me to interpret in terms of real units). On a log10 scale, I see a big spike at zero (about 60,000 wells) and a distinct and separate lump that looks fairly normal (corresponding to a lognormal distribution in the raw data) centered at around 2 (90,000 wells with log10(As) between 2.0 and 2.1) and nothing in the range 0.1 < x <  1.

The simple thing to do in modeling this would be to represent the data with a mixture of two normal distributions, one with a mean near zero and small variance and the other with a larger mean and variance. But a naive formulation would make the parameters of the two normal distributions non-identifiable because the distributions are invariant under swapping (mu_1, sigma_1) with (mu_2, sigma_2). And if I am doing a two-level model (a national-level (completely pooled) two-component mixture model with parameters mu_1, sigma_2, mu_2, and sigma_2, and then 3700 site-level (partially pooled) distributions with means mu_1 + delta_mu_1[i] and mu_2 + delta_mu_2[i]) there will be thousands of parameters so I have to assume that there will be a fair bit of label swapping as the MCMC does its sampling.

I would love advice about how to think about this.  Since empirically I see that the two components of my proposed mixture are well separated, I could use the empirical data to impose restrictive priors that reduce the chance of parameter swapping to low probabilities. I could also impose an ordering condition on the means. I think I wouldn't run into problems of ambiguity with ordered means because empirically the two parts of the distribution are so cleanly separated.

But I'm a newbie at this kind of analysis and would appreciate any advice on whether there's a better approach or if there are pitfalls I should watch out for beyond those mentioned in the Stan manual chapters on Mixture Models and Label Switching.

What I'm most interested in as an output is predictions of arsenic for new wells at the sites in my database, not the values of parameters for their own sake, so marginalizing out inconvenient parameters would be acceptable where that helps.

messages.body_plain:
A paper needs to be written on all this!

> On Jun 30, 2015, at 10:53 AM, Jonathan Gilligan <jonathan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you. This is very clear and helpful. I had felt that I understand using R hat, traceplots, and autocorrelation plots as diagnostics but I did not understand the HMC/NUTS specific diagnostics at all. This summary is a big help.  Thanks also to Ben Goodrich for his answers and for pointing me to the cmd-stan manual.
>
> On Tuesday, June 30, 2015 at 3:40:26 AM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > Unfortunately we’re overdo for a serious rewrite of the manual,
> > especially given our rapidly evolving understanding of subtle
> > theoretical MCMC issues.  I have everything collected into
> > slides, but turning it into text will have to wait until I have some
> > free time.  But I’ll summarize the results here.
> >
> > MCMC is just a method for numerically estimating integrals,
> > which is hard in high dimensions because of something called
> > concentration of measure.  Essentially the only parameters
> > that contribute to integrals lie on a hyper surface in parameter
> > space and if we want to estimate integrals then we need to
> > find that hyper surface and then explore it.  That’s exactly
> > what a Markov chain does — eventually we have a series
> > of states distributed across the hyper surface, { y_{n} }, that
> > we can use as a grid for doing really simple quadrature,
> >
> > \int dy p(y) f(y) ~ 1/N sum_{n = 1}^{N} f(y_{n})
> >
> > Everything relies on our being able to find and then explore
> > the _entire_ hyper surface (which we call the typical set).
> > This is incredibly hard to determine theoretically so we’re
> > left with a bunch of necessary but not sufficient diagnostics
> > to identify when we’re not exploring everything.
> >
> > All of these apply only to samples — because we dynamically
> > adapt sampling parameters in warmup those samples will
> > behave very differently.  Again, ignore anything you see
> > in warmup.
> >
> > Traceplots:
> >
> > The characteristic way pathologies manifest is the Markov
> > chain getting stuck in the boundary of a pathological region
> > of parameter space.  If you run long enough you’ll literally
> > see the chain get stuck for long periods of time.  You can
> > also compare chains to identify multi modality and other
> > problems.
> >
> > R-hat:
> >
> > If our Markov chain can explore the entire target distribution
> > then any realization of it should look the same.  R-hat
> > essentially performs an analysis of variance on a bunch of
> > chains (and subsets of chains) looking for any deviations.
> > The more chains you use the more sensitive you’ll be to
> > potential pathologies.
> >
> > n-divergent:
> >
> > Hamiltonian Monte Carlo has a unique diagnostic — regions
> > of the typical set that are hard to explore induce particular
> > numerical divergences that we can capture and report.  This
> > is much more sensitive then looking at trace plots! If
> > you see any divergences in sampling then you have to be
> > careful.  For a few divergences you can increase the target
> > acceptance probability, but for any nontrivial number of
> > divergences you’ll probably have to consider tweaking your
> > model to use stronger priors or different parameterizations.
> >
> > In RStan you can grab the divergences with
> >
> > fit <- stan(file='model_name.stan', data=input_data,
> >             iter=2000, chains=1, seed=4938483)
> >
> > count_divergences <- function(fit) {
> >   sampler_params <- get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)
> >   sum(sapply(sampler_params, function(x) c(x[,'n_divergent__']))[,1])
> > }
> >
> > Finally the treedepth issue is not so much a diagnostic of a
> > bad Markov chain but rather a safeguard we’ve built in to
> > avoid infinite loops caused by ill-formed posteriors which
> > require the sampler to explore all the way to infinity in back
> > (requiring an infinite tree depth an infinite time).  Sometimes
> > your sampler will need to explore beyond our default safeguard
> > value, in which case you have to increase it manually — this
> > doesn’t effect the validity of your results, just the performance
> > of the algorithm.
> >
> > I like looking at a histogram of the treedepths,
> >
> > hist_treedepth <- function(fit) {
> >   sampler_params <- get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)
> >   hist(sapply(sampler_params, function(x) c(x[,'treedepth__']))[,1], breaks=0:20, main="", xlab="Treedepth")
> >   abline(v=10, col=2, lty=1)
> > }
> >
> > Technically the sampler tries one more step after maxdepth
> > which is why you might see it exceed that value by one.  I
> > can never remember the indexing and ordering to state whether
> > you should see maxdepth or maxdepth + 1 but in the end it
> > doesn’t really matter as the bad behavior (histogram saturating
> > at a large value) is pretty obvious.
> >

> > > Now that's something I understand how to fix!  I'll move the discussion

> > > Here's the issue tracker link:

> > > https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1508#issuecomment-116940132
> > >

messages.subject: Re: Modeling of multimodal data distributions
messages.body_plain:
Any chance that the spike around zero is caused by censoring? In other words, is it possible that under a certain threshold for the true concentration, the measured concentrations turn out as zero? Not an uncommon phenomenon, which can be easily modeled by either:

1) integrating out the censored observations, using cumulative distribution functions, or
2) sampling the values under the threshold value (i.e. specifying them as parameters bounded between zero and the detection threshold).

Depending on the data and model, 1) or 2) may be more efficient. In one of my own applications I found the second to be more efficient, although I'm not quite sure why. Anyway, this approach doesn't require mixture distributions (if it applies to your problem).

Luc

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Modeling of multimodal data distributions
messages.body_plain:
Hey—arsenic, that’s one of my topics!  Quick answer is that you can avoid the aliasing problem by restricting mu_1 to be less than mu_2.  You also want to put informative priors on the variance parameters, otherwise the fit can blow up with variance estimates near 0.

> On Jun 30, 2015, at 4:21 PM, Jonathan Gilligan <jonathan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Can anyone offer advice for an analysis problem I'm working on.  I want to apply a partial-pooling approach like the radon examples in chapter 12 of ARM to analyzing a database of arsenic concentration in well-water. I have a measured arsenic concentrations in roughly 465,000 wells distrtibuted among roughly 3700 sites with the number or wells per site  ranging from 1 to roughly 2300 (the median is 82).
>
> Right now, I'm getting started by trying a partially pooled analysis of mean arsenic and uncertainty at each site, similar to figure 12.1 in ARM. Once I'm confident this is working, I plan to build on this to add parameters that account for the effect of well depth, stratigraphic characteristics, and ultimately to consider spatial effects (e.g., draw inferences from the nearest neighbor sites).
>
> The precision of arsenic measurements is sufficiently poor that it's reasonable for me to add 1 part per billion to every measurement (to deal with the measurements that are nominally zero parts per billion) and then take the log (base 10 to make it easier for me to interpret in terms of real units). On a log10 scale, I see a big spike at zero (about 60,000 wells) and a distinct and separate lump that looks fairly normal (corresponding to a lognormal distribution in the raw data) centered at around 2 (90,000 wells with log10(As) between 2.0 and 2.1) and nothing in the range 0.1 < x <  1.
>
> The simple thing to do in modeling this would be to represent the data with a mixture of two normal distributions, one with a mean near zero and small variance and the other with a larger mean and variance. But a naive formulation would make the parameters of the two normal distributions non-identifiable because the distributions are invariant under swapping (mu_1, sigma_1) with (mu_2, sigma_2). And if I am doing a two-level model (a national-level (completely pooled) two-component mixture model with parameters mu_1, sigma_2, mu_2, and sigma_2, and then 3700 site-level (partially pooled) distributions with means mu_1 + delta_mu_1[i] and mu_2 + delta_mu_2[i]) there will be thousands of parameters so I have to assume that there will be a fair bit of label swapping as the MCMC does its sampling.
>
> I would love advice about how to think about this.  Since empirically I see that the two components of my proposed mixture are well separated, I could use the empirical data to impose restrictive priors that reduce the chance of parameter swapping to low probabilities. I could also impose an ordering condition on the means. I think I wouldn't run into problems of ambiguity with ordered means because empirically the two parts of the distribution are so cleanly separated.
>
> But I'm a newbie at this kind of analysis and would appreciate any advice on whether there's a better approach or if there are pitfalls I should watch out for beyond those mentioned in the Stan manual chapters on Mixture Models and Label Switching.
>
> What I'm most interested in as an output is predictions of arsenic for new wells at the sites in my database, not the values of parameters for their own sake, so marginalizing out inconvenient parameters would be acceptable where that helps.
>
